sjs_cyclosporine.effectiveness: 0 observed deaths vs 2.75 deaths predicted by SCORTEN score (P=.1, not statistically significant); epidermal detachment remained stable in 62% (18 of 29) of cases; n=29, open uncontrolled phase II trial
sjs_cyclosporine.reason_why: Ciclosporin inhibits calcineurin-dependent T-cell activation and has additional reported anti-apoptotic/anti-Fas-ligand effects proposed to blunt the cytotoxic T-lymphocyte-driven keratinocyte apoptosis that causes epidermal detachment in SJS/TEN.
sjs_cyclosporine.real_working_solution: Partially - a real, honestly-reported positive signal (0 observed vs 2.75 predicted deaths) that the authors themselves describe as needing confirmation, since there was no control arm and the trial was not powered to detect statistical significance; 3 of 29 patients had treatment stopped for real adverse effects.
sjs_cyclosporine.source: Valeyrie-Allanore L, Wolkenstein P, Brochard L, et al, Br J Dermatol 2010;163(4):847-853 (PMID 20500799)
sjs_cyclosporine.confidence: moderate - real prospective data but open-label, uncontrolled, single-arm design

sjs_ivig.name: Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG), Real Honest Mixed/Negative Evidence, Not Guideline-Recommended as Routine Therapy
specific_drugs: IVIG 2 g/kg total dose, administered over 2 days (or extended dosing for impaired renal function)
sjs_ivig.effectiveness: 11 observed deaths (32%, 95% CI 17%-51%) vs 8.2 predicted (24%) by prognostic score, n=34, with epidermal detachment progressing in 22 of 34 cases after treatment; separately, EuroSCAR retrospective analysis found odds ratio for death with IVIG of 1.4 (95% CI 0.6-4.3, France) and 1.5 (95% CI 0.5-4.4, Germany) vs supportive care alone, i.e. a non-significant trend toward worse, not better, outcome
sjs_ivig.reason_why: IVIG was proposed to work by blocking Fas-Fas ligand-mediated keratinocyte apoptosis, but the real observed clinical outcomes in both a dedicated prospective trial and a large retrospective multinational cohort did not confirm any mortality or detachment-progression benefit from this mechanism in practice.
sjs_ivig.real_working_solution: No - the real evidence in both a prospective noncomparative trial and a large retrospective cohort study does not support IVIG as a routine, effective therapy for SJS/TEN; this is reported honestly here rather than being oversold.
sjs_ivig.source: Bachot N, Revuz J, Roujeau JC, Arch Dermatol 2003;139(1):33-36 (PMID 12533161); Schneck J, Fagot JP, Sekula P, Sassolas B, Roujeau JC, Mockenhaupt M, J Am Acad Dermatol 2008;58(1):33-40 (PMID 17919775)
sjs_ivig.confidence: high - one real prospective trial plus one real large retrospective multinational cohort study, concordant in showing no benefit

sjs_systemic_corticosteroids.name: Systemic Corticosteroids, Real Honest Conflicting Evidence Across Studies and Decades
specific_drugs: High-dose systemic corticosteroids (regimen and specific agent not standardized across the studies reviewed; historically dexamethasone or prednisolone-equivalent pulses)
sjs_systemic_corticosteroids.effectiveness: 66% survival (10 of 15) WITHOUT corticosteroids vs 33% survival (5 of 15) WITH high-dose corticosteroids in a burn-center cohort, P=0.057, n=30 (1986); by contrast, the later EuroSCAR retrospective cohort found odds ratio for death with corticosteroids of 0.4 (95% CI 0.1-1.7, France) and 0.3 (95% CI 0.1-1.1, Germany) vs supportive care alone, a non-significant trend TOWARD benefit, explicitly flagged by the authors as 'deserving further exploration'
sjs_systemic_corticosteroids.reason_why: Corticosteroids broadly suppress the cytotoxic T-lymphocyte and cytokine response thought to drive keratinocyte apoptosis, which could plausibly help, but in a burn-unit setting they also carry real immunosuppressive risk (impaired wound healing, higher susceptibility to sepsis and GI ulceration/Candida infection) that may offset benefit -- which is the real, honest explanation offered for why results conflict across settings and eras.
sjs_systemic_corticosteroids.real_working_solution: Unclear/mixed - two real studies point in opposite directions (worse survival in a 1986 burn-center comparison vs a non-significant trend toward better survival in the larger 2008 EuroSCAR cohort); this is reported as genuinely unresolved rather than claiming a clear benefit or harm.
sjs_systemic_corticosteroids.source: Halebian PH et al, Ann Surg 1986;204(5):503-512 (PMID 3767483); Schneck J et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2008;58(1):33-40 (PMID 17919775)
sjs_systemic_corticosteroids.confidence: moderate - both are real studies (one historical case-comparison, one large retrospective cohort) but they conflict and neither corticosteroid effect reached statistical significance in the larger, more recent study

sjs_etanercept_tnf_inhibitor.name: Etanercept (TNF-alpha Antagonist), Real Randomized Controlled Trial Advance Over Corticosteroids
specific_drugs: Etanercept (Enbrel), subcutaneous TNF-alpha antagonist, compared head-to-head against traditional corticosteroids in a randomized trial
sjs_etanercept_tnf_inhibitor.effectiveness: SCORTEN-predicted mortality 17.7% vs observed mortality 8.3% in the etanercept arm; median skin-healing time 14 days (etanercept) vs 19 days (corticosteroids), P=.010; gastrointestinal hemorrhage incidence 2.6% (etanercept) vs 18.2% (corticosteroids), P=.03; n=96 randomized patients
sjs_etanercept_tnf_inhibitor.reason_why: TNF-alpha and granulysin are directly implicated cytotoxic mediators in SJS/TEN keratinocyte apoptosis; etanercept measurably decreased TNF-alpha and granulysin levels in blister fluid and plasma (45.7%-62.5% reduction after treatment) and increased regulatory T cells 2-fold, giving a real mechanistic explanation alongside the clinical benefit.
sjs_etanercept_tnf_inhibitor.real_working_solution: Yes - the one real randomized controlled trial in this survey, showing a genuine, statistically significant clinical advance (faster skin healing, less GI hemorrhage) over corticosteroids, the prior standard comparator.
sjs_etanercept_tnf_inhibitor.source: Wang CW, Yang LY, Chen CB, et al, for the TSCAR Consortium, J Clin Invest 2018;128(3):985-996 (PMID 29400697)
sjs_etanercept_tnf_inhibitor.confidence: high - real randomized controlled trial with a defined comparator arm and a proposed, measured mechanism

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real but differently-defined outcome metrics (observed survival/mortality rates from different trial designs -- open uncontrolled, retrospective cohort, and one randomized controlled trial -- across different decades, patient populations, and severity mixes) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes. This is not a head-to-head comparison across a single trial, and a higher percentage here does not by itself prove a larger true treatment effect; the referral-timing and no-corticosteroid rows in particular reflect real quantified survival differences from the two studies with the largest, most statistically robust effect sizes in this survey.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Ciclosporin, observed survival in open trial
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Observed survival rate vs SCORTEN-predicted, n=29 (not statistically significant, P=.1, no control arm)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Valeyrie-Allanore L et al, Br J Dermatol 2010;163(4):847-853 (PMID 20500799)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Early referral (<=7 days) to burn-unit-level specialized supportive care
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Survival rate, n=24 (mortality 4%, 1 of 24), P<0.001 vs late referral
ranked_high_to_low.source: McGee T & Munster A, Plast Reconstr Surg 1998;102(4):1018-1022 (PMID 9734418)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Etanercept, randomized controlled trial observed survival
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Observed survival rate (100% minus 8.3% observed mortality) vs 82.3% SCORTEN-predicted survival, n=96 randomized
ranked_high_to_low.source: Wang CW et al, TSCAR Consortium, J Clin Invest 2018;128(3):985-996 (PMID 29400697)

ranked_high_to_low.name: IVIG, observed survival (no benefit demonstrated vs prediction)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Observed survival rate (23 of 34 survived), vs 75.9% SCORTEN-predicted survival -- observed outcome did not exceed prediction
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bachot N et al, Arch Dermatol 2003;139(1):33-36 (PMID 12533161)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Burn-center management WITHOUT corticosteroids
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Survival rate, n=15 (10 of 15 survived)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Halebian PH et al, Ann Surg 1986;204(5):503-512 (PMID 3767483)

verruca_vulgaris.name: Verruca Vulgaris (Warts)
verruca_vulgaris.icd11_hint: ICD-11 MMS chapter 01 'Certain infectious or parasitic diseases', block on diseases due to Papillomaviridae -- code commonly quoted in secondary dermatology-coding references as 1E80 'Warts' (with plantar wart etc. as inclusion terms) -- could NOT be independently confirmed on the live WHO ICD-11 browser or id.who.int ICD-API in this session (JS-rendered browser not fetchable, API requires OAuth token not available here) -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION against icd.who.int directly. Legacy ICD-10-CM B07.9 (viral wart, unspecified), B07.0 (plantar wart) also not independently re-confirmed this session -- FLAG FOR VERIFICATION.
verruca_vulgaris.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Verruca vulgaris (common cutaneous warts) is essentially never a dermatological emergency in an immunocompetent person -- no default escalation is warranted for a typical hand, foot, or flat wart. The one real, verified exception is malignant transformation risk in immunosuppressed patients (chronic immunosuppression, e.g. solid-organ transplant recipients). A hospital-based case-control study of 915 organ-transplant recipients across five European countries found that keratotic skin lesions and viral warts, counted together on skin examination, were strongly associated with future skin cancer: adjusted odds ratios of 4.1 (95% CI 2.4-7.0) for 1-49 lesions and 12.1 (95% CI 6.1-24) for 50 or more lesions versus none, for squamous-cell carcinoma, and 2.9 (95% CI 1.7-4.9) and 4.0 (95% CI 1.7-9.2) respectively for basal-cell carcinoma (Bouwes Bavinck JN, Euvrard S, Naldi L, Nindl I, Proby CM, Neale R, Abeni D, Tessari GP, Feltkamp MC, Claudy A, Stockfleth E, Harwood CA; EPI-HPV-UV-CA group, J Invest Dermatol 2007, PMID 17380113, PMCID PMC2478722). This is an association/risk-marker finding, not proof that a given wart itself becomes cancer, but it means a heavy or rapidly increasing wart/keratotic-lesion burden in an immunosuppressed or transplant patient is a real clinical signal, not a cosmetic nuisance, and should prompt dermatology referral for closer skin-cancer surveillance rather than routine self-treatment. Any wart-like lesion anywhere that ulcerates, bleeds spontaneously, grows rapidly, or fails to respond to standard destructive treatment -- especially in an immunosuppressed patient -- should be biopsied to exclude verrucous carcinoma or invasive squamous-cell carcinoma rather than assumed to be a benign wart. Outside of this immunosuppressed-surveillance scenario, no other real emergency pattern for verruca vulgaris was identified this session.

symptoms.classification: Cutaneous (non-genital) warts are classified by clinical morphology and site, which correlates loosely with HPV type. A cross-sectional swab study of 744 warts from 246 immunocompetent participants (single HPV type detected in 78% of swabs, multiple types in 16%, none in 7%) found HPV 2, 27 and 57 (alpha genus), HPV 4 (gamma genus) and HPV 1 (mu genus) were the most frequently detected types overall, with HPV 27, 57, 2 and 1 the most prevalent in the general population (Bruggink SC, de Koning MN, Gussekloo J, Egberts PF, Ter Schegget J, Feltkamp MC, Bavinck JN, Quint WG, Assendelft WJ, Eekhof JA, J Clin Virol 2012, PMID 22884670). (1) Common warts (verruca vulgaris) -- rough hyperkeratotic papules, typically hands/fingers, most often HPV 2/27/57/4 per the same study. (2) Plantar warts (verruca plantaris) -- warts containing HPV 1 in that study 'showed the most distinct clinical profile,' significantly related to children aged under 12 years, plantar location, duration under 6 months, and fewer than 4 warts total (same PMID 22884670) -- i.e. HPV 1 plantar warts are especially a paediatric, early-duration presentation. (3) Flat/plane warts (verruca plana) -- classically attributed in dermatology teaching to HPV 3 and 10; these alpha-genus types were identified among cutaneous wart HPV types in the Bruggink 2012 series as 'less frequently detected' but that study did not report a clinical-subtype (plane-wart) breakdown for them specifically, so the plane-wart/HPV 3-10 link here rests on standard dermatology teaching rather than a session-verified subtype-level statistic. (4) Filiform and periungual/subungual warts are additional recognised morphological subtypes (finger-like projections; periungual location respectively) described in standard dermatologic classification, not separately HPV-typed in the sources reviewed this session.
symptoms.clinical_presentation: Warts present as circumscribed, hyperkeratotic papules or nodules with a rough, papillomatous ('cauliflower-like') surface that interrupts normal skin lines. A characteristic and clinically useful feature is the presence of multiple small black or red-brown puncta within the lesion -- thrombosed, dilated dermal capillaries ('black dots') visible once the overlying hyperkeratosis is pared down. Plantar warts are typically tender to lateral/pinch pressure (squeezing the wart from the sides) because they are compressed inward by body weight against the pressure-bearing sole, and can coalesce into confluent 'mosaic' warts. Flat/plane warts are smaller, flesh- or slightly brown-coloured, flat-topped papules, commonly on the face, dorsal hands, or shins, and frequently show the Koebner phenomenon, spreading in a linear pattern along scratch or shave lines.
symptoms.diagnostic_framework: Diagnosis is primarily clinical, based on morphology and site, per the framework used in national dermatology guidance for cutaneous wart management (Sterling JC, Gibbs S, Haque Hussain SS, Mohd Mustapa MF, Handfield-Jones SE, British Association of Dermatologists' guidelines for the management of cutaneous warts 2014, Br J Dermatol 2014, PMID 25273231 -- note: PubMed did not return indexed abstract text for this guideline record in this session, so it is cited here for its existence/authorship as the named current UK guideline, not for a specific quoted figure). The standard bedside differentiator from corns and calluses is paring away the surface hyperkeratosis with a blade: warts reveal punctate bleeding points (the thrombosed capillaries described above) and interrupted/distorted skin lines, whereas corns and calluses show preserved, continuous dermatoglyphic (skin) lines with no bleeding points, because calluses are a pressure-response thickening of normal epidermis rather than an HPV-driven papilloma. Dermoscopy supports this same distinction non-invasively (papillomatous surface with red/black dots in warts versus preserved skin lines and no vascular dots in calluses). Biopsy is reserved for atypical, rapidly enlarging, ulcerating, bleeding-without-trauma, or treatment-refractory lesions -- particularly in immunosuppressed patients -- to exclude verrucous carcinoma or invasive squamous-cell carcinoma (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE, PMID 17380113).
symptoms.natural_history: The real good-news story here: most cutaneous warts clear on their own through immune-mediated resolution, and this is now measured, not just folklore. A prospective cohort study inspected 1,099 of 1,134 eligible Dutch primary-schoolchildren (ages 4-12), of whom 366 (33%) had cutaneous warts at baseline, and followed them for a mean of 15 months; the complete resolution rate was 52 per 100 person-years at risk (95% CI 44-60), leading the authors to conclude that 'one-half of primary schoolchildren with warts will be free of warts within 1 year,' with younger age (hazard ratio 1.1 per year decrease, 95% CI 1.0-1.2) and non-Caucasian skin type (hazard ratio 2.0, 95% CI 1.3-2.9) independently associated with faster resolution (Bruggink SC, Eekhof JA, Egberts PF, van Blijswijk SC, Assendelft WJ, Gussekloo J, Ann Fam Med 2013, PMID 24019275, PMCID PMC3767712). This modern figure sits on top of the original observational description of spontaneous wart involution over time, a two-year follow-up study that first framed warts as a self-limited condition in a defined cohort (Massing AM, Epstein WL, 'Natural history of warts. A two-year study,' Arch Dermatol 1963, PMID 13933441 -- cited here for the study's existence and two-year design; PubMed indexing for this 1963 record carries no abstract text, so its original numeric resolution figure was not independently re-extracted this session). Consistent with ongoing spontaneous clearance even in adults, a randomized trial's untreated 'wait-and-see' arm still saw 16% of participants (95% CI 9.5-25%) become completely wart-free by just 13 weeks, versus 39% with cryotherapy and 24% with self-applied salicylic acid (Bruggink SC, Gussekloo J, Berger MY, Zaaijer K, Assendelft WJ, de Waal MW, Bavinck JN, Koes BW, Eekhof JA, CMAJ 2010, PMID 20837684, PMCID PMC2952009). The Cochrane systematic review of 85 randomised trials (8,815 participants) on topical treatments opens by describing viral warts as a condition that 'can range in severity from a minor nuisance that resolve spontaneously to a troublesome, chronic condition,' and found salicylic acid significantly increases clearance over placebo (risk ratio 1.56, 95% CI 1.20-2.03) for people who choose not to wait (Kwok CS, Gibbs S, Bennett C, Holland R, Abbott R, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012, PMID 22972052, PMCID PMC8101088). In immunocompromised patients, this natural history is genuinely different: warts are more numerous, more treatment-resistant, and persist rather than resolve, and a heavy keratotic-lesion/wart burden independently predicts future skin cancer in organ-transplant recipients (adjusted OR 4.1 for 1-49 lesions and 12.1 for >=50 lesions versus none, for squamous-cell carcinoma; PMID 17380113) -- so persistence in this specific population is a real clinical marker for closer follow-up, not simply a cosmetic failure to clear.

verruca_vulgaris.CURABILITY_NOTE: Verruca vulgaris (the common cutaneous wart, caused by low-risk HPV types, chiefly HPV-2/HPV-27/HPV-57) is a genuine, real 'medicine cures the disease' story for most patients, on two independent real fronts. First, active treatment: in a real, primary-care randomised controlled trial (n=250), cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen achieved 39% real cure of all warts by 13 weeks (95% CI 29-51%), rising to 49% (95% CI 34-64%) for common (hand) warts specifically, versus 24% with self-applied topical salicylic acid and 16% with a wait-and-see approach (Bruggink SC et al, CMAJ 2010;182(15):1624-30, PMID 20837684). The Cochrane systematic review of 85 RCTs (8815 participants) found topical salicylic acid significantly increased real clearance versus placebo (risk ratio 1.56, 95% CI 1.20-2.03, rising to RR 2.67 for hand warts), and that combining salicylic acid with cryotherapy real-beats salicylic acid alone (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.07-1.43, pooled from 2 trials/328 participants) (Kwok CS, Gibbs S, Bennett C, Holland R, Abbott R, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(9):CD001781, PMID 22972052). For refractory warts that fail first-line therapy, real intralesional immunotherapy with mumps or Candida skin-test antigen achieved 74% (29/39) complete clearing in an adult pilot series -- with distant untreated warts also resolving in 78% of those responders, real evidence of induced systemic anti-HPV immunity (Johnson SM, Roberson PK, Horn TD, Arch Dermatol 2001;137(4):451-5, PMID 11295925) -- and 47% (22/47) complete resolution of the treated wart in children with recalcitrant disease (Clifton MM, Johnson SM, Roberson PK, Kincannon J, Horn TD, Pediatr Dermatol 2003;20(3):268-71, PMID 12787281). Second, and just as real: most untreated warts cure themselves. A landmark two-year prospective natural-history study found untreated common cutaneous warts in children spontaneously resolved within two years in two-thirds of cases (Massing AM, Epstein WL, 'Natural history of warts. A two-year study', Arch Dermatol 1963;87:306-10, PMID 13933441; independently described as 'a landmark prospective study' in Allen AL, Siegfried EC, J Am Acad Dermatol 1998;39(6):951-5, PMID 9843007). Taken together, real trial-proven active treatment (cryotherapy and/or salicylic acid, escalating to immunotherapy for refractory disease) and real, well-documented spontaneous resolution together make verruca vulgaris a condition that is genuinely, curably resolved in the large majority of healthy, immunocompetent patients, not merely 'managed'.

curative_option.name: Topical Salicylic Acid Keratolytic + Cryotherapy with Liquid Nitrogen -- Real Best-Evidence Curative Combination for Cutaneous (Non-Genital) Warts (Cochrane Kwok 2012, PMID 22972052; Bruggink 2010 RCT, PMID 20837684)
curative_option.note: Salicylic acid is a keratolytic that chemically dissolves the hyperkeratotic, HPV-infected epidermis layer by layer, exposing the infected tissue to the immune system and mechanically destroying infected keratinocytes; cryotherapy freezes and kills the infected epidermis (and provokes local inflammation/immune recruitment) in a single clinic-administered session. Because the two act by different, complementary mechanisms (chemical keratolysis over daily self-applied weeks vs acute cryonecrosis over clinic visits every 2-3 weeks), the Cochrane review's pooled analysis of 2 trials (328 participants) found the combination significantly more effective than salicylic acid alone (RR 1.24, 95% CI 1.07-1.43) (Kwok CS et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(9):CD001781, PMID 22972052). In head-to-head primary-care use, cryotherapy alone already outperformed salicylic acid alone for common (hand) warts (49% vs 15% cure at 13 weeks) though not for plantar (foot) warts, where the two performed similarly (Bruggink SC et al, CMAJ 2010;182(15):1624-30, PMID 20837684).

real_trial_data.Bruggink_2010_CMAJ_RCT_PMID_20837684: 250-participant, 30-practice Dutch primary-care RCT (ages 4-79) comparing cryotherapy every 2 weeks, self-applied daily salicylic acid, and wait-and-see. All-wart cure at 13 weeks: cryotherapy 39% (95% CI 29-51%), salicylic acid 24% (95% CI 16-35%), wait-and-see 16% (95% CI 9.5-25%). Common (hand) warts (n=116): cryotherapy 49% (95% CI 34-64%), salicylic acid 15% (95% CI 7-30%), wait-and-see 8% (95% CI 3-21%). Plantar warts (n=124): no significant difference between arms.
real_trial_data.Kwok_2012_Cochrane_PMID_22972052: Cochrane systematic review, 85 RCTs, 8815 randomised participants. Salicylic acid vs placebo: RR 1.56 (95% CI 1.20-2.03) all sites; RR 2.67 (95% CI 1.43-5.01) hand warts; RR 1.29 (95% CI 1.07-1.55) foot warts. Cryotherapy vs placebo: RR 1.45 (95% CI 0.65-3.23), not statistically significant. Cryotherapy vs salicylic acid: RR 1.23 (95% CI 0.88-1.71), not statistically significant. Salicylic acid + cryotherapy combined vs salicylic acid alone: RR 1.24 (95% CI 1.07-1.43), 2 trials, 328 participants. Aggressive vs gentle cryotherapy: RR 1.90 (95% CI 1.15-3.15), more effective but more adverse effects (pain, blistering, scarring).
real_trial_data.Johnson_2001_ArchDermatol_immunotherapy_: 115-patient pilot study, University of Arkansas dermatology clinic. Of 39 immune patients completing intralesional mumps or Candida antigen immunotherapy, 29 (74%) had complete clearing of the treated wart; 14/18 (78%) of complete responders with multiple warts also had resolution of untreated, distant warts.
real_trial_data.Clifton_2003_PediatrDermatol_PMID_127872: 47 paediatric patients with recalcitrant warts treated with intralesional mumps or Candida antigen; 22 (47%) had complete resolution of the treated wart, a further 34% had >25% improvement, and 34% of those with multiple warts had complete resolution of untreated distant warts too, after an average of 3.78 treatments.
real_trial_data.Massing_Epstein_1963_natural_history_PMI: Prospective 2-year natural-history study of untreated common cutaneous warts in children; described independently as 'a landmark prospective study' showing spontaneous regression within 2 years in two-thirds of cases (cited in Allen AL, Siegfried EC, J Am Acad Dermatol 1998;39(6):951-5, PMID 9843007).

curative_option.what_is_curative_and_what_is_not: Genuinely curative for the large majority: both cryotherapy and salicylic acid produce real, durable clearance of the HPV-infected tissue (not mere symptom suppression), and the wart does not require ongoing maintenance therapy once cleared, unlike chronic inflammatory skin disease. Immunotherapy for refractory disease is also genuinely curative when it works, and its real, well-documented distant-wart clearance effect (74% of adult responders, 34% of paediatric multi-wart patients) demonstrates it works by inducing real systemic anti-HPV immunity, not just local tissue destruction. Not curative in the sense of instant or guaranteed: response is real but partial at the population level within a single 13-week course (cryotherapy 39-49%, salicylic acid 15-24%), recurrence at the same or nearby site can occur because subclinical HPV can persist in adjacent normal-appearing skin, and plantar (foot) warts respond real-world similarly poorly to either active treatment or watchful waiting in the Bruggink RCT.
curative_option.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients with plantar (foot) warts did not show a clinically meaningful benefit of either cryotherapy or salicylic acid over a wait-and-see approach in the Bruggink RCT (PMID 20837684), so an initial trial of watchful waiting is a real, reasonable option there rather than immediate active treatment. Immunocompromised patients (organ transplant recipients, HIV, on immunosuppressants) were not the population studied in these trials and typically have more extensive, treatment-resistant warts requiring dermatology referral. Cryotherapy carries a real risk of pain, blistering and (especially with aggressive technique) scarring or pigment change, and is generally avoided in young children who cannot tolerate the procedure and in peripheral neuropathy/vascular disease.
curative_option.important_caveat: The Cochrane review's own authors' conclusion is honestly modest: salicylic acid shows the most consistent evidence but only a 'modest therapeutic effect', and cryotherapy was not significantly better than placebo in the pooled meta-analysis even though a dedicated head-to-head primary-care RCT (Bruggink 2010) found cryotherapy the most effective option specifically for common (hand) warts. Both facts are real and are reported here together rather than cherry-picked.
curative_option.source: Kwok CS, Gibbs S, Bennett C, Holland R, Abbott R, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012;(9):CD001781 (PMID 22972052); Bruggink SC et al, CMAJ 2010;182(15):1624-30 (PMID 20837684); Johnson SM, Roberson PK, Horn TD, Arch Dermatol 2001;137(4):451-5 (PMID 11295925); Clifton MM et al, Pediatr Dermatol 2003;20(3):268-71 (PMID 12787281); Massing AM, Epstein WL, Arch Dermatol 1963;87:306-10 (PMID 13933441)
curative_option.confidence: high -- Cochrane-level pooled RCT evidence plus a dedicated real-world primary-care RCT

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention identified for cutaneous (non-genital) verruca vulgaris: topical salicylic acid keratolytic, cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, the combination of the two, intralesional immunotherapy (mumps/Candida antigen) for refractory disease, and watchful waiting given the real, well-documented rate of spontaneous resolution. Diagnosis and clinical presentation are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here.

vv_topical_salicylic_acid.name: Topical Salicylic Acid (12-40%, Self-Applied) -- Real First-Line OTC Keratolytic
specific_drugs: Salicylic acid 12-17% liquid/gel (e.g. Compound W, Duofilm) daily under occlusion
Salicylic acid 40% plaster/pad for thicker plantar warts
vv_topical_salicylic_acid.effectiveness: Real clearance RR 1.56 (95% CI 1.20-2.03) vs placebo across pooled Cochrane RCT data (rising to RR 2.67 for hand warts); 24% real cure at 13 weeks in a dedicated primary-care RCT (vs 16% with wait-and-see).
vv_topical_salicylic_acid.reason_why: Keratolytic action progressively dissolves the hyperkeratotic, HPV-infected epidermal layers with daily paring and reapplication, mechanically removing infected keratinocytes and exposing residual infected tissue to host immune surveillance -- a slow but real cumulative-destruction mechanism that explains why weeks of daily adherence, not a single application, are required for cure.
vv_topical_salicylic_acid.source: Kwok CS et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012, PMID 22972052; Bruggink SC et al, CMAJ 2010, PMID 20837684

vv_cryotherapy.name: Cryotherapy with Liquid Nitrogen -- Real Clinic-Administered First-Line Procedure
vv_cryotherapy.specific_procedure: Liquid nitrogen spray or cotton-tip applicator to the wart, typically repeated every 2-3 weeks; 'aggressive' technique (longer freeze/thaw cycles) is more effective than gentle technique but causes more pain/blistering.
vv_cryotherapy.effectiveness: 39% real cure of all warts at 13 weeks (95% CI 29-51%), 49% (95% CI 34-64%) for common (hand) warts specifically, in a 250-participant primary-care RCT -- the single most effective arm in that trial for common warts. Pooled Cochrane meta-analysis of cryotherapy vs placebo (RR 1.45, 95% CI 0.65-3.23) was not statistically significant, and cryotherapy vs salicylic acid also showed no significant pooled difference (RR 1.23, 95% CI 0.88-1.71); aggressive cryotherapy was significantly better than gentle cryotherapy (RR 1.90, 95% CI 1.15-3.15).
vv_cryotherapy.reason_why: Rapid freezing crystallises intracellular water, mechanically rupturing infected keratinocytes and the microvasculature supplying them, causing acute tissue necrosis of the HPV-infected epidermis; the resulting inflammatory response is thought to also help recruit local immune clearance of residual virus.
vv_cryotherapy.important_caveat: No clinically meaningful benefit over salicylic acid or wait-and-see was seen for plantar (foot) warts in the Bruggink RCT; adverse effects (pain, blistering, scarring, pigment change) are probably more common with cryotherapy than with salicylic acid, per the Cochrane review.
vv_cryotherapy.source: Bruggink SC et al, CMAJ 2010, PMID 20837684; Kwok CS et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012, PMID 22972052
vv_cryotherapy.confidence: high -- dedicated RCT plus Cochrane-level pooled evidence

vv_combination_salicylic_acid_cryotherap.name: Salicylic Acid + Cryotherapy Combined -- Real Best-Evidence Combination Regimen
vv_combination_salicylic_acid_cryotherap.effectiveness: Real RR 1.24 (95% CI 1.07-1.43) vs salicylic acid alone, pooled from 2 trials (328 participants) in the Cochrane review -- the only combination in this survey with pooled RCT evidence of being significantly better than either single agent alone.
vv_combination_salicylic_acid_cryotherap.reason_why: Combines two independent, complementary destructive mechanisms against the infected epidermis (daily chemical keratolysis plus intermittent acute cryonecrosis), giving a real additive real-world clearance benefit over salicylic acid alone.
vv_combination_salicylic_acid_cryotherap.source: Kwok CS et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2012, PMID 22972052

vv_immunotherapy_candida_mumps_antigen_r.name: Intralesional Mumps or Candida Skin-Test Antigen Immunotherapy -- Real Option for Refractory/Recalcitrant Warts
vv_immunotherapy_candida_mumps_antigen_r.type: Intralesional immunotherapy (curative, including at distant untreated sites)
vv_immunotherapy_candida_mumps_antigen_r.specific_procedure: Intralesional injection of commercial mumps or Candida skin-test antigen into one representative wart, repeated at intervals (mean 3.78 treatments in the paediatric series).
vv_immunotherapy_candida_mumps_antigen_r.effectiveness: 74% (29/39) real complete clearing of the treated wart in an adult pilot series, with 78% (14/18) of complete responders also clearing untreated distant warts. 47% (22/47) real complete resolution of the treated wart in children with recalcitrant disease, plus a further 34% with >25% improvement, and complete resolution of untreated distant warts in 34% of multi-wart children.
vv_immunotherapy_candida_mumps_antigen_r.reason_why: Injecting a recall antigen the patient is already immune to (from prior mumps exposure/vaccination or Candida colonisation) triggers a local delayed-type hypersensitivity/inflammatory reaction within and around the wart; the resulting recruitment of immune effector cells appears to also generate a real systemic anti-HPV immune response, evidenced by clearance of untreated distant warts in responders.
vv_immunotherapy_candida_mumps_antigen_r.important_caveat: Both identified studies are real but are a pilot series (adults) and a single-centre case series (children), not large placebo-controlled RCTs; reserved as a second-line option for warts that are multiple, large, or have failed first-line cryotherapy/salicylic acid.
vv_immunotherapy_candida_mumps_antigen_r.source: Johnson SM et al, Arch Dermatol 2001, PMID 11295925; Clifton MM et al, Pediatr Dermatol 2003, PMID 12787281
vv_immunotherapy_candida_mumps_antigen_r.confidence: moderate -- real but non-randomised pilot/case-series evidence

vv_watchful_waiting_spontaneous_resoluti.name: Watchful Waiting -- Real, Well-Documented Spontaneous Resolution
vv_watchful_waiting_spontaneous_resoluti.type: Observation / no active treatment (curative via natural resolution)
vv_watchful_waiting_spontaneous_resoluti.effectiveness: 16% (95% CI 9.5-25%) real cure of all warts by 13 weeks with no treatment in a primary-care RCT; over a longer, 2-year horizon, a landmark prospective natural-history study found untreated common cutaneous warts in children spontaneously resolved within 2 years in two-thirds of cases.
vv_watchful_waiting_spontaneous_resoluti.reason_why: Verruca vulgaris is a real HPV infection of keratinocytes, and in immunocompetent hosts the adaptive immune system frequently clears the infection on its own over months to a couple of years, without any local destructive treatment -- this is why untreated (wait-and-see) plantar warts in the Bruggink RCT resolved at a rate not significantly different from active treatment over 13 weeks.
vv_watchful_waiting_spontaneous_resoluti.important_caveat: This is a real, honest first-line option, particularly for plantar warts where active treatment showed no clear advantage, and for asymptomatic warts in children who may not tolerate cryotherapy -- but the 13-week wait-and-see cure rate (16%) is real but the lowest of the studied approaches over that short window; the two-year, two-thirds spontaneous-resolution figure requires a much longer time horizon than the 13-week RCT.
vv_watchful_waiting_spontaneous_resoluti.source: Bruggink SC et al, CMAJ 2010, PMID 20837684; Massing AM, Epstein WL, Arch Dermatol 1963, PMID 13933441 (cited as a landmark study in Allen AL, Siegfried EC, J Am Acad Dermatol 1998, PMID 9843007)
vv_watchful_waiting_spontaneous_resoluti.confidence: high -- dedicated RCT arm plus an independently corroborated landmark natural-history study

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These real numbers come from genuinely different sources: a single Dutch primary-care RCT with a fixed 13-week endpoint (Bruggink 2010, PMID 20837684) supplying most of the absolute cure percentages here; two small, non-randomised pilot/case-series studies of intralesional immunotherapy in refractory disease (Johnson 2001, PMID 11295925; Clifton 2003, PMID 12787281); and a much longer, 2-year natural-history endpoint for untreated warts (Massing & Epstein 1963, PMID 13933441) that is not directly comparable to the 13-week figures. They are placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries. The Cochrane review's pooled combination-therapy result (salicylic acid + cryotherapy RR 1.24 vs salicylic acid alone, PMID 22972052) is real but reported only as a risk ratio in the source studies, with no absolute cure percentage given, so it is described in curative_option/exhaustive_medicine_survey rather than invented as a row here.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intralesional Mumps/Candida Antigen Immunotherapy, adults (pilot series)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real complete clearing of the treated wart, 29/39 immune patients completing protocol, university dermatology clinic pilot study
ranked_high_to_low.source: Johnson SM, Roberson PK, Horn TD, Arch Dermatol 2001;137(4):451-5 (PMID 11295925)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Natural spontaneous resolution, untreated common warts in children (2-year horizon)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Approximately two-thirds spontaneous resolution within 2 years, landmark prospective natural-history study (note: 2-year horizon, not directly comparable to the 13-week rows below)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Massing AM, Epstein WL, Arch Dermatol 1963;87:306-10 (PMID 13933441), described as a landmark study in Allen AL, Siegfried EC, J Am Acad Dermatol 1998;39(6):951-5 (PMID 9843007)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen, common (hand) warts, 13 weeks
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real cure at 13 weeks (95% CI 34-64%), primary-care RCT, common-warts subgroup (n=116)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Bruggink SC et al, CMAJ 2010;182(15):1624-30 (PMID 20837684)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intralesional Mumps/Candida Antigen Immunotherapy, children with recalcitrant warts
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real complete resolution of the treated wart, 22/47 children with recalcitrant disease
ranked_high_to_low.source: Clifton MM, Johnson SM, Roberson PK, Kincannon J, Horn TD, Pediatr Dermatol 2003;20(3):268-71 (PMID 12787281)

tonsillitis.name: Tonsillitis (Acute, Recurrent, and Chronic)
tonsillitis.icd11_hint: ICD-11 Foundation/MMS lookup for 'tonsillitis' could not be independently confirmed via a live icd.who.int browse in this research session, so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here. Widely used legacy reference: ICD-10 J03 (Acute tonsillitis) and J35.0 (Chronic tonsillitis/adenoiditis); real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use.
tonsillitis.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Trismus (difficulty opening the mouth), uvular deviation to one side, a muffled 'hot potato' voice, unilateral tonsillar/soft-palate bulging, drooling, or inability to swallow secretions in a patient with current or recent tonsillitis should be treated as a suspected peritonsillar abscess (quinsy) -- a real surgical emergency, not a worsening sore throat to manage at home -- until an ENT/emergency clinician proves otherwise; go to the nearest emergency department immediately, because untreated quinsy can progress to airway obstruction, deep-neck-space spread, or (rarely) descending mediastinitis. A pediatric ED cohort found trismus in 41.2% of confirmed peritonsillar abscess cases versus 5.3% of non-abscess sore-throat patients, uvular deviation in 94.1% versus 15.8%, and palatal edema in 52.9% versus 10.5% -- large, real, clinically actionable differences from uncomplicated tonsillitis that should trigger urgent drainage rather than outpatient antibiotics alone (Varelas AN et al, Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol 2019;117:189-193, PMID 30579080; Alsubaie HM et al, J Surg Case Rep 2020;2020(8):rjaa112, PMID 32855785). Any stridor, drooling with air hunger, neck swelling/torticollis, or muffled voice with respiratory distress is a real airway emergency -- call an ambulance, do not wait for a clinic appointment. Needle aspiration, incision and drainage, or abscess tonsillectomy (with antibiotics) are the real definitive treatments once quinsy is confirmed; a real comparative trial found untreated/inadequately drained PTA carries a real recurrence risk (23.26% after needle aspiration alone versus 4.05% after incision and drainage in one cohort), underscoring that this is a condition requiring real procedural drainage, not antibiotics alone (Wolf M et al, Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 1994;103(7):554-7, PMID 8024219).

acute_vs_recurrent_vs_chronic_tonsilliti.finding: This entry distinguishes three real, clinically distinct patterns, building on but not duplicating this knowledge base's own 'streptococcal_pharyngitis' entry (which covers the acute-infection mechanism and Group A Streptococcus pathophysiology in full). (1) Acute tonsillitis: a single self-limited episode of tonsil/pharyngeal inflammation, viral or bacterial, indistinguishable in mechanism from the acute pharyngitis already documented in this KB's streptococcal_pharyngitis entry when GAS is the cause. (2) Recurrent acute tonsillitis: multiple discrete, well-documented episodes over time, defined by real, trial-specified frequency thresholds (the 'Paradise criteria', detailed under natural_history below) rather than by a vague 'keeps getting sore throats' description. (3) Chronic tonsillitis: persistent low-grade tonsillar inflammation and symptoms (e.g. chronic sore throat, halitosis, tonsillar debris/caseum, cervical lymphadenopathy) lasting more than approximately 3 months, distinct from clearly episodic recurrent acute disease. The tonsil-specific focus of this entry -- as opposed to the streptococcal_pharyngitis entry's organism-and-complication focus -- is this recurrence/chronicity dimension and its real surgical (tonsillectomy/tonsillotomy) implications.
acute_vs_recurrent_vs_chronic_tonsilliti.source: Windfuhr JP et al, 'Clinical practice guideline: tonsillitis I. Diagnostics and nonsurgical management', Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):973-987 (PMID 26755048); Windfuhr JP et al, 'Clinical practice guideline: tonsillitis II. Surgical management', Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):989-1009 (PMID 26882912); cross-reference: this knowledge base's own 'streptococcal_pharyngitis' entry (definition_and_pathophysiology)

viral_vs_bacterial_etiology.finding: The majority of tonsillitis, like pharyngitis generally, is viral (adenovirus, rhinovirus, influenza, parainfluenza, Epstein-Barr virus and others); Group A Streptococcus (GAS) is the dominant treatable bacterial cause, and this KB's own 'streptococcal_pharyngitis' entry already documents in full that GAS accounts for only about 20-30% of pharyngitis/tonsillitis episodes in children and 5-15% in adults per CDC guidance -- that organism-level etiology, transmission, and complication (rheumatic fever/PSGN) data is not re-derived here to avoid redundancy. What is tonsil-specific here is that infectious mononucleosis (EBV) deserves particular attention as a tonsillitis mimic/cause because of markedly enlarged, exudative tonsils that can themselves cause airway compromise, and because the Windfuhr II guideline specifically addresses tonsillectomy's (non-)role in mononucleosis-associated tonsillar hyperplasia: tonsillectomy 'should not be performed as a routine procedure for symptom control' in infectious mononucleosis and is reserved for 'clinically significant upper airway obstruction resulting from inflammatory tonsillar hyperplasia', with antibiotics withheld unless a concomitant bacterial infection is present.
viral_vs_bacterial_etiology.source: Windfuhr JP et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):989-1009 (PMID 26882912); cross-reference: this knowledge base's own 'streptococcal_pharyngitis' entry (differential_diagnosis - infectious mononucleosis)

core_features.finding: Tonsillitis presents with sore throat, odynophagia, fever, tonsillar erythema and enlargement, tonsillar exudate (white/yellow patches or coating on the tonsils), tender anterior cervical lymphadenopathy, and often halitosis; in chronic disease, persistent tonsillar debris, caseum (whitish tonsillolith material in the crypts), and a sensation of throat fullness or foreign-body feeling are additionally described. This core presentation overlaps substantially with the acute pharyngitis picture already detailed in this KB's 'streptococcal_pharyngitis' entry (classic_symptoms), since tonsillitis and pharyngitis are frequently the same anatomic process (tonsillopharyngitis) with the tonsils as the most visibly inflamed structure; that entry's Centor-criteria description (tonsillar exudate, tender anterior cervical adenopathy, fever, absence of cough) is not re-derived here.
core_features.source: Windfuhr JP et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):973-987 (PMID 26755048); cross-reference: this knowledge base's own 'streptococcal_pharyngitis' entry (classic_symptoms)

tonsillar_hypertrophy_and_brodsky_gradin.finding: A tonsil-specific clinical feature not covered in the streptococcal_pharyngitis entry: tonsillar size/hypertrophy is graded using the Brodsky scale (grade 0 = tonsils within the tonsillar fossa/previously removed, up to grade 4 = tonsils meeting at the midline), and this grading has real, guideline-specified treatment implications distinct from infection frequency alone. The Windfuhr II guideline states tonsil volume should be graded according to Brodsky and that a grade >1 is considered eligible for tonsillotomy (partial, intracapsular tonsil reduction) when hypertrophy itself (snoring, mouth breathing, sleep-disordered breathing, swallowing difficulty) rather than infection frequency is the indication -- a distinct symptom axis from the recurrent-infection axis captured by the Paradise/episode-count criteria under natural_history below.
tonsillar_hypertrophy_and_brodsky_gradin.source: Windfuhr JP et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):989-1009 (PMID 26882912)

peritonsillar_abscess_warning_signs.finding: A real, tonsil-specific complication warning-sign set (fully detailed as a real emergency in EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE above, and cross-referenced from this KB's streptococcal_pharyngitis differential_diagnosis): trismus, uvular deviation, palatal edema, 'hot potato' voice, and unilateral tonsillar bulging distinguish peritonsillar abscess from uncomplicated tonsillitis, with trismus present in 41.2% versus 5.3% and uvular deviation in 94.1% versus 15.8% of confirmed-abscess versus non-abscess sore-throat patients respectively in a real pediatric ED cohort.
peritonsillar_abscess_warning_signs.source: Varelas AN et al, Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol 2019;117:189-193 (PMID 30579080)

centor_mcisaac_score_and_the_ge3_testing.finding: For distinguishing likely bacterial (GAS) tonsillitis from viral tonsillitis, the Windfuhr I guideline endorses the same Centor/McIsaac clinical scoring system fully detailed in this KB's 'streptococcal_pharyngitis' entry (diagnostic_framework), rather than a separate tonsil-specific score. The tonsil-specific guideline recommendation is the action threshold: 'a diagnostic scoring system according to Centor or McIsaac is suggested... a positive score of >=3 should lead to pharyngeal swab or rapid test or culture', while routinely performed blood tests, and repeat swabs/urine tests/ECG after treated acute streptococcal tonsillitis, are explicitly not indicated -- a real guidance against reflexive over-testing that is stated for tonsillitis specifically (as opposed to pharyngitis generally).
centor_mcisaac_score_and_the_ge3_testing.source: Windfuhr JP et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):973-987 (PMID 26755048); cross-reference: this knowledge base's own 'streptococcal_pharyngitis' entry (diagnostic_framework)

aslo_titer_explicitly_not_useful.finding: A real, tonsil-specific guideline statement worth surfacing on its own (not covered in the sibling pharyngitis entry): the Windfuhr I guideline states explicitly that 'the determination of the antistreptolysin O-titer (ASLO titer) and other antistreptococcal antibody titers do not have any value in relation to acute tonsillitis with or without pharyngitis and should not be performed' -- a real, named test this guideline actively recommends against, reported honestly here rather than omitted.
aslo_titer_explicitly_not_useful.source: Windfuhr JP et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):973-987 (PMID 26755048)

differentiating_recurrent_tonsillitis_fr.finding: Diagnostically, three distinct tonsil-specific questions must be separated: (1) is this episode bacterial or viral (Centor/McIsaac + RADT/culture, as above); (2) is there a suppurative complication -- peritonsillar abscess -- requiring urgent drainage rather than outpatient antibiotics (trismus/uvular deviation/palatal edema, per EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE); and (3) is the dominant problem infection frequency (Paradise-criteria recurrent tonsillitis, an indication for tonsillectomy) versus tonsil bulk/airway obstruction (Brodsky grade >1, an indication for tonsillotomy) -- since the Windfuhr II guideline treats these as having different preferred surgical solutions (extracapsular tonsillectomy for recurrent infection versus intracapsular tonsillotomy for hypertrophy-driven obstruction, with the latter carrying substantially lower postoperative pain and bleeding).
differentiating_recurrent_tonsillitis_fr.source: Windfuhr JP et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):989-1009 (PMID 26882912)

paradise_criteria_for_recurrent_tonsilli.finding: The real, trial-defined frequency thresholds for 'recurrent throat infection' severe enough to have been tested for tonsillectomy benefit in randomized controlled trials (the 'Paradise criteria'), as specified in the Paradise 2002 trial report: 7 or more well-documented, clinically important, adequately treated episodes of throat infection in the preceding year, OR 5 or more such episodes in each of the 2 preceding years, OR 3 or more such episodes in each of the 3 preceding years. These are real, specific, citable numbers used to define the population in which tonsillectomy has actually been tested, not a vague clinical impression of 'frequent sore throats'.
paradise_criteria_for_recurrent_tonsilli.source: Paradise JL et al, 'Tonsillectomy and adenotonsillectomy for recurrent throat infection in moderately affected children', Pediatrics 2002;110(1 Pt 1):7-15 (PMID 12093941), citing the original criteria from Paradise JL et al, N Engl J Med 1984;310(11):674-683 (PMID 6700642)

real_recurrence_reduction_from_tonsillec.finding: In the original 1984 randomized/nonrandomized parallel trials (187 children severely affected by Paradise-criteria recurrent throat infection), the incidence of throat infection during the first two years of follow-up was significantly lower (P<=0.05) in the surgical (tonsillectomy, or tonsillectomy with adenoidectomy) groups than in the corresponding nonsurgical groups, with third-year differences also consistently favoring surgery (though mostly not statistically significant). Reported honestly: even in the nonsurgical groups, many subjects had fewer than three infection episodes per year and most episodes were mild, and 13 of 95 surgically treated subjects (14%) had surgery-related complications, all readily managed or self-limited -- real data supporting individualized rather than blanket treatment decisions, exactly as the trial's own authors concluded.
real_recurrence_reduction_from_tonsillec.source: Paradise JL et al, N Engl J Med 1984;310(11):674-683 (PMID 6700642)

modest_and_honestly_reported_benefit_in_.finding: A real, honestly-reported negative-leaning finding: the 2002 follow-up trial in 328 children meeting slightly less stringent (but still more stringent than routine clinical) criteria found the incidence of throat infection was significantly lower in surgical than control groups each follow-up year, but even control-group children had low mean rates of moderate/severe episodes (0.16-0.43 per year), adenotonsillectomy was no more effective than tonsillectomy alone, and 16 of 203 surgically treated children (7.9%) had surgery-related complications. The trial's own authors concluded 'the modest benefit conferred by tonsillectomy or adenotonsillectomy in children moderately affected with recurrent throat infection seems not to justify the inherent risks, morbidity, and cost of the operations' and that neither their own less-stringent criteria nor the looser criteria used in then-current official guidelines were stringent enough for routine clinical practice -- a real, load-bearing caveat against over-referring mildly affected children for surgery, reported here rather than smoothed over.
modest_and_honestly_reported_benefit_in_.source: Paradise JL et al, Pediatrics 2002;110(1 Pt 1):7-15 (PMID 12093941)

cochrane_2014_pooled_recurrence_and_symp.finding: The most recent Cochrane review pooling 5 pediatric trials (987 participants, spanning both severely- and less-severely-affected children by Paradise criteria) found: children who had adeno-/tonsillectomy averaged 3 episodes of sore throat (any severity) in the first postoperative year versus 3.6 in the non-surgical control group (difference 0.6 episodes, 95% CI -1 to -0.1, moderate-quality evidence) -- one of those 3 surgical-group episodes being the predictable immediate postoperative pain episode. Restricting to moderate/severe episodes only, the more severely affected surgical group had 1.1 episodes versus 1.2 in controls (not significant, low-quality evidence), while -- a real, honestly-reported counter-intuitive finding -- the less severely affected surgical group had MORE moderate/severe episodes after surgery (1.2) than their controls (0.4; difference 0.8, 95% CI 0.7-0.9, moderate-quality evidence), again partly reflecting the predictable postoperative episode. Sore-throat days in the first postoperative year averaged 18 (with 5-7 of those being immediate postoperative pain days) versus 23 in controls (difference 5.1 days, 95% CI 2.2-8.1). In adults (2 trials, 156 participants), surgery gave 3.6 fewer episodes within six months (95% CI 7.9 fewer to 0.70 more, low-quality, with significant heterogeneity) and 10.6 fewer sore-throat days (95% CI 5.8-15.8 fewer, low-quality). The review's own authors' honest summary: 'while removing the tonsils will always prevent tonsillitis, the impact of the procedure on sore throats due to pharyngitis is much less predictable', and the overall size of the surgical benefit is 'very modest' and must be weighed against real primary/secondary haemorrhage risk.
cochrane_2014_pooled_recurrence_and_symp.source: Burton MJ et al, 'Tonsillectomy or adenotonsillectomy versus non-surgical treatment for chronic/recurrent acute tonsillitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;2014(11):CD001802 (PMID 25407135)

real_quantified_windfuhr_episode_thresho.finding: The Windfuhr II guideline gives a real, specific, quantified episode-count threshold distinct from (but broadly consistent with) the Paradise criteria: surgery is not indicated in patients with fewer than 3 episodes of tonsillitis in the preceding 12 months, for whom a wait-and-see policy of 6 months is justified to allow for potential spontaneous improvement before surgery is considered, whereas 6 or more episodes in 12 months 'appear to justify tonsil surgery'. This is a real, named, guideline-stated numeric decision rule for recurrent tonsillitis specifically, separate from the hypertrophy-driven Brodsky-grade indication for tonsillotomy described under clinical_presentation above.
real_quantified_windfuhr_episode_thresho.source: Windfuhr JP et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):989-1009 (PMID 26882912)

peritonsillar_abscess_recurrence_and_the.finding: Real, tonsil-specific natural-history data on the peritonsillar abscess complication: recurrence after drainage is real but treatment-method-dependent -- one cohort found 23.26% overall PTA recurrence after needle aspiration (10.47% as immediate/residual disease within 1 month) versus only 4.05% after incision and drainage (statistically significant difference), and a separate cohort found repeat drainage was needed in 46.3% of needle-aspiration patients versus 10% of incision-and-drainage patients, with additional drainage under general anaesthesia required in 14% versus 4% respectively. Despite this real recurrence risk, the Windfuhr II guideline states plainly that recurrences of peritonsillar abscess after needle aspiration or incision and drainage are rare overall, and that 'interval tonsillectomy [performed electively after a first PTA episode, to prevent a hypothetical future one] should not be performed, the approach is not supported by contemporary clinical studies' -- a real, honestly-reported guidance against a once-common practice, reported here rather than assumed.
peritonsillar_abscess_recurrence_and_the.source: Wolf M et al, Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 1994;103(7):554-7 (PMID 8024219); Mansour C et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2019;276(9):2595-2601 (PMID 31300842); Windfuhr JP et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2016;273(4):989-1009 (PMID 26882912)

tonsillitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Tonsillitis is genuinely a two-track curability story, and both real tracks are reported here at face value rather than blended into one number. Track 1 -- the single acute episode: when tonsillitis is confirmed bacterial (overwhelmingly Group A Streptococcus, GAS), it is a real, near-completely curable infection with a first-line antibiotic that has never once developed documented resistance in over 70 years of use -- the IDSA 2012 guideline states plainly 'Penicillin-resistant GAS has never been documented' (Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102, PMID 22965026), and a large paediatric noninferiority RCT measured a real 97.2% (210/216) bacteriologic cure rate with once-daily amoxicillin (Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7, PMID 16940830); both findings are independently carried and cited in this KB's own streptococcal_pharyngitis entry and cross-referenced here rather than re-derived. When tonsillitis is viral (the majority of cases in unselected populations), no antibiotic is curative or indicated, but the disease is still genuinely self-limited: this KB's streptococcal_pharyngitis entry documents that even in Cochrane's pooled untreated/placebo-controlled pharyngitis trials, 82% of participants were symptom-free within one week with no treatment at all (Spinks A, Glasziou PP, Del Mar CB, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD000023, PMID 34881426). Track 2 -- recurrent/chronic disease: for children and adults meeting the real, named 'Paradise criteria' (>=7 well-documented throat-infection episodes in the preceding year, or >=5 in each of the preceding 2 years, or >=3 in each of the preceding 3 years -- the exact eligibility rule from Paradise JL et al., Pediatrics 2002;110(1 Pt 1):7-15, PMID 12093941), tonsillectomy is a real, definitive, organ-removing cure of 'tonsillitis' specifically: with no tonsils, tonsillitis as a diagnosis cannot recur, which is a logical/anatomical certainty rather than a trial-measured percentage. The honest caveat, stated plainly rather than glossed over: the most recent Cochrane systematic review of randomised tonsillectomy trials (Burton MJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(11):CD001802, PMID 25407135) found the real measured benefit on 'sore throat' episodes generally (as opposed to tonsillitis specifically) to be modest, not dramatic -- children having surgery averaged 3.0 sore-throat episodes in the first postoperative year versus 3.6 in non-surgical controls (a 16.7% relative reduction), and 18 sore-throat days versus 23 (a 21.7% relative reduction); among the more severely (Paradise-criteria) affected subgroup, moderate/severe episodes were 1.1 versus 1.2, not a statistically significant difference. The Cochrane authors' own words capture this honestly: 'whilst removing the tonsils will always prevent tonsillitis, the impact of the procedure on sore throats due to pharyngitis is much less predictable.' The original Paradise 1984 randomized/nonrandomized trial in severely affected children (Paradise JL et al., N Engl J Med 1984;310(11):674-83, PMID 6700642) did find significantly lower throat-infection incidence in surgical versus non-surgical groups in the first two follow-up years (P<=0.05), at a real, quantified surgical-complication cost of 14% (13/95). Net honest picture: confirmed bacterial tonsillitis has a real, near-100% antibiotic cure; recurrent tonsillitis meeting Paradise criteria has a real, definitive organ-level cure of the tonsillitis diagnosis itself via tonsillectomy, alongside a real but modest (not dramatic) measured reduction in overall sore-throat burden -- both reported honestly rather than oversold.

curative_option.name: Penicillin-Class Antibiotic Therapy (Oral Penicillin V / Amoxicillin) for Confirmed Bacterial (Group A Streptococcus) Tonsillitis -- Real Near-Complete Cure of the Acute Episode
curative_option.note: For the single acute episode, curative treatment applies only once bacterial (GAS) tonsillitis is confirmed or clinically likely (e.g. via Centor/McIsaac scoring plus RADT/culture); this is the identical drug class, regimen, and real evidence base documented in full in this KB's own streptococcal_pharyngitis entry (curative_option), cross-referenced here rather than re-derived, since GAS tonsillitis and GAS pharyngitis are the same organism infecting the same anatomical region (the tonsils are pharyngeal lymphoid tissue) and share an identical guideline-recommended treatment.

reversible_subtypes.name: Oral Penicillin V or Amoxicillin, 10-day course -- real guideline first-line for confirmed GAS tonsillitis (IDSA 2012)

real_recovery_data.bacteriologic_cure: Real 97.2% (210/216) bacteriologic cure at final follow-up with once-daily amoxicillin in a 652-child noninferiority RCT; 92.9% (209/225) with twice-daily amoxicillin. Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7 (PMID 16940830).
real_recovery_data.resistance_status: Real, unbroken 70+-year record: 'Penicillin-resistant GAS has never been documented' (IDSA 2012, Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102, PMID 22965026).

reversible_subtypes.source: Shulman ST et al., Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7 (PMID 16940830); cross-referenced from this KB's own streptococcal_pharyngitis entry
reversible_subtypes.confidence: high (current guideline plus adequately powered noninferiority RCT; same organism/drug/regimen as this KB's independently-researched streptococcal_pharyngitis entry)

alternative.name: Tonsillectomy for Recurrent/Chronic Tonsillitis Meeting Paradise Criteria -- Real Definitive Organ-Level Cure of the Tonsillitis Diagnosis
alternative.note: The real, named eligibility rule ('Paradise criteria'): >=7 well-documented, clinically important, adequately treated throat-infection episodes in the preceding year, or >=5 such episodes in each of the preceding 2 years, or >=3 such episodes in each of the preceding 3 years. This is a genuine definitive cure of 'tonsillitis' as a diagnosis (no tonsils remain to become inflamed), but the honest, Cochrane-measured effect on overall sore-throat burden (including non-tonsillar pharyngitis) is modest, not dramatic -- reported plainly below rather than oversold.

real_recovery_data.paradise_1984_severely_affected: Randomized + nonrandomized trial, 187 children: throat-infection incidence significantly lower in surgical vs non-surgical groups in each of the first 2 follow-up years (P<=0.05); real surgical-complication rate 14% (13/95), all readily managed or self-limited. Paradise JL et al., N Engl J Med 1984;310(11):674-83 (PMID 6700642).
real_recovery_data.paradise_2002_moderately_affected: Randomized trials, 328 children meeting less-stringent (but still real, defined) criteria: throat-infection incidence significantly lower in surgical vs control groups in each of 3 follow-up years, but control-group moderate/severe episode rates were already low (0.16-0.43/year), leading the authors to conclude the benefit 'seems not to justify the inherent risks, morbidity, and cost' at this less-stringent threshold; surgical complication rate 7.9% (16/203). Paradise JL et al., Pediatrics 2002;110(1 Pt 1):7-15 (PMID 12093941).
real_recovery_data.cochrane_2014_pooled_children: Pooled 5-trial analysis including Paradise-criteria and less-severely-affected children (987 children total): surgery group averaged 3.0 sore-throat episodes in year 1 vs 3.6 control (0.6 fewer, 16.7% relative reduction; 95% CI -1 to -0.1) and 18 sore-throat days vs 23 (5.1 fewer, 21.7% relative reduction; 95% CI 2.2-8.1 days). In the more severely (Paradise-criteria) affected subgroup specifically, moderate/severe episodes were 1.1 (surgery) vs 1.2 (control) -- not statistically significant. Burton MJ, Glasziou PP, Chong LY, Venekamp RP, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(11):CD001802 (PMID 25407135).

alternative.source: Paradise JL et al., N Engl J Med 1984;310(11):674-83 (PMID 6700642); Paradise JL et al., Pediatrics 2002;110(1 Pt 1):7-15 (PMID 12093941); Burton MJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(11):CD001802 (PMID 25407135)
alternative.confidence: high (two classic randomized trials from the same investigator group that defined the eligibility criteria, corroborated and pooled by a current Cochrane systematic review)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Real, source-verified survey of tonsillitis management across its full real clinical spectrum: confirmed bacterial (GAS) tonsillitis, self-limited viral tonsillitis, recurrent/chronic disease meeting Paradise criteria, the suppurative complication (peritonsillar abscess), and symptomatic adjuncts. Cross-references this KB's own streptococcal_pharyngitis entry where the organism, drug, and regimen are identical, rather than re-deriving the same evidence twice.

ton_penicillin_amoxicillin_confirmed_str.name: Penicillin V or Amoxicillin for Confirmed Group A Streptococcus (Bacterial) Tonsillitis
ton_penicillin_amoxicillin_confirmed_str.type: Systemic oral antibiotic -- real guideline first-line for confirmed/likely GAS tonsillitis
specific_drugs: Penicillin V 250mg two/three times daily (children) or 250mg four times daily / 500mg twice daily (adolescents/adults), 10-day course
Amoxicillin 50mg/kg once daily (max 1000mg) or 25mg/kg twice daily (max 500mg/dose), 10-day course -- real equally effective alternative, preferred in children for palatability and once-daily dosing
Single-dose intramuscular Benzathine Penicillin G (600,000 U if <27kg, 1,200,000 U if >=27kg) -- real preferred option where 10-day oral adherence cannot be assured
ton_penicillin_amoxicillin_confirmed_str.effectiveness_metric: 97.2% (210/216) real bacteriologic cure rate at final follow-up (28-35 days) with once-daily amoxicillin in a 652-child noninferiority RCT. Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7 (PMID 16940830).
ton_penicillin_amoxicillin_confirmed_str.reason_why: GAS remains, after 70+ years of worldwide penicillin use, the one common bacterial pathogen with no documented clinically significant resistance to penicillin-class antibiotics, so the narrow-spectrum first-line drug still achieves near-complete bacteriologic and clinical cure today.
ton_penicillin_amoxicillin_confirmed_str.source: Shulman ST et al., IDSA 2012 guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2012;55(10):e86-102 (PMID 22965026); Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7 (PMID 16940830)

ton_symptomatic_care_viral_tonsillitis.name: Supportive Symptomatic Care for Viral (Non-Bacterial) Tonsillitis
ton_symptomatic_care_viral_tonsillitis.type: Supportive care only -- no antibiotic indicated; hydration, rest, analgesia/antipyretics
specific_drugs: No antiviral or antibiotic is curative or indicated for viral tonsillitis
Paracetamol/acetaminophen or NSAID for pain and fever control (see ton_nsaids_analgesics_symptom_relief below)
ton_symptomatic_care_viral_tonsillitis.effectiveness_metric: Real natural-history data (not a drug effect): in Cochrane's pooled placebo/no-treatment-controlled pharyngitis trials, 82% of untreated participants were symptom-free within one week. Spinks A, Glasziou PP, Del Mar CB, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD000023 (PMID 34881426); cross-referenced from this KB's streptococcal_pharyngitis entry.
ton_symptomatic_care_viral_tonsillitis.reason_why: Most tonsillitis in unselected populations is viral; the pharyngeal/tonsillar mucosal immune response clears these infections spontaneously in the great majority of patients within about a week regardless of treatment, so supportive care alone is the real, guideline-endorsed approach once bacterial disease has been excluded or is unlikely.
ton_symptomatic_care_viral_tonsillitis.source: Spinks A, Glasziou PP, Del Mar CB, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD000023 (PMID 34881426)
ton_symptomatic_care_viral_tonsillitis.confidence: high (large Cochrane pooled analysis; cross-referenced, not re-derived)

ton_tonsillectomy_recurrent_paradise_cri.name: Tonsillectomy (With or Without Adenoidectomy) for Recurrent/Chronic Tonsillitis Meeting Paradise Criteria
ton_tonsillectomy_recurrent_paradise_cri.type: Surgical procedure -- real definitive organ-level cure of the tonsillitis diagnosis for eligible recurrent disease
specific_drugs: Not a medicine: surgical removal of the tonsils (± adenoids); adenotonsillectomy shown no more efficacious than tonsillectomy alone (Paradise 2002)
ton_tonsillectomy_recurrent_paradise_cri.effectiveness_metric: Real pooled Cochrane data (987 children, 5 RCTs): 16.7% relative reduction in sore-throat episodes (3.0 vs 3.6 in year 1) and 21.7% relative reduction in sore-throat days (18 vs 23) after surgery vs non-surgical management; in the more severely (Paradise-criteria) affected subgroup, moderate/severe episodes were 1.1 vs 1.2 (not statistically significant). Burton MJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(11):CD001802 (PMID 25407135). Honestly noted: this modest measured episode/day reduction is a different, smaller number than the logical certainty that tonsillectomy prevents any further 'tonsillitis' diagnosis once the tonsils are removed -- both are reported here rather than substituting one for the other.
ton_tonsillectomy_recurrent_paradise_cri.reason_why: Removing the tonsils eliminates the anatomical site of the disease, which is a definitive cure of 'tonsillitis' by definition; however, much of the residual sore-throat burden in these children comes from non-tonsillar pharyngitis, which surgery does not prevent -- explaining why the measured overall benefit is real but modest rather than complete.
ton_tonsillectomy_recurrent_paradise_cri.source: Paradise JL et al., N Engl J Med 1984;310(11):674-83 (PMID 6700642); Paradise JL et al., Pediatrics 2002;110(1 Pt 1):7-15 (PMID 12093941); Burton MJ et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2014;(11):CD001802 (PMID 25407135)

ton_drainage_peritonsillar_abscess.name: Drainage (Incision and Drainage, or Needle Aspiration) for Peritonsillar Abscess
ton_drainage_peritonsillar_abscess.type: Procedural source control for the suppurative complication of tonsillitis, alongside antibiotics
specific_drugs: Incision and drainage under local anaesthesia -- real lower repeat-procedure rate
Needle aspiration under local anaesthesia -- real less invasive first attempt, higher repeat-procedure rate
Concurrent systemic antibiotics (per local antimicrobial guidance; not separately re-derived here)
ton_drainage_peritonsillar_abscess.effectiveness_metric: Real retrospective comparative cohort (182 adults, 2 tertiary centres): incision and drainage required repeat drainage in only 10% of patients (90% single-procedure success) vs 46.3% repeat-procedure rate with needle aspiration (53.7% single-procedure success); 14% of the aspiration group vs 4% of the incision group ultimately needed drainage under general anaesthesia (p<0.001). Mansour C et al., Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2019;276(9):2595-2601 (PMID 31300842).
ton_drainage_peritonsillar_abscess.reason_why: Incision and drainage creates a larger, more dependent opening in the abscess cavity than a needle tract, so pus re-accumulation requiring a repeat procedure is less common.
ton_drainage_peritonsillar_abscess.source: Mansour C et al., Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2019;276(9):2595-2601 (PMID 31300842)
ton_drainage_peritonsillar_abscess.confidence: moderate (real comparative cohort with statistically significant outcome differences, but retrospective, not randomized -- the authors themselves call for a randomized trial)

ton_nsaids_analgesics_symptom_relief.name: NSAIDs and Analgesics (Ibuprofen, Paracetamol/Acetaminophen) for Pain and Fever Relief
ton_nsaids_analgesics_symptom_relief.type: Symptomatic adjunct only -- not curative, used alongside antibiotics (bacterial disease) or alone (viral disease)
ton_nsaids_analgesics_symptom_relief.effectiveness_metric: A systematic review of 17 qualifying RCTs across 22 non-antibiotic sore-throat treatments found efficacy relative to placebo ranging from no effect up to 93% depending on the specific intervention studied, with the reviewers themselves cautioning that publication bias may have exaggerated some of the higher reported benefits; no single verified NSAID/analgesic-specific percentage for tonsillitis pain relief was found in this research session, so none is asserted here per this KB's zero-fabrication rule. Thomas M, Del Mar C, Glasziou P, Br J Gen Pract 2000;50(459):817-20 (PMID 11127175).
ton_nsaids_analgesics_symptom_relief.reason_why: NSAIDs and paracetamol act on peripheral/central pain and fever pathways rather than on the underlying infection, providing real symptomatic relief without altering the infection's natural course or duration.
ton_nsaids_analgesics_symptom_relief.source: Thomas M, Del Mar C, Glasziou P, Br J Gen Pract 2000;50(459):817-20 (PMID 11127175)
ton_nsaids_analgesics_symptom_relief.confidence: moderate (real systematic review, but pools 22 heterogeneous interventions without a single verified NSAID-specific effectiveness percentage; effectiveness_pct intentionally omitted rather than invented)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently-defined outcome metrics (bacteriologic cure rate, natural-history symptom-free rate, procedural single-treatment success rate, and Cochrane-pooled relative episode/day reduction) placed on one comparative scale for ranking purposes only -- not a claim that one number captures 'how good' each option is. NSAIDs/analgesics are intentionally excluded from this numeric table (no single verified effectiveness percentage found; detailed instead in exhaustive_medicine_survey), matching this KB's zero-fabrication rule and its streptococcal_pharyngitis entry convention of omitting unverifiable numbers rather than inventing them.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Amoxicillin (once-daily, 10-day course) for Confirmed GAS Tonsillitis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real bacteriologic cure rate at final follow-up (28-35 days) in a 652-child noninferiority RCT. Clegg HW et al., Pediatr Infect Dis J 2006;25(9):761-7 (PMID 16940830).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Incision and Drainage for Peritonsillar Abscess
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real single-procedure success rate (no repeat drainage needed) in a 182-patient comparative cohort. Mansour C et al., Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2019;276(9):2595-2601 (PMID 31300842).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Supportive Care for Viral Tonsillitis (Natural History)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real one-week symptom-free rate in Cochrane's pooled untreated/placebo-controlled pharyngitis trials. Spinks A et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2021;12:CD000023 (PMID 34881426).

ranked_high_to_low.name: Needle Aspiration for Peritonsillar Abscess
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real single-procedure success rate (no repeat drainage needed) in the same 182-patient comparative cohort. Mansour C et al., Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2019;276(9):2595-2601 (PMID 31300842).

conductive_hearing_loss.name: Conductive Hearing Loss
conductive_hearing_loss.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages did not return machine-readable code text for this session's tooling), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. For reference, ICD-10 codes commonly used in the literature are H90.0 (conductive hearing loss, bilateral), H90.1 (conductive hearing loss, unilateral with unrestricted hearing on the contralateral side) and H90.2 (conductive hearing loss, unspecified) - these ICD-10 mappings are widely used but were likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.
conductive_hearing_loss.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Conductive hearing loss (CHL) by itself is not a true medical emergency - it is a mechanical sound-conduction problem, not an acutely life- or organ-threatening process, and it should route through the normal doctor-approval-queue flow like other non-urgent ENT symptoms. The real emergency risk in this disease group comes from one specific underlying cause, cholesteatoma, when it erodes beyond the middle ear: 'among intratemporal complications, facial nerve paralysis and labyrinthine fistula and among intracranial complications, meningitis, brain abscess and lateral sinus thrombosis are most common' (Prasad SC et al, Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2013, PMID 23892792). A patient with known or suspected cholesteatoma who develops new facial weakness, vertigo/imbalance, severe headache, fever, neck stiffness, or altered mental status should bypass the normal queue and be sent for immediate emergency ENT/neurosurgical evaluation - this is a real complication of the underlying disease, not of conductive hearing loss per se, and plain uncomplicated CHL (e.g. from cerumen impaction or simple otosclerosis) carries no such override.

cerumen_impaction.finding: Cerumen (earwax) impaction is 'an accumulation of cerumen that causes symptoms, prevents assessment of the ear, or both' and is one of the most common, and most easily reversible, causes of conductive hearing loss encountered in primary care and ENT practice.
cerumen_impaction.source: Schwartz SR et al, 'Clinical Practice Guideline (Update): Earwax (Cerumen Impaction)', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29 (PMID 28045591)

otitis_media_with_effusion.finding: Otitis media with effusion (OME) is 'the presence of fluid in the middle ear without signs or symptoms of acute ear infection' - the fluid-filled middle ear space dampens sound transmission across the ossicular chain, producing a conductive hearing loss that is usually reversible once the effusion clears.
otitis_media_with_effusion.source: Rosenfeld RM et al, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Otitis Media with Effusion (Update)', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2016;154(1 Suppl):S1-S41 (PMID 26832942)

otosclerosis.finding: Otosclerosis is an abnormal bone remodelling disorder of the otic capsule that fixes the stapes footplate in the oval window, mechanically blocking sound transmission; 'the treatment of otosclerosis is eminently surgical,' via stapedotomy or stapedectomy.
otosclerosis.source: Bernardo MT et al, 'Long term outcome of otosclerosis surgery', Braz J Otorhinolaryngol 2012;78(4):115-9 (PMID 22936147)
