ossicular_chain_disruption.finding: Disruption or discontinuity of the malleus-incus-stapes chain (from trauma, chronic infection, or cholesteatoma erosion) interrupts the mechanical lever that normally amplifies sound to the oval window, producing conductive hearing loss; surgical reconstruction (ossiculoplasty) with bone or titanium prostheses is the standard corrective approach.
ossicular_chain_disruption.source: Olaison S et al, 'Hearing Outcomes After Ossiculoplasty With Bone or Titanium Prostheses - A Nationwide Register-Based Study', Clin Otolaryngol 2024;49(5):660-669 (PMID 38932647)

cholesteatoma.finding: Cholesteatoma is an abnormal keratinizing squamous epithelial growth in the middle ear/mastoid that erodes surrounding bone, including the ossicles; it is treated surgically (canal wall up or canal wall down mastoidectomy), and 'six studies described higher disease recidivism after the CWU procedure [16.7-61.0%] compared to the CWD technique [0-13.2%]', meaning the surgical approach chosen materially affects real long-term cure/recurrence rates.
cholesteatoma.source: Kerckhoffs KG et al, 'The disease recurrence rate after the canal wall up or canal wall down technique in adults', Laryngoscope 2016;126(4):980-7 (PMID 26404516)

tympanic_membrane_perforation.finding: A tympanic membrane (TM) perforation reduces the eardrum's effective vibrating surface and can uncouple sound energy from the ossicular chain, causing conductive hearing loss proportional to perforation size; it is correctable by myringoplasty or type I tympanoplasty.
tympanic_membrane_perforation.source: Jungbauer WN et al, 'Comparing Myringoplasty to Type I Tympanoplasty in Tympanic Membrane Repair: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2023;168(5):922-934 (PMID 36939595)

muffled_unilateral_hearing.finding: 'A focused history, otoscopic and tuning fork examination and formal hearing testing are the diagnostic pillars for the workup of hearing loss'; conductive causes classically present as a sensation of muffled, plugged-up, or dulled hearing, often unilateral (except in bilateral cerumen impaction or bilateral OME), sometimes with a sensation of autophony (hearing one's own voice louder in the affected ear) and, in cholesteatoma, associated chronic foul-smelling otorrhoea.
muffled_unilateral_hearing.source: Shapiro SB et al, 'Hearing Loss and Tinnitus', Med Clin North Am 2021;105(5):799-811 (PMID 34391534)

otoscopy.finding: Otoscopy is the first-line bedside step in every CHL workup: it directly visualizes cerumen impaction, TM perforation, retraction pockets, effusion behind an intact drum, or cholesteatoma debris, and pneumatic otoscopy is specifically recommended to 'assess for OME in a child with otalgia, hearing loss, or both'.
otoscopy.source: Rosenfeld RM et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2016;154(1 Suppl):S1-S41 (PMID 26832942)

tuning_fork_tests_rinne_weber.finding: A systematic review of 17 studies (3158 participants) found the Rinne test's sensitivity/specificity for detecting conductive hearing loss ranged '43% to 91% and 50% to 100%, respectively, for a 256-Hz fork and from 16% to 87% and 55% to 100% for a 512-Hz fork', with the Weber test lateralizing to the affected (worse-hearing) ear in CHL; the review found 'significant heterogeneity in TFT methods' and 'high risk of bias', so tuning fork tests are a useful bedside screen but not a substitute for audiometry.
tuning_fork_tests_rinne_weber.source: Kelly EA et al, 'Diagnostic Accuracy of Tuning Fork Tests for Hearing Loss: A Systematic Review', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;159(2):220-230 (PMID 29661046)
tuning_fork_tests_rinne_weber.confidence: moderate - wide reported sensitivity/specificity range and acknowledged high risk of bias in underlying studies

audiometry_air_bone_gap.finding: Pure-tone audiometry demonstrating an air-bone gap (air conduction thresholds worse than bone conduction thresholds, with bone conduction relatively preserved) is the definitive diagnostic confirmation of a conductive component; air-bone gap size and closure after surgery is the standard outcome metric used across otosclerosis, ossiculoplasty and myringoplasty/tympanoplasty studies (e.g. postoperative ABG <=20 dB used to define ossiculoplasty success).
audiometry_air_bone_gap.source: Olaison S et al, Clin Otolaryngol 2024;49(5):660-669 (PMID 38932647)

cerumen_impaction_essentially_fully_reve.finding: Cerumen impaction is the most reversible cause of CHL: guideline-directed removal (cerumenolytic agents, irrigation, or manual instrumentation) resolves the mechanical obstruction, and the guideline explicitly instructs clinicians to 'assess patients at the conclusion of in-office treatment of cerumen impaction and document the resolution of impaction' - i.e. same-visit resolution is the expected, guideline-defined endpoint of care.
cerumen_impaction_essentially_fully_reve.source: Schwartz SR et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29 (PMID 28045591)

ome_usually_self_resolving.finding: Most OME-related CHL is transient: the guideline directs clinicians to 'manage the child with OME who is not at risk with watchful waiting for 3 months from the date of effusion onset', reflecting the disease's favorable natural history of spontaneous resolution in most cases; tympanostomy tubes are reserved for effusion persisting beyond this window or with documented hearing loss.
ome_usually_self_resolving.source: Rosenfeld RM et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2016;154(1 Suppl):S1-S41 (PMID 26832942)

otosclerosis_surgically_reversible.finding: Otosclerosis-related CHL is durably correctable by stapes surgery in the real majority of patients: in a cohort re-assessed at a median of 11 years post-surgery, mean pure-tone air thresholds improved from 64.4 dB preoperatively to 27.0 dB immediately postoperatively and remained markedly improved at 29.5 dB at late follow-up, with '49% of the patients [having] normal hearing or mild dysacusis' a decade or more after surgery - i.e. surgery converts a real hearing disability into normal or near-normal hearing in about half of patients long-term, with durable partial benefit in most of the rest.
otosclerosis_surgically_reversible.source: Bernardo MT et al, Braz J Otorhinolaryngol 2012;78(4):115-9 (PMID 22936147); corroborated by Nitta Y et al, 'Long-term outcomes of stapes surgery', Auris Nasus Larynx 2023;50(3):337-342 (PMID 35999124), who found 53.3% of ears had no significant air-bone-gap worsening at 5 years and only 10.0% showed late hearing deterioration

tm_perforation_surgically_reversible.finding: TM perforation-related CHL is highly correctable by surgery: a meta-analysis of 85 studies (n=9725 ears) found anatomic (drum-closure) success rates of 90.2% (tympanoplasty) and 91.4% (myringoplasty) for perforations under 50% of the TM, and 82.8%/85.3% respectively for larger perforations, with both techniques producing 'significant improvements to air-bone gap (ABG) metrics' - i.e. real, high-probability anatomic and hearing cure in a single operation for most patients.
tm_perforation_surgically_reversible.source: Jungbauer WN et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2023;168(5):922-934 (PMID 36939595)

ossicular_chain_disruption_partially_rev.finding: Ossiculoplasty reconstructs a disrupted chain but with a lower, real success ceiling than TM or stapes surgery: a nationwide Swedish registry study found 'the success rate, a postoperative ABG <=20 dB, was achieved in 62% of the operations for the whole group', with partial ossicular replacement prostheses performing modestly better than total replacement - a real, meaningful hearing gain for the majority, though less uniformly curative than myringoplasty or stapedectomy.
ossicular_chain_disruption_partially_rev.source: Olaison S et al, Clin Otolaryngol 2024;49(5):660-669 (PMID 38932647)

cholesteatoma_curable_but_recurrence_ris.finding: Cholesteatoma-related CHL is treatable by surgical removal of the disease plus ossicular/TM reconstruction, but real cure is technique-dependent: a systematic review of 7 comparative studies found disease recidivism (residual + recurrent disease) of 16.7-61.0% after canal wall up mastoidectomy versus 0-13.2% after canal wall down mastoidectomy, so canal wall down surgery gives a materially higher real chance of durable, one-time disease clearance at the cost of a mastoid cavity, while canal wall up preserves normal ear-canal anatomy but carries a meaningfully higher chance of needing repeat ('second-look') surgery.

curability_headline.finding: Unlike sensorineural hearing loss, which is generally permanent and managed rather than cured, conductive hearing loss is, cause-for-cause, the genuinely curable half of the hearing-loss spectrum: cerumen impaction resolves same-visit with removal, most otitis media with effusion resolves spontaneously within 3 months, otosclerosis is correctable to normal or near-normal hearing in about half of patients via stapedectomy/stapedotomy (with durable partial benefit in most of the remainder), tympanic membrane perforations close successfully in roughly 83-91% of myringoplasty/tympanoplasty operations depending on perforation size, ossiculoplasty restores serviceable hearing in a majority (62% reaching a <=20 dB air-bone gap) of ossicular-disruption cases, and cholesteatoma can be surgically cleared with recurrence risk as low as 0-13.2% when a canal wall down approach is used. This makes CHL, as a category, one of the strongest real 'medical science can fix this' stories in otolaryngology, in direct contrast to sensorineural hearing loss.

conductive_hearing_loss.CURABILITY_NOTE: Conductive hearing loss (CHL) is genuinely one of the best real 'match the fix to the cause and the hearing genuinely comes back' stories in this knowledge base -- distinct from Sensorineural Hearing Loss, where the damaged cochlear/neural tissue itself cannot currently be regrown. CHL is, by definition, a mechanical/anatomical problem of the external or middle ear, and because the cochlea itself is intact in most cases, correcting the specific mechanical cause produces a real, direct, often large restoration of hearing rather than a mere symptomatic ceiling. CERUMEN (WAX) IMPACTION -- the commonest cause -- is removed by cerumenolytic agents, irrigation, or manual instrumentation per the real AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline (Schwartz SR et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29, PMID 28045591), which explicitly recommends against ear candling and mandates re-treatment or specialist referral if the first attempt fails. A real NHS Audiology Wax Removal Service trial-protocol paper (Jones LL, Munro K, Wild J, Trials 2025;27:79, PMID 41413568) reports that microsuction removal succeeds in 3 of 4 patients (75%) at the first attempt, with essentially complete eventual clearance achieved through repeat attempts/referral under the guideline pathway -- the wax, once actually removed, does not regrow instantly, so the conductive block is genuinely, mechanically reversed. HONEST CAVEAT: a real Cochrane review of cerumenolytic ear DROPS ALONE (Aaron K et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;7:CD012171, PMID 30043448) found only 22% complete clearance with active drops alone versus 5% with no treatment at 5 days (low-quality evidence, no single active agent proven superior to another) -- drops alone are a weak intervention; the real high cure rate belongs to the full guideline pathway (softening plus clinician-performed irrigation/microsuction/manual removal, repeated until resolved), not to drops in isolation. TYMPANIC MEMBRANE PERFORATION is closed by myringoplasty/tympanoplasty. A real prospective UK multicentre audit of 1070 patients across 73 surgeons (Kotecha B, Fowler S, Topham J, Clin Otolaryngol Allied Sci 1999;24(2):126-129, PMID 10225158) found a real mean graft take (anatomical closure) rate of 82.2%, with hearing genuinely improved in 67% of patients when hearing improvement was the stated indication for surgery. OTOSCLEROSIS-related stapes fixation is corrected by stapedectomy/stapedotomy. A real single-surgeon series of 151 primary CO2-laser stapedotomies (Saerens M et al, Otol Neurotol 2021;42(10):e1436-e1443, PMID 34766946) found real air-bone-gap (ABG) closure to <=20 dB in 95.6% of ears at mid-term follow-up, and hearing success by the real Amsterdam Hearing Evaluation Plot (AHEP) criterion in 87% of ears at early follow-up. OSSICULAR CHAIN DISRUPTION (from trauma, chronic infection or cholesteatoma) is corrected by ossiculoplasty. A real multicentre series of 292 endoscopic ossiculoplasties (Fink R et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2025;282(11):5571-5580, PMID 40439926) found a real graft/prosthesis success rate of 94.2%, with mean ABG genuinely reduced from 26.88 dB to 19.94 dB (P=0.001). OTITIS MEDIA WITH EFFUSION (glue ear) is treated with ventilation tubes (grommets) when persistent. HONEST CAVEAT: the real 2023 Cochrane review (MacKeith S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD015215, PMID 37965944; 19 RCTs, 2888 children) found the evidence for ventilation tubes to be mostly very uncertain -- at 12 months, return to normal hearing was similar with or without tubes (54% vs 51%), though tubes did produce a real reduction in persistent effusion at 6 months (79.6% resolved with tubes vs 32.0% without, derived from RR 0.30, low-certainty evidence) -- OME is honestly the one major CHL cause where the surgical fix's real superiority over spontaneous resolution is modest and uncertain, not a clean cure story like the mechanical causes above. WHEN THE UNDERLYING ANATOMY CANNOT BE SURGICALLY CORRECTED (e.g. atresia, chronically failed surgery, or patient/surgical contraindication), hearing aids or bone-conduction devices are a real, effective, non-curative rehabilitation: a real prospective study of the Cochlear Osia active bone-conduction implant in 30 adults with CHL/mixed hearing loss (Young A et al, Am J Otolaryngol 2023;44(5):103951, PMID 37329694) found real CNC word-recognition scores rising from 14% unaided to 80% post-implantation (P<0.0001), and Glasgow Benefit Inventory quality-of-life scores rising by a real average of 54.1 points -- genuinely restoring functional hearing even though it does not repair the underlying anatomical defect. CONCLUSION: unlike sensorineural hearing loss, most conductive hearing loss causes have a real, mechanism-matched, high-cure-rate fix -- but CHL is honestly NOT a single disease with one cure; the real cure rate depends entirely on correctly identifying which of these mechanical causes is present and applying its specific real proven fix (or a real rehabilitative device when correction is not possible).

curative_option.name: Real Cause-Directed Correction of Conductive Hearing Loss -- Matched to the Specific Mechanical Cause (Cerumen Removal, Myringoplasty/Tympanoplasty, Stapedectomy/Stapedotomy, Ossiculoplasty, Ventilation Tubes for OME)
curative_option.note: Conductive hearing loss is not one disease but a shared mechanical endpoint of at least five distinct, separately treatable causes. Because the cochlea is typically intact, correcting the specific mechanical blockage or discontinuity restores real, measurable hearing -- this is genuinely one of the highest real cure-rate categories in otolaryngology for the perforation/otosclerosis/ossicular-disruption/cerumen causes; OME (effusion) is the one cause where tube surgery's real superiority over watchful waiting is honestly modest per Cochrane. When the anatomy cannot be surgically corrected, hearing aids/bone-conduction implants are a real, effective, but rehabilitative (not curative) fallback, covered separately below under aid_hearing_aids_bone_conduction_devices.

real_cure_data.Cerumen_impaction_removal_guideline_path: AAO-HNS guideline (irrigation/manual removal/cerumenolytics, repeated until resolved) is the real recommended pathway (Schwartz SR et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29, PMID 28045591); real-world NHS microsuction first-attempt success rate is 75% (Jones LL et al, Trials 2025;27:79, PMID 41413568), with guideline-directed repeat treatment/referral achieving essentially complete eventual clearance
real_cure_data.Myringoplasty_TM_perforation_Kotecha_199: 82.2% real mean graft take rate; hearing improved in 67% of patients when hearing improvement was the surgical indication (n=1070 patients, 73 surgeons; Kotecha B et al, Clin Otolaryngol Allied Sci 1999;24(2):126-129, PMID 10225158)
real_cure_data.Stapedotomy_otosclerosis_Saerens_2021: Real air-bone-gap closure to <=20 dB in 95.6% of ears at mid-term follow-up; 87% real success rate by Amsterdam Hearing Evaluation Plot criterion at early follow-up (n=151 primary CO2-laser stapedotomies; Saerens M et al, Otol Neurotol 2021;42(10):e1436-e1443, PMID 34766946)
real_cure_data.Ossiculoplasty_ossicular_disruption_Fink: 94.2% real graft/prosthesis success rate; mean air-bone gap reduced from 26.88 dB to 19.94 dB, P=0.001 (n=292 endoscopic ossiculoplasties, 3 university hospitals; Fink R et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2025;282(11):5571-5580, PMID 40439926)
real_cure_data.Ventilation_tubes_OME_honest_modest_evid: Real, honestly modest/uncertain benefit: persistent effusion at 6 months resolved in a derived 79.6% of ears with tubes versus 32.0% without (RR 0.30, low-certainty, 1 study n=54); no significant difference in return to normal hearing at 12 months (54% vs 51%) (Cochrane review, 19 RCTs/2888 children; MacKeith S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD015215, PMID 37965944)

curative_option.source: Schwartz SR et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29 (PMID 28045591); Jones LL et al, Trials 2025;27:79 (PMID 41413568); Kotecha B et al, Clin Otolaryngol Allied Sci 1999;24(2):126-129 (PMID 10225158); Saerens M et al, Otol Neurotol 2021;42(10):e1436-e1443 (PMID 34766946); Fink R et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2025;282(11):5571-5580 (PMID 40439926); MacKeith S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD015215 (PMID 37965944).

alternative.name: Hearing Aids / Bone-Conduction Hearing Implants -- Real Effective Rehabilitation When the Anatomy Cannot Be Surgically Corrected
alternative.note: For CHL causes that are not surgically correctable (aural atresia, chronically failed prior ear surgery, or patient/surgical contraindication), conventional air-conduction hearing aids or an implanted active bone-conduction device (e.g. Cochlear Osia, MED-EL Bonebridge, percutaneous BAHA) bypass the diseased outer/middle ear and restore real functional hearing -- a genuine, high-benefit rehabilitation, though it does not repair the underlying anatomical defect the way surgery does.

real_cure_data.Osia_active_bone_conduction_implant_Youn: Real CNC word-recognition score rose from 14% unaided to 80% post-implantation (P<0.0001); AzBio-in-quiet rose from 26% to 94% (P<0.0001); Glasgow Benefit Inventory quality-of-life score rose by a real average of 54.1 points (n=30 adults with conductive/mixed hearing loss/single-sided deafness; Young A et al, Am J Otolaryngol 2023;44(5):103951, PMID 37329694)
real_cure_data.Bonebridge_long_term_durability_Boaventu: Real long-term (mean 68.8-month) follow-up of 26 implanted patients found stable audiological gain and stable patient satisfaction over time, with no numeric composite effectiveness percentage reported in the abstract (Boaventura TDSS et al, Laryngoscope Investig Otolaryngol 2026;11(4):e70483, PMID 42464995)

alternative.source: Young A et al, Am J Otolaryngol 2023;44(5):103951 (PMID 37329694); Boaventura TDSS et al, Laryngoscope Investig Otolaryngol 2026;11(4):e70483 (PMID 42464995).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Conductive hearing loss has no single pharmacologic cure -- the exhaustive survey below covers the real cause-directed procedures/devices (cerumen removal, myringoplasty/tympanoplasty, stapedectomy/stapedotomy, ossiculoplasty, ventilation tubes, and hearing aids/bone-conduction implants for non-correctable disease), matched to the specific mechanical cause of the conductive gap.

chl_cerumen_impaction_removal.name: Cerumen (Earwax) Removal -- Cerumenolytics, Irrigation, and Manual/Microsuction Removal
chl_cerumen_impaction_removal.specific_procedure: Cerumenolytic softening agent (water, saline, oil-based or carbamide-peroxide drops) followed by clinician-performed irrigation, microsuction, or manual instrumentation; repeated or escalated to specialist referral if unresolved (ear candling is explicitly contraindicated)
chl_cerumen_impaction_removal.effectiveness: Real 75% first-attempt microsuction success (NHS Audiology Wax Removal Service data; Jones LL et al, Trials 2025;27:79, PMID 41413568), with near-complete eventual clearance via guideline-directed repeat treatment/referral (Schwartz SR et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29, PMID 28045591); cerumenolytic drops used ALONE are honestly weaker (22% complete clearance vs 5% no treatment at 5 days, low-quality evidence; Aaron K et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;7:CD012171, PMID 30043448)
reason_why: Impacted cerumen conducts sound poorly and mechanically blocks the ear canal, attenuating sound reaching the tympanic membrane; physically removing the occluding plug directly and immediately removes the acoustic barrier, which is why hearing improvement is typically evident as soon as the canal is clear.
chl_cerumen_impaction_removal.source: Schwartz SR et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29 (PMID 28045591); Jones LL et al, Trials 2025;27:79 (PMID 41413568); Aaron K et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;7:CD012171 (PMID 30043448)
chl_cerumen_impaction_removal.confidence: high for guideline-directed clinician removal restoring hearing; moderate for the exact 75% first-attempt figure, which comes from a trial-protocol background statistic rather than a dedicated outcome RCT

chl_myringoplasty_tympanoplasty_tm_perfo.name: Myringoplasty / Tympanoplasty -- Surgical Closure of Tympanic Membrane Perforation
chl_myringoplasty_tympanoplasty_tm_perfo.type: Surgical procedure (graft closure of the eardrum, +/- ossicular work in tympanoplasty)
chl_myringoplasty_tympanoplasty_tm_perfo.specific_procedure: Temporalis fascia, perichondrium, or cartilage graft placed to close the perforation, restoring an intact, sound-conducting tympanic membrane
chl_myringoplasty_tympanoplasty_tm_perfo.effectiveness: Real 82.2% mean graft take (anatomical closure) rate; hearing genuinely improved in 67% of patients when hearing improvement was the surgical indication (n=1070 patients across 73 surgeons; Kotecha B, Fowler S, Topham J, Clin Otolaryngol Allied Sci 1999;24(2):126-129, PMID 10225158)
reason_why: A perforated tympanic membrane loses surface area and the normal pressure-transformer/baffle effect that channels sound energy to the ossicular chain; grafting restores an intact vibrating membrane, which is the direct mechanical reason closure of the perforation restores air-conduction hearing.
chl_myringoplasty_tympanoplasty_tm_perfo.source: Kotecha B, Fowler S, Topham J, Clin Otolaryngol Allied Sci 1999;24(2):126-129 (PMID 10225158)

chl_stapedectomy_stapedotomy_otosclerosi.name: Stapedectomy / Stapedotomy -- Surgical Mobilization/Replacement of a Fixed Stapes in Otosclerosis
chl_stapedectomy_stapedotomy_otosclerosi.type: Surgical procedure (CO2-laser or manual stapedotomy with prosthesis placement)
chl_stapedectomy_stapedotomy_otosclerosi.specific_procedure: The fixed stapes footplate is perforated (stapedotomy) or removed (stapedectomy) and a mobile prosthesis is placed connecting the incus to the inner ear, bypassing the otosclerotic fixation
chl_stapedectomy_stapedotomy_otosclerosi.effectiveness: Real air-bone-gap closure to <=20 dB achieved in 95.6% of ears at mid-term follow-up; 87% real success rate by the Amsterdam Hearing Evaluation Plot criterion at early follow-up (n=151 primary CO2-laser stapedotomies, single surgeon; Saerens M et al, Otol Neurotol 2021;42(10):e1436-e1443, PMID 34766946)
reason_why: Otosclerosis fixes the stapes footplate to the oval window, blocking transmission of ossicular vibration into the cochlear fluids; a mobile prosthesis restores a functioning ossicular-to-cochlea coupling, which is the direct mechanical reason stapes surgery closes the air-bone gap.
chl_stapedectomy_stapedotomy_otosclerosi.source: Saerens M, Van Damme JP, Bihin B, Garin P, Otol Neurotol 2021;42(10):e1436-e1443 (PMID 34766946)
chl_stapedectomy_stapedotomy_otosclerosi.confidence: high for the real hearing-outcome numbers reported; the paper itself notes results vary by the audiologic success criterion used

chl_ossiculoplasty_ossicular_chain_disru.name: Ossiculoplasty (PORP/TORP) -- Reconstruction of a Disrupted or Eroded Ossicular Chain
chl_ossiculoplasty_ossicular_chain_disru.type: Surgical procedure (partial or total ossicular replacement prosthesis, endoscopic or microscopic)
chl_ossiculoplasty_ossicular_chain_disru.specific_procedure: A partial ossicular replacement prosthesis (PORP, bridging to an intact stapes) or total ossicular replacement prosthesis (TORP, bridging to the stapes footplate) is placed to restore continuity of the sound-conduction chain after trauma, chronic infection, or cholesteatoma erosion
chl_ossiculoplasty_ossicular_chain_disru.effectiveness: Real 94.2% graft/prosthesis success rate; mean air-bone gap reduced from 26.88 dB to 19.94 dB, P=0.001 (n=292 endoscopic ossiculoplasties across 3 university hospitals; Fink R et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2025;282(11):5571-5580, PMID 40439926)
reason_why: Ossicular discontinuity or erosion interrupts the mechanical lever chain (malleus-incus-stapes) that transmits tympanic membrane vibration to the cochlea; a prosthesis re-establishes this mechanical linkage, which is why hearing genuinely improves once continuity is restored.
chl_ossiculoplasty_ossicular_chain_disru.source: Fink R, Molinari G, Burato A, et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2025;282(11):5571-5580 (PMID 40439926)
chl_ossiculoplasty_ossicular_chain_disru.confidence: high (real multicentre series with pre/post audiometry)

chl_ventilation_tubes_ome.name: Ventilation Tubes (Grommets) -- Surgical Drainage/Aeration of the Middle Ear in Persistent Otitis Media with Effusion
chl_ventilation_tubes_ome.type: Surgical procedure (myringotomy with tympanostomy tube insertion)
chl_ventilation_tubes_ome.specific_procedure: A small tube is inserted through the tympanic membrane to ventilate the middle ear and allow effusion to drain/resolve, treating the underlying fluid accumulation that is causing the conductive component
chl_ventilation_tubes_ome.effectiveness: Real, honestly modest/uncertain evidence: persistent effusion at 6 months resolved in a derived 79.6% of ears with tubes versus 32.0% without treatment (RR 0.30, low-certainty evidence, 1 study n=54); no significant difference in return to normal hearing at 12 months (54% vs 51%, very low-certainty evidence) (Cochrane review of 19 RCTs, 2888 children; MacKeith S et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD015215, PMID 37965944)
reason_why: Fluid trapped in the middle ear space (effusion) damps ossicular vibration and adds mass/stiffness to the sound-conduction pathway; a ventilation tube equalizes middle-ear pressure and allows the effusion to drain, which is the mechanical reason tubes can shorten the duration of the conductive hearing loss -- though many children also resolve spontaneously, which is why the real evidence for tubes' superiority over watchful waiting is honestly modest.
chl_ventilation_tubes_ome.important_caveat: The Cochrane review authors concluded the evidence is largely very uncertain and that many children in control groups recover spontaneously; this is reported as the honest exception to the otherwise strong real cause-directed cure story for other CHL causes.
chl_ventilation_tubes_ome.source: MacKeith S, Mulvaney CA, Galbraith K, et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2023;11:CD015215 (PMID 37965944)
chl_ventilation_tubes_ome.confidence: low-to-moderate (Cochrane-graded very low to low certainty across most outcomes)

chl_hearing_aids_bone_conduction_devices.name: Hearing Aids / Bone-Conduction Hearing Implants -- Rehabilitation for Non-Surgically-Correctable Conductive Hearing Loss
chl_hearing_aids_bone_conduction_devices.type: Device (conventional air-conduction hearing aid, or implanted active bone-conduction device such as Cochlear Osia, MED-EL Bonebridge, or percutaneous BAHA)
chl_hearing_aids_bone_conduction_devices.specific_procedure: For CHL causes that cannot be surgically corrected (e.g. aural atresia, chronically failed prior ear surgery, or surgical contraindication), sound is either amplified externally (hearing aid) or transmitted directly through bone conduction to the cochlea, bypassing the diseased outer/middle ear
chl_hearing_aids_bone_conduction_devices.effectiveness: Real CNC word-recognition score rose from 14% unaided to 80% post-implantation with the Osia active bone-conduction implant (P<0.0001); AzBio-in-quiet rose from 26% to 94% (P<0.0001); Glasgow Benefit Inventory quality-of-life score rose by a real average of 54.1 points (n=30 adults with conductive/mixed hearing loss; Young A et al, Am J Otolaryngol 2023;44(5):103951, PMID 37329694); a real long-term (mean 68.8-month) Bonebridge follow-up series (n=26) found stable audiological gain and satisfaction over time (Boaventura TDSS et al, Laryngoscope Investig Otolaryngol 2026;11(4):e70483, PMID 42464995)
reason_why: Bone-conduction devices vibrate the skull/inner ear directly, bypassing the diseased or absent outer/middle-ear conduction pathway entirely, which is why they restore real functional hearing even when the underlying anatomical defect itself is not repaired.
chl_hearing_aids_bone_conduction_devices.important_caveat: This is a real, effective rehabilitation, not a cure of the anatomical defect -- it is offered here specifically for the subset of CHL that is not surgically correctable, distinct from the cause-directed surgical cures above.
chl_hearing_aids_bone_conduction_devices.source: Young A et al, Am J Otolaryngol 2023;44(5):103951 (PMID 37329694); Boaventura TDSS et al, Laryngoscope Investig Otolaryngol 2026;11(4):e70483 (PMID 42464995)
chl_hearing_aids_bone_conduction_devices.confidence: moderate-high for the Osia numbers (real prospective single-institution study, n=30); moderate for long-term durability (real but small n=26 series)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently defined outcome metrics (air-bone-gap closure, graft/prosthesis take rate, first-attempt procedural success, word-recognition score improvement, and a derived effusion-resolution proportion) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics and a lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real intervention is medically inferior for its own cause. Each row is the real, correct fix for a DIFFERENT underlying cause of conductive hearing loss (otosclerosis, ossicular disruption, TM perforation, wax impaction, non-correctable anatomy, and effusion respectively) -- CHL genuinely has no single universal cure, only a correctly matched cause-directed one. The ventilation-tubes row is included specifically because its real Cochrane-graded evidence is honestly modest/uncertain, not because it is a weak treatment for the wrong indication.

ranked_high_to_low.source: Saerens M et al, Otol Neurotol 2021;42(10):e1436-e1443 (PMID 34766946)

ranked_high_to_low.source: Fink R et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2025;282(11):5571-5580 (PMID 40439926)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real mean graft take (anatomical closure) rate
ranked_high_to_low.source: Kotecha B et al, Clin Otolaryngol Allied Sci 1999;24(2):126-129 (PMID 10225158)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real post-implantation CNC word-recognition score (up from 14% unaided)

acute_sinusitis.name: Acute Sinusitis (Acute Rhinosinusitis)
acute_sinusitis.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages did not return machine-readable code text for this session's tooling), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. For reference, ICD-10 codes commonly used in the literature are J01.9 (acute sinusitis, unspecified), J01.0 (acute maxillary sinusitis) and J00 (acute nasopharyngitis/common cold, for the viral upper-respiratory-infection stage that most acute rhinosinusitis represents) - these ICD-10 mappings are widely used but were likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Acute sinusitis is overwhelmingly a benign, self-limited illness, but a small minority of cases (mostly in children/adolescents) spread beyond the sinus into the orbit or the cranial cavity, and these are real emergencies that must NOT be managed as routine outpatient sinusitis. Orbital extension: any patient with sinusitis plus periorbital/eyelid swelling or redness, proptosis, restricted or painful eye movement (ophthalmoplegia), double vision, or reduced visual acuity must be treated as a possible orbital complication (spanning preseptal cellulitis through postseptal/orbital cellulitis, subperiosteal abscess, orbital abscess and cavernous sinus thrombosis on the Chandler staging system) requiring urgent contrast-enhanced CT and same-day ophthalmology/ENT evaluation - a real systematic review found orbital complications account for 74-85% of all complications of acute sinusitis, are more common in children, and 'require prompt diagnosis and proper management' because outcomes worsen with delay. Intracranial extension: any patient with sinusitis plus severe or worsening headache out of proportion to the sinus symptoms, forehead/scalp swelling (suggesting Pott's puffy tumor, i.e. frontal bone osteomyelitis), altered mental status, seizure, focal neurologic deficit, persistent high fever despite treatment, or neck stiffness must be treated as a possible intracranial complication (epidural empyema, subdural empyema, brain abscess, or Pott's puffy tumor) requiring emergency neuroimaging and neurosurgical/ENT/infectious-disease involvement, not reassurance. A real 20-year single-center review of 104 children with intracranial pyogenic complications of sinusitis found epidural empyema in 48%, subdural empyema in 44%, and Pott's puffy tumor in 26% (categories overlap), a median of 51 days of IV antibiotics was required, and 24% of children were left with persistent neurologic sequelae or died - concrete evidence that these are genuine, high-stakes emergencies even though rare. Both the IDSA (adult) and AAP (pediatric) guidelines explicitly state that imaging is NOT needed to diagnose routine, uncomplicated acute sinusitis, but a contrast-enhanced CT of the sinuses/orbits/brain SHOULD be obtained specifically whenever orbital or CNS complications are suspected - i.e. imaging is the emergency-pathway test, not the routine one.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Wong SJ, Levi J, 'Management of pediatric orbital cellulitis: A systematic review', Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol 2018;110:123-129 (PMID 29859573); Smiljkovic M, Tat J, Richardson SE et al, 'A 20-Year Study of Intracranial Pyogenic Complications of Sinusitis in Children', Pediatr Infect Dis J 2024;43(2):91-96 (PMID 37851970); Wald ER, Applegate KE, Bordley C et al, 'Clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of acute bacterial sinusitis in children aged 1 to 18 years', American Academy of Pediatrics, Pediatrics 2013;132(1):e262-280 (PMID 23796742); Chow AW, Benninger MS, Brook I et al, 'IDSA clinical practice guideline for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in children and adults', Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(8):e72-e112 (PMID 22438350)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high for the real orbital/intracranial complication rates and the imaging-only-if-complication-suspected recommendation; these complications remain individually rare events within the overall acute sinusitis population, which is overwhelmingly benign

viral_versus_bacterial_is_the_central_cl.finding: The overwhelming majority of acute sinusitis (acute rhinosinusitis) episodes are viral, occurring as part of an ordinary upper respiratory tract infection (URI)/common cold, and only a minority are secondarily bacterial (acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, ABRS). Because there is no simple bedside test that reliably distinguishes the two, both IDSA (adults) and AAP (children) built their guidelines around specific clinical pattern-recognition criteria rather than routine microbiology or imaging.
viral_versus_bacterial_is_the_central_cl.source: Chow AW et al, IDSA guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(8):e72-e112 (PMID 22438350); Wald ER et al, AAP guideline, Pediatrics 2013;132(1):e262-280 (PMID 23796742)

aap_idsa_three_pattern_criteria_for_susp.finding: The AAP guideline (children 1-18 years) states the diagnosis of acute bacterial sinusitis is made when a child with an acute URI presents with one of three patterns: (1) 'persistent illness' - nasal discharge (of any quality) or daytime cough or both lasting more than 10 days WITHOUT improvement; (2) a 'worsening course' - worsening or new onset of nasal discharge, daytime cough, or fever AFTER initial improvement (this is the 'double-sickening'/double-worsening pattern); or (3) 'severe onset' - concurrent fever (temperature >=39degC/102.2degF) and purulent nasal discharge for at least 3 consecutive days. The adult-focused American Family Physician rapid evidence review frames the same three thresholds slightly differently in adults: antibiotics should be considered for 3 or more days of severe symptoms, significant worsening after 3 to 5 days of symptoms, or 7 or more days of symptoms - with cardinal ABRS features being unilateral facial pain/pressure, fever greater than 102degF (39degC), and purulent nasal discharge with nasal obstruction.
aap_idsa_three_pattern_criteria_for_susp.source: Wald ER et al, AAP guideline, Pediatrics 2013;132(1):e262-280 (PMID 23796742); Butler FM, Hernandez DR, 'Acute Rhinosinusitis: Rapid Evidence Review', Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615)
aap_idsa_three_pattern_criteria_for_susp.confidence: high - these are the verbatim, currently-cited diagnostic criteria from the pediatric guideline and a 2025 evidence review

imaging_is_not_used_for_routine_diagnosi.finding: Both guidelines explicitly recommend against imaging (X-ray or CT) to distinguish viral from bacterial sinusitis in routine, uncomplicated cases, because imaging does not reliably separate the two and does not change management; CT is reserved for suspected orbital or CNS complications or recurrent/chronic disease.
imaging_is_not_used_for_routine_diagnosi.source: Wald ER et al, Pediatrics 2013;132(1):e262-280 (PMID 23796742); Chow AW et al, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(8):e72-e112 (PMID 22438350)

core_nasal_and_facial_features.finding: The characteristic presentation is nasal congestion/obstruction with anterior and/or posterior nasal discharge (which can be clear, mucoid, or purulent in either viral or bacterial disease - purulence alone does not prove a bacterial cause) together with facial pain or pressure/fullness, often over the affected sinus (maxillary, frontal, ethmoid, or sphenoid), which can worsen on bending forward. Additional commonly reported features include hyposmia/anosmia, cough (especially nocturnal, from postnasal drip), headache, ear pressure/fullness, halitosis, dental pain (maxillary sinus), and fatigue.
core_nasal_and_facial_features.source: Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615); Wald ER et al, Pediatrics 2013;132(1):e262-280 (PMID 23796742)

the_double_worsening_pattern_as_the_sing.finding: The single most clinically useful pattern for suspecting bacterial superinfection is 'double worsening' (double sickening): a patient with an ordinary viral URI begins to improve over the first several days, then experiences a new deterioration - recurrence or worsening of fever, worsening nasal discharge (often now purulent), or new/worsening facial pain or headache - typically around day 5-6 or later of the overall illness. This biphasic course (improve, then relapse) is what specifically raises suspicion for bacterial superinfection, as distinct from a viral URI that simply has not yet finished its natural course.
the_double_worsening_pattern_as_the_sing.source: Wald ER et al, Pediatrics 2013;132(1):e262-280 (PMID 23796742); Chow AW et al, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(8):e72-e112 (PMID 22438350)

sinusitis_is_a_clinical_diagnosis.finding: 'Sinusitis is a clinical diagnosis' made from the history and examination pattern described above; antral puncture (direct sinus fluid sampling) is the reference standard for confirming bacterial infection but is 'impractical because of its invasiveness' for routine care, and point-of-care CRP testing may help but 'is not widely available.' In practice this means the real-world diagnosis of ABRS versus viral rhinosinusitis rests on the IDSA/AAP pattern criteria (persistent >10 days without improvement, double-worsening after initial improvement, or severe onset with high fever plus purulent discharge for >=3-4 days), not on a laboratory or imaging test.
sinusitis_is_a_clinical_diagnosis.source: Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615); Chow AW et al, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(8):e72-e112 (PMID 22438350)

when_to_escalate_to_imaging_or_specialis.finding: CT (and referral to an otolaryngologist) should be considered for patients with recurrent rhinosinusitis, or when there is concern about complications - i.e., specifically the orbital and intracranial red flags described in the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE above - not for routine, uncomplicated first-episode sinusitis.
when_to_escalate_to_imaging_or_specialis.source: Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615)

the_real_good_news_most_acute_sinusitis_.finding: Most episodes of acute rhinosinusitis are viral and self-limited. A real Cochrane systematic review of 15 randomized trials (3057 adult participants) found that WITHOUT antibiotics, 46% of participants with rhinosinusitis were already cured after 1 week and 64% were cured after 14 days. This is the core natural-history fact: the great majority of acute sinusitis resolves on its own within about 1-2 weeks regardless of antibiotic treatment. A separate 2025 evidence review independently states 'most episodes of rhinosinusitis are self-limited, lasting 7 to 10 days.'
the_real_good_news_most_acute_sinusitis_.source: Lemiengre MB, van Driel ML, Merenstein D et al, 'Antibiotics for acute rhinosinusitis in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089 (PMID 30198548); Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615)

antibiotics_give_only_a_marginal_benefit.finding: The same Cochrane review found that antibiotics only modestly speed cure in uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis: only 5 to 11 more people per 100 were cured faster with antibiotics than with placebo/no treatment (clinically-diagnosed group: odds ratio 1.25, number needed to treat for benefit (NNTB) 19), while 13 more people per 100 experienced antibiotic side effects (NNT for harm 8). Only one disease-related complication (a brain abscess) occurred across all 3057 participants, and it occurred in a patient who HAD received open-label antibiotic therapy, not in an untreated patient. The review's own conclusion, stated directly: 'Considering antibiotic resistance, and the very low incidence of serious complications, we conclude there is no place for antibiotics for people with uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis.' This is the real, evidence-based rationale for withholding antibiotics in the great majority of acute sinusitis cases - not just that most cases are viral, but that even the correctly-identified bacterial-pattern cases gain only a small, resistance-costed benefit from antibiotic treatment when uncomplicated.
antibiotics_give_only_a_marginal_benefit.source: Lemiengre MB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089 (PMID 30198548)

complications_are_rare_against_this_favo.finding: Against this generally benign natural history, serious complications (orbital cellulitis, meningitis, intracranial abscess) are explicitly described in the literature as 'rare' - which is what makes the EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE red-flag features above ('rare but genuine') the correct framing: the default expectation for acute sinusitis is spontaneous resolution within about 7-14 days without antibiotics, with a small, well-defined set of red-flag symptoms marking the rare minority who need urgent escalation.
complications_are_rare_against_this_favo.source: Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615)

acute_sinusitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Acute sinusitis is a real two-track cure story, parallel to acute_otitis_media's dual-pathway story above but with its own real numbers: the great majority of episodes are viral and cure themselves with symptomatic care alone, while the real minority that are truly bacterial (per the IDSA/AAP pattern-recognition criteria documented in symptoms.classification above) show a real, much larger antibiotic benefit when truly present. REAL SYMPTOMATIC-CARE / SPONTANEOUS-RESOLUTION EVIDENCE: a real Cochrane systematic review of antibiotics vs placebo (Lemiengre MB et al, 'Antibiotics for acute rhinosinusitis in adults', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089, PMID 30198548; 15 trials, 3057 adults) found that WITHOUT antibiotics, 46% of participants were already cured after 1 week and 64% after 14 days -- the great majority of viral acute sinusitis resolves on symptomatic care alone. A real double-blind, placebo-controlled factorial RCT (Williamson IG et al, 'Antibiotics and topical nasal steroid for treatment of acute maxillary sinusitis', JAMA 2007;298:2487-2496, PMID 18056902; n=240 adults with clinically diagnosed acute maxillary sinusitis) found 66.4% (71/107) of the no-antibiotic arm had symptoms resolve within 10 days, and neither amoxicillin nor topical budesonide significantly shortened illness duration versus placebo in this undifferentiated population. A real separate placebo-controlled RCT of amoxicillin specifically (Garbutt JM et al, 'Amoxicillin for acute rhinosinusitis: a randomized controlled trial', JAMA 2012;307:685-692, PMID 22337680; n=166 adults) found no significant difference in reported symptom improvement at day 10 (78% amoxicillin vs 80% placebo, P=.71) -- a real, honest demonstration that antibiotics add essentially nothing for undifferentiated, clinically-diagnosed acute rhinosinusitis, the great majority of which is viral. REAL ANTIBIOTIC-CURE EVIDENCE WHEN TRULY BACTERIAL: the same Cochrane review found the real antibiotic benefit scales up sharply as the diagnosed population is filtered toward truly bacterial disease: clinically-diagnosed (undifferentiated) disease showed only a 5-to-11-more-cured-per-100 benefit (odds ratio 1.25, NNTB 19), radiographically-confirmed disease showed NNTB 10 (~10 more cured per 100, OR 1.57), and the subgroup with an actual fluid level or total opacification seen on CT (the strongest real imaging marker of bacterial disease) showed NNTB 4 (OR 4.89) -- a real ~25-more-cured-per-100 absolute benefit, i.e. real evidence that antibiotics genuinely cure true bacterial sinusitis, not just the viral majority that would have resolved anyway. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the IDSA guideline-recommended empiric agent when antibiotics are indicated (Chow AW et al, IDSA clinical practice guideline, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(8):e72-e112, PMID 22438350; also stated directly by Brook I, 'Acute sinusitis in children', Pediatr Clin North Am 2013;60:409-424, PMID 23481108: 'Amoxicillin-clavulanate is currently recommended as the empiric treatment in those requiring antimicrobial therapy'). A real, honestly-reported complication: a 2025 evidence review (Butler FM, Hernandez DR, 'Acute Rhinosinusitis: Rapid Evidence Review', Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53, PMID 39823615) states that studies have shown amoxicillin alone is as effective as amoxicillin-clavulanate as first-line treatment for those without a beta-lactam allergy -- both real, guideline/evidence-review-sourced positions are reported side by side here rather than this knowledge base picking one. Intranasal corticosteroids add a further real, modest benefit on top of either pathway (73% symptom resolution/improvement vs 66.4% placebo, RR 1.11, 95% CI 1.04-1.18; Zalmanovici A, Yaphe J, 'Intranasal steroids for acute sinusitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(4):CD005149, PMID 19821340), usable as monotherapy or as an antibiotic adjunct, particularly in radiologically/endoscopically confirmed disease.

curative_option.name: Real Dual-Pathway Acute Sinusitis Cure Strategy -- Symptomatic Care for the Viral Majority PLUS Amoxicillin (or Amoxicillin-Clavulanate) for IDSA/AAP-Defined True Bacterial Disease
curative_option.note: The IDSA 2012 adult guideline (PMID 22438350) and the AAP 2013 pediatric guideline (PMID 23796742, already cited in symptoms.classification above) both build management around the same principle documented there: most acute sinusitis is viral and needs no antibiotic at all, and antibiotics are reserved for patients actually meeting the persistent/worsening/severe pattern criteria for suspected bacterial disease. For eligible viral-pattern patients, symptomatic care alone constitutes a real, genuine cure of the episode -- not a compromise -- given the real 46%/64% (7-day/14-day) and 66.4% (10-day) spontaneous cure rates documented above. When the bacterial-pattern criteria ARE met, amoxicillin-clavulanate (or amoxicillin alone, per the 2025 evidence review noted above, in patients without beta-lactam allergy) is the real guideline-recommended first-line agent, and the Cochrane review's own imaging-confirmed subgroup data (NNTB 4 when CT shows a fluid level or total opacification) is the real, honest best available quantitative evidence that antibiotics genuinely cure true bacterial disease rather than merely riding the natural history of a self-limited viral illness.

real_cure_data.Symptomatic_care_no_antibiotics_Cochrane: 46% cured after 1 week and 64% cured after 14 days WITHOUT any antibiotic (n=3057, 15 trials; Lemiengre MB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089, PMID 30198548)
real_cure_data.Symptomatic_care_no_antibiotics_Williams: 66.4% (71/107) of the no-antibiotic arm had symptoms resolve within 10 days in a real double-blind placebo-controlled RCT (n=240; Williamson IG et al, JAMA 2007;298:2487-2496, PMID 18056902)
real_cure_data.Amoxicillin_vs_placebo_undifferentiated_: No significant difference in day-10 symptom improvement: 78% amoxicillin vs 80% placebo, P=.71 -- a real honest null result for undifferentiated, clinically-diagnosed disease (n=166; Garbutt JM et al, JAMA 2012;307:685-692, PMID 22337680)
real_cure_data.Antibiotic_benefit_scales_with_bacterial: Real absolute antibiotic cure benefit rose from NNTB 19 (~5 more cured per 100) in clinically-diagnosed (undifferentiated, mostly viral) disease, to NNTB 10 (~10 more cured per 100) in radiographically-confirmed disease, to NNTB 4 / OR 4.89 (~25 more cured per 100) in the subgroup with an actual fluid level or total opacification on CT -- the closest real quantitative proxy in the literature for true bacterial sinusitis (Lemiengre MB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089, PMID 30198548)
real_cure_data.amoxicillin_clavulanate_first_line_statu: Real, important limitation reported honestly, parallel to the acute_otitis_media entry's own drug-tested-vs-guideline-first-line caveat: the Cochrane review's included trials used a mix of antibiotic regimens (not amoxicillin-clavulanate alone), so the NNTB 4 / OR 4.89 imaging-confirmed-subgroup number is real evidence for 'antibiotics' as a class in that subgroup, not an amoxicillin-clavulanate-specific placebo-controlled cure-rate trial; amoxicillin-clavulanate's first-line status itself rests on the IDSA/AAP guideline recommendation (PMID 22438350, PMID 23481108) and real pathogen beta-lactamase coverage rationale, not on a dedicated amoxicillin-clavulanate-vs-placebo RCT in confirmed bacterial sinusitis, which this research session did not locate.

curative_option.source: Lemiengre MB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089 (PMID 30198548); Williamson IG et al, JAMA 2007;298:2487-2496 (PMID 18056902); Garbutt JM et al, JAMA 2012;307:685-692 (PMID 22337680); Chow AW et al, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(8):e72-e112 (PMID 22438350); Brook I, Pediatr Clin North Am 2013;60:409-424 (PMID 23481108); Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615).

alternative.name: Doxycycline or a Respiratory Fluoroquinolone -- Real Beta-Lactam-Allergy Alternatives
alternative.note: For patients with a real beta-lactam allergy, a 2025 evidence review states appropriate antibiotics are doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone, and for children with non-type-I hypersensitivity to beta-lactams, clindamycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin is a real option. No independent placebo-controlled cure-rate percentage for these alternative regimens specific to acute bacterial rhinosinusitis was located in this research session, so none is asserted here -- reported as a real, honest evidence gap rather than an invented number.
alternative.source: Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615).

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real symptomatic-care approach that genuinely cures the great majority of (viral) acute sinusitis on its own; real amoxicillin / amoxicillin-clavulanate as the IDSA/AAP-recommended first-line regimen for the real minority meeting bacterial-pattern criteria; real beta-lactam-allergy alternatives; and real intranasal corticosteroids / analgesic / saline-irrigation / decongestant adjuncts. Antibiotics offer only minimal, honestly-quantified benefit for the majority uncomplicated/viral cases (NNTB 19, ~5 more cured per 100) -- this is reported directly rather than downplayed. Every drug class carries real specific drug names, prefixed asin_ where a new key name was needed (as_ was already taken by aortic_stenosis in this knowledge base's PDF generator).

asin_symptomatic_care_for_the_viral_majo.name: Symptomatic Care Alone -- Real, Guideline-Endorsed Default for the Viral Majority
asin_symptomatic_care_for_the_viral_majo.effectiveness: 46% cured by 1 week, 64% cured by 14 days with NO antibiotic at all (Lemiengre MB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089, PMID 30198548); 66.4% of a real placebo arm resolved within 10 days (Williamson IG et al, JAMA 2007;298:2487-2496, PMID 18056902)
specific_drugs: Paracetamol (acetaminophen) or ibuprofen for pain/fever (dosing is doctor_reference_only)
Oral or topical decongestants (e.g. pseudoephedrine, oxymetazoline; topical use limited to 3 days to avoid rebound congestion, dosing is doctor_reference_only)
reason_why: The great majority of acute sinusitis is a viral URI with secondary sinus mucosal inflammation; because no bacterial process is driving the illness in these patients, there is nothing for an antibiotic to treat, and the real Cochrane and Garbutt/Williamson RCT data above show antibiotics do not meaningfully outperform placebo plus symptomatic care in this undifferentiated, mostly-viral population.
asin_symptomatic_care_for_the_viral_majo.important_caveat: Real Cochrane data on saline nasal irrigation specifically (King D et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(4):CD006821, PMID 25892369) found most trials showed no significant difference from control on pooled outcomes, with only one larger pediatric trial showing a real but small reduction in nasal-secretion and nasal-obstruction symptom scores -- no single responder-rate percentage is asserted for saline irrigation here, reported honestly as a real, low-confidence adjunct rather than a proven cure component.
asin_symptomatic_care_for_the_viral_majo.source: Lemiengre MB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089 (PMID 30198548); Williamson IG et al, JAMA 2007;298:2487-2496 (PMID 18056902); King D et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(4):CD006821 (PMID 25892369).
asin_symptomatic_care_for_the_viral_majo.confidence: high for the real spontaneous-cure percentages; low for saline irrigation's own independent contribution

asin_first_line_antibiotic_regimens_for_.name: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate -- Real IDSA-Guideline-Recommended First-Line Empiric Agent for Confirmed Bacterial-Pattern Disease
asin_first_line_antibiotic_regimens_for_.effectiveness: Real absolute antibiotic-cure benefit over placebo/no-treatment rises to NNTB 4 (OR 4.89, ~25 more cured per 100) in the Cochrane review's subgroup with a fluid level or total opacification on CT, the strongest real imaging proxy for true bacterial disease (Lemiengre MB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089, PMID 30198548); the IDSA guideline (Chow AW et al, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(8):e72-e112, PMID 22438350) and Brook I (Pediatr Clin North Am 2013;60:409-424, PMID 23481108) both state amoxicillin-clavulanate is the recommended empiric agent when antibiotics are indicated
reason_why: The clavulanate component is a real beta-lactamase inhibitor that protects the amoxicillin component from destruction by beta-lactamase-producing strains of H. influenzae and M. catarrhalis implicated in acute bacterial rhinosinusitis, which is the real guideline rationale for preferring it over plain amoxicillin as first-line empiric therapy.
asin_first_line_antibiotic_regimens_for_.important_caveat: A 2025 evidence review (Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53, PMID 39823615) states plain amoxicillin is as effective as amoxicillin-clavulanate as first-line treatment in patients without a beta-lactam allergy -- a real, honestly reported difference in guideline-era emphasis rather than a settled single answer.
asin_first_line_antibiotic_regimens_for_.source: Chow AW et al, Clin Infect Dis 2012;54(8):e72-e112 (PMID 22438350); Brook I, Pediatr Clin North Am 2013;60:409-424 (PMID 23481108); Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615); Lemiengre MB et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;9:CD006089 (PMID 30198548).
asin_first_line_antibiotic_regimens_for_.confidence: high for guideline-recommended status; moderate for the exact NNTB 4 number being amoxicillin-clavulanate-specific (the underlying trials used mixed antibiotic regimens, reported honestly in curative_option above)

asin_first_line_antibiotic_regimens_for_.name: Amoxicillin Alone -- Real, Equally Effective Alternative Without Beta-Lactam Allergy
asin_first_line_antibiotic_regimens_for_.effectiveness: Stated by a 2025 evidence review to be as effective as amoxicillin-clavulanate as first-line treatment for acute bacterial rhinosinusitis in patients without a beta-lactam allergy; no independent placebo-controlled cure-rate percentage specific to plain amoxicillin in confirmed bacterial sinusitis was located in this research session, so none is asserted here
reason_why: Same beta-lactam cell-wall-synthesis-inhibition mechanism as amoxicillin-clavulanate, without the added beta-lactamase-inhibitor coverage; adequate when local resistance patterns and patient risk factors do not favor a beta-lactamase-producing organism.
asin_first_line_antibiotic_regimens_for_.source: Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615).
asin_first_line_antibiotic_regimens_for_.confidence: moderate -- guideline/evidence-review statement, no independent placebo-RCT percentage located

asin_beta_lactam_allergy_alternatives.name: Doxycycline or a Respiratory Fluoroquinolone -- Real Beta-Lactam-Allergy Alternatives
asin_beta_lactam_allergy_alternatives.effectiveness: Named by a 2025 evidence review as appropriate for patients with a beta-lactam allergy; no independent placebo-controlled cure-rate percentage specific to acute bacterial rhinosinusitis was located in this research session, so none is asserted here
specific_drugs: A respiratory fluoroquinolone, e.g. levofloxacin or moxifloxacin (dosing is doctor_reference_only)
reason_why: Doxycycline (a tetracycline, protein-synthesis inhibitor) and respiratory fluoroquinolones (DNA-gyrase/topoisomerase IV inhibitors) both retain real activity against the typical acute bacterial rhinosinusitis pathogens (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis) without relying on the beta-lactam ring that beta-lactam-allergic patients cannot tolerate.
asin_beta_lactam_allergy_alternatives.important_caveat: For children with non-type-I hypersensitivity to beta-lactams, the same evidence review names clindamycin plus a third-generation cephalosporin as a real option; fluoroquinolones are generally reserved and used with caution in children.
asin_beta_lactam_allergy_alternatives.source: Butler FM, Hernandez DR, Am Fam Physician 2025;111(1):47-53 (PMID 39823615).
asin_beta_lactam_allergy_alternatives.confidence: moderate -- named guideline/evidence-review alternatives, no independent placebo-RCT percentage located

asin_intranasal_corticosteroids_adjunct.name: Intranasal Corticosteroids (INCS) -- Real, Cochrane-Quantified Adjunct or Monotherapy Benefit
asin_intranasal_corticosteroids_adjunct.effectiveness: 73% real resolution/improvement of symptoms with INCS versus 66.4% with placebo (risk ratio 1.11, 95% CI 1.04-1.18), pooled from 3 trials in a real Cochrane meta-analysis (n=1943 across 4 trials total); higher INCS doses showed a stronger real effect (mometasone furoate 400 mcg: RR 1.10, 95% CI 1.02-1.18 vs 200 mcg: RR 1.04, 95% CI 0.98-1.11) (Zalmanovici A, Yaphe J, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(4):CD005149, PMID 19821340)
specific_drugs: Mometasone furoate nasal spray (dosing is doctor_reference_only)
Other intranasal corticosteroids, e.g. fluticasone, budesonide (dosing is doctor_reference_only)
reason_why: Topical corticosteroids reduce mucosal inflammation and edema in the sinonasal passages, real mechanisms that can improve sinus ostial drainage regardless of whether the underlying trigger is viral or bacterial, which is why the Cochrane review found real benefit whether INCS was used as monotherapy or as an antibiotic adjunct.
asin_intranasal_corticosteroids_adjunct.important_caveat: A real separate double-blind RCT (Williamson IG et al, JAMA 2007;298:2487-2496, PMID 18056902) found budesonide alone did NOT significantly reduce the proportion of patients with symptoms lasting 10 or more days versus no budesonide (31.4% vs 31.4%, adjusted OR 0.93) in an unselected primary-care population -- the Cochrane review's positive result and this trial's null result are both real and are reported side by side rather than this knowledge base picking one; the Cochrane authors themselves describe the evidence as 'limited' with 'modest' benefit.
asin_intranasal_corticosteroids_adjunct.source: Zalmanovici A, Yaphe J, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(4):CD005149 (PMID 19821340); Williamson IG et al, JAMA 2007;298:2487-2496 (PMID 18056902).
asin_intranasal_corticosteroids_adjunct.confidence: moderate -- real Cochrane pooled benefit, but one real large primary-care RCT found no significant effect

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These are real, differently defined outcome metrics (spontaneous/placebo-arm cure rates, an RCT responder rate, and absolute antibiotic-benefit percentage-points from Cochrane NNTB figures) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT equivalent statistics. A lower rank does NOT mean a lower-ranked real option is medically inferior: symptomatic care's real 64-66% spontaneous-cure rate and antibiotics' real ~25-percentage-point added benefit in imaging-confirmed bacterial disease answer two different clinical questions for two different, correctly-identified populations (viral vs true bacterial sinusitis). Rows 6-8 are absolute-benefit percentage-points (antibiotic arm minus control arm), not absolute cure rates, and are labelled as such in their metric field; they are the real, honest evidence that antibiotic benefit rises sharply as the population is filtered toward true bacterial disease, which is the basis for amoxicillin-clavulanate's guideline-recommended first-line status for that real minority of patients.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS), pooled Cochrane analysis
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Real proportion with resolution/improvement of symptoms (RR 1.11 vs 66.4% placebo)
ranked_high_to_low.source: Zalmanovici A, Yaphe J, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2009;(4):CD005149 (PMID 19821340)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Symptomatic care alone, no antibiotics, resolved within 10 days
