A distinct, real subgroup is aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD, historically 'Samter's triad'): the clinical triad of asthma, nasal polyps/CRSwNP, and respiratory reactions (bronchospasm, rhinorrhoea) precipitated by aspirin/NSAIDs (COX-1 inhibitors), first characterised by Samter M and Beers RF, 'Intolerance to aspirin: clinical studies and consideration of its pathogenesis,' Ann Intern Med 1968;68:975-983 (PMID 5646829). AERD patients characteristically have severe, recurrent, treatment-refractory nasal polyposis with rapid polyp regrowth after surgery, and require specific recognition (oral aspirin/NSAID avoidance or supervised aspirin desensitisation under specialist care) distinct from routine CRSwNP management (Buchheit KM et al, 'The importance of timely diagnosis of aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease for patient health and safety,' World J Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2020;6:203-208, PMID 33336174). EPOS2020 (PMID 32077450) devotes a dedicated chapter to aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease as a distinct CRS-related entity.
natural_history.real_treatment_response_context_not_this: Symptom-side note only (full treatment/curability detail is a separate fork's scope): unlike most chronic upper-airway disease, CRSwNP now has real, randomised-trial-proven disease-modifying options at both ends of the severity spectrum. For severe, Type-2 CRSwNP refractory to standard therapy, the anti-IL-4Ralpha biologic dupilumab produced, at 24 weeks versus placebo, a least-squares mean difference in nasal polyp score of -2.06 (95% CI -2.43 to -1.69, p<0.0001) in SINUS-24 and -1.80 (-2.10 to -1.51, p<0.0001) in SINUS-52, nasal congestion/obstruction score differences of -0.89 and -0.87 respectively (both p<0.0001), and Lund-Mackay CT score differences of -7.44 and -5.13 respectively (both p<0.0001) (Bachert C et al, Lancet 2019;394:1638-1650, PMID 31543428; consistent with the earlier phase 2 result in Bachert C et al, JAMA 2016;315:469-479, PMID 26836729). For medically-refractory CRS more broadly, endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) is the established real high-success-rate procedural option. These are documented here only to correctly frame CRS's real natural history as a condition with genuine disease-modifying solutions available, not to duplicate the dedicated treatment-side entry.
natural_history.source: Fokkens WJ et al, EPOS2020, Rhinology 2020;58(Suppl S29):1-464, PMID 32077450; Tomassen P et al, J Allergy Clin Immunol 2016;137:1449-1456, PMID 26949058; Samter M, Beers RF, Ann Intern Med 1968;68:975-983, PMID 5646829; Buchheit KM et al, World J Otorhinolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2020;6:203-208, PMID 33336174; Bachert C et al, Lancet 2019;394:1638-1650, PMID 31543428; Bachert C et al, JAMA 2016;315:469-479, PMID 26836729
natural_history.confidence: high

chronic_rhinosinusitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS) - inflammation of the nose and paranasal sinuses persisting 12 weeks or longer, occurring with (CRSwNP) or without (CRSsNP) nasal polyps - is NOT curable in the sense of permanently erasing the underlying mucosal inflammatory tendency (type 2/eosinophilic in most CRSwNP; mixed/non-type-2 in much CRSsNP), but two real interventions produce dramatic, trial-proven improvement that goes well beyond ordinary day-to-day symptom suppression: IL-4/IL-13-blocking biologic therapy in CRSwNP, and endoscopic sinus surgery (ESS) for disease that has failed medical therapy. Dupilumab, a fully human monoclonal antibody blocking the shared IL-4 receptor alpha subunit used by both IL-4 and IL-13, was tested in two pivotal multinational randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 3 trials - LIBERTY NP SINUS-24 and LIBERTY NP SINUS-52 - in adults with severe CRSwNP who had already failed intranasal corticosteroids, systemic corticosteroids, and/or sinus surgery (Bachert C et al., Lancet 2019;394:1638-1650, PMID 31543428). At 24 weeks, dupilumab reduced the bilateral endoscopic Nasal Polyp Score (standard 0-8 scale, 0-4 per nostril) by a least-squares mean of 2.06 points more than placebo in SINUS-24 (95% CI -2.43 to -1.69; p<0.0001) and 1.80 points more in SINUS-52 (95% CI -2.10 to -1.51; p<0.0001) - 25.8% and 22.5% of the full 8-point scale, computed 2.06/8 and 1.80/8. Sinus opacification on CT (Lund-Mackay score, standard 0-24 scale) improved 7.44 points more than placebo in SINUS-24 (95% CI -8.35 to -6.53; p<0.0001) - 31.0% of the 24-point scale, computed 7.44/24 - and nasal congestion/obstruction severity (standard 0-3 daily symptom scale) improved 0.89 points more than placebo in SINUS-24 (95% CI -1.07 to -0.71; p<0.0001) - 29.7% of the 3-point scale, computed 0.89/3. These are real, dramatic, disease-altering reductions in polyp burden and sinus opacification, large enough that dupilumab is now used specifically to avoid or defer repeat sinus surgery in patients who would otherwise need it. Endoscopic sinus surgery is the second real, high-success option, reserved for CRS (with or without polyps) that stays symptomatic despite medical therapy. In the largest published outcome dataset, the prospective English National Comparative Audit of Surgery for Nasal Polyposis and Chronic Rhinosinusitis followed 3,128 patients who underwent ESS; among the 1,459 (52.2%) with 5-year follow-up, the mean Sino-Nasal Outcome Test-22 (SNOT-22) score was 28.2 at 5 years, described in the paper as 'a 14-point improvement over the baseline score' - a baseline of approximately 42.2 (computed 28.2+14) and therefore a 33.2% reduction (computed 14/42.2) that was durable, essentially unchanged from the 3-month result (25.5), showing the benefit does not fade over time (Hopkins C et al., Laryngoscope 2009;119:2459-2465, PMID 19780032). Revision surgery was needed in 19.1% of the 5-year respondents (20.6% of polyp patients vs 15.5% of CRS-alone patients), and this is the honest boundary of surgical benefit here - most patients get large, lasting symptom relief, but roughly one in five eventually needs a further operation. REAL WORKING SOLUTION for the person who actually has CRS: (1) confirm the diagnosis endoscopically and/or radiologically and classify as CRSwNP or CRSsNP per EPOS2020 criteria (Fokkens WJ et al., Rhinology 2020, PMID 32226949); (2) start first-line medical therapy - a daily intranasal corticosteroid plus regular high-volume saline irrigation - which is real, guideline-first-line, and produces a documented 178% higher chance of symptom improvement versus placebo/no treatment (relative risk 2.78, 95% CI 1.76-4.40, 109 participants, computed (2.78-1)x100; Chong LY et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016, PMID 27115217); (3) for CRSwNP that stays uncontrolled on maximal medical therapy, or for the patient who wants to avoid or defer another operation, dupilumab is the real, trial-proven, dramatic-improvement option detailed above - omalizumab and mepolizumab are real biologic alternatives with weaker but genuine phase 3 trial support, detailed in exhaustive_medicine_survey; and (4) for disease that remains symptomatic and structurally obstructed despite steps 2-3, endoscopic sinus surgery gives real, durable, high-magnitude relief in the great majority of patients and is the correct definitive step for medically-refractory CRS - it is a proven, guideline-endorsed, high-success real intervention, not a low-expectation last resort.

curative_option.name: Dupilumab (Anti-IL-4Ra Biologic) for Severe CRSwNP - Real Trial-Proven Dramatic Reduction in Nasal Polyp Burden and Sinus Opacification, LIBERTY NP SINUS-24/SINUS-52 Phase 3 Trials; Disease-Modifying in Magnitude for Type 2 CRSwNP, Not a Permanent Cure of the Underlying Eosinophilic/Type-2 Inflammatory Tendency
curative_option.note: Dupilumab is the real special case among CRS treatments for the subset with nasal polyps: every other pharmacologic option in this survey (intranasal corticosteroids, saline irrigation, short-course oral corticosteroids) works only while it is being used and is far smaller in effect size. Dupilumab blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signalling, the key drivers of the type 2 inflammation that builds nasal polyps, and produces polyp-score and sinus-opacification reductions of a magnitude that changes clinical decisions - it is explicitly used to let patients avoid or defer a repeat sinus operation. It is described here as producing real dramatic improvement, and NOT as an absolute cure, because: benefit requires continued dosing (durability after stopping is not established the way it is for allergen immunotherapy in allergic rhinitis), it is approved specifically for CRSwNP (not CRSsNP), and the underlying type 2 inflammatory tendency is suppressed, not eliminated.

real_trial_data.sinus_24_and_sinus_52_coprimary_endpoint: Bachert C et al., 'Efficacy and safety of dupilumab in patients with severe chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (LIBERTY NP SINUS-24 and LIBERTY NP SINUS-52)', Lancet 2019;394:1638-1650 (PMID 31543428): two multinational, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group phase 3 trials, 276 patients (SINUS-24) and 448 patients (SINUS-52) with severe CRSwNP despite prior systemic corticosteroids and/or surgery. At week 24, least-squares mean difference vs placebo in Nasal Polyp Score (0-8 scale) was -2.06 in SINUS-24 (95% CI -2.43 to -1.69; p<0.0001, 25.8% of the scale, computed 2.06/8) and -1.80 in SINUS-52 (95% CI -2.10 to -1.51; p<0.0001, 22.5% of the scale, computed 1.80/8); nasal congestion/obstruction score (0-3 scale) difference was -0.89 in SINUS-24 (95% CI -1.07 to -0.71; p<0.0001, 29.7% of the scale) and -0.87 in SINUS-52 (95% CI -1.03 to -0.71; p<0.0001, 29.0% of the scale); Lund-Mackay sinus CT score (0-24 scale) difference was -7.44 in SINUS-24 (95% CI -8.35 to -6.53; p<0.0001, 31.0% of the scale) and -5.13 in SINUS-52 (95% CI -5.80 to -4.46; p<0.0001, 21.4% of the scale). All coprimary endpoints met statistical significance in both trials; the most common adverse events (nasopharyngitis, headache, epistaxis, injection-site erythema) were more frequent with placebo than dupilumab.

alternative.name: Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (ESS) for Medically-Refractory CRS (With or Without Polyps) - Real, Large-Cohort, Durable High-Magnitude Symptom Relief, English National Comparative Audit
alternative.real_outcome_data: Hopkins C et al., 'Long-term outcomes from the English national comparative audit of surgery for nasal polyposis and chronic rhinosinusitis', Laryngoscope 2009;119:2459-2465 (PMID 19780032): prospective cohort of 3,128 patients undergoing ESS for CRS (with or without polyps) in England and Wales; 1,459 (52.2%) responded at 5-year follow-up. Mean SNOT-22 score was 28.2 at 5 years, 'a 14-point improvement over the baseline score' (baseline approximately 42.2, computed 28.2+14) - a 33.2% reduction (computed 14/42.2) - essentially unchanged from the 3-month result (25.5), 12-month result (27.7) and 36-month result (27.7), indicating no meaningful decline in benefit from 12 to 60 months. Polyp patients reported better 5-year scores (mean 26.2) than CRS-alone patients (mean 33.3). Revision surgery was required in 19.1% of respondents over 5 years (20.6% of polyp patients vs 15.5% of CRS-alone patients); patients who received additional sinus surgery beyond simple polypectomy were significantly less likely to need revision surgery after adjustment for baseline characteristics (adjusted OR 0.66; p=0.04).
alternative.important_caveat: Real high success at the population level, but not universal: roughly one in five patients needs a further operation within 5 years, and about half of the original 3,128-patient cohort did not respond to the 5-year survey (attrition, not necessarily treatment failure). Surgery clears obstructing disease and restores sinus drainage/ventilation; it does not by itself eliminate the underlying mucosal inflammatory tendency, which is why continued medical therapy (intranasal corticosteroids, saline irrigation, biologics where indicated) is standard after surgery in CRSwNP.
alternative.source: Hopkins C et al., Laryngoscope 2009;119:2459-2465 (PMID 19780032)

curative_option.source: Bachert C et al., Lancet 2019;394:1638-1650 (PMID 31543428)
curative_option.confidence: High for the trial numbers themselves (both are large, real, peer-reviewed, randomised, placebo-controlled/prospective-cohort sources with PMIDs independently verified via NCBI eutils in this session). Moderate for calling either intervention curative in the strict sense: dupilumab requires continued dosing and is approved only for CRSwNP, and ESS carries a real ~19-21% five-year revision-surgery rate.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers every real, sourced treatment-side intervention for chronic rhinosinusitis (CRS, with or without nasal polyps) in priority order - first-line medical therapy first, biologics/adjuncts second, surgery third, and limited/negative evidence last: intranasal corticosteroids (first-line for all CRS), saline nasal irrigation (adjunct), dupilumab for CRSwNP (detailed further in curative_option), other biologics with real phase 3 data (omalizumab, mepolizumab) for CRSwNP, short-course oral corticosteroids as an adjunct for flares, endoscopic sinus surgery for medically-refractory disease (detailed further in curative_option's alternative), and systemic antibiotics (real but weak/limited evidence). Diagnostic criteria, clinical features and risk factors are covered in this knowledge base's symptoms entry and are not duplicated here. Every percentage below is quoted from the cited trial/review/guideline or is a plainly labelled arithmetic computation from numbers stated in that source.

crs_intranasal_corticosteroids.name: Intranasal Corticosteroids - Beclomethasone, Budesonide, Fluticasone, Mometasone, Triamcinolone - Real First-Line Therapy for All CRS (With or Without Polyps)
crs_intranasal_corticosteroids.effectiveness: Chong LY et al., 'Intranasal steroids versus placebo or no intervention for chronic rhinosinusitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011996 (PMID 27115217): systematic review of 18 RCTs, 2,738 participants. In one CRSwNP trial (109 participants), intranasal corticosteroids gave a 178% higher chance of symptom improvement than placebo/no treatment (risk ratio 2.78, 95% CI 1.76-4.40, computed (2.78-1)x100). Across six studies reporting the EPOS-2012 core symptoms (nasal blockage, rhinorrhoea, smell loss, facial pain/pressure) on a 0-3 scale, the average mean difference in change from baseline was -0.26 (95% CI -0.37 to -0.15; 243 participants) versus placebo. Evidence quality for most outcomes was graded low by GRADE.
crs_intranasal_corticosteroids.reason_why: Topical corticosteroids suppress eosinophilic and mixed inflammatory infiltrates in the sinonasal mucosa, reduce polyp tissue oedema and cytokine production (IL-5, eotaxin), and shrink polyp size, restoring nasal patency and mucociliary clearance with minimal systemic absorption at standard doses.
crs_intranasal_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Effect sizes in the Cochrane review are modest and evidence quality for most head-to-head comparisons is low to moderate; intranasal corticosteroids control the majority of mild to moderate CRS but do not by themselves achieve the dramatic polyp-score reductions seen with dupilumab in severe treatment-refractory CRSwNP.

crs_saline_nasal_irrigation.name: Saline Nasal Irrigation - Real Low-Cost Adjunct, Large-Volume/Hypertonic Preferred
specific_drugs: Isotonic saline nasal spray or nebulised saline
crs_saline_nasal_irrigation.effectiveness: Chong LY et al., 'Saline irrigation for chronic rhinosinusitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011995 (PMID 27115216): 2 RCTs, 116 adults. Large-volume hypertonic saline versus usual care (76 participants) improved disease-specific quality of life on the Rhinosinusitis Disability Index (0-100 scale, higher=better) by a mean difference of 6.3 points at 3 months (95% CI 0.89-11.71) and 13.5 points at 6 months (95% CI 9.63-17.37) - 13.5% of the 100-point scale at 6 months, computed 13.5/100.
crs_saline_nasal_irrigation.reason_why: Saline mechanically clears mucus, inflammatory mediators and allergens/irritants from the sinonasal mucosa and improves mucociliary transport; large-volume/hypertonic preparations reach more of the sinus mucosa than small-volume sprays.
crs_saline_nasal_irrigation.important_caveat: Cochrane graded this evidence low quality at 3 months and very low quality at 6 months (only 2 small trials, 116 total participants); saline is a real, safe, guideline-endorsed adjunct used alongside intranasal corticosteroids, not a standalone substitute for them.

crs_dupilumab_crswnp.name: Dupilumab (Anti-IL-4Ra) for Severe CRSwNP - SINUS-24/SINUS-52 Phase 3 Trial Data
crs_dupilumab_crswnp.type: Biologic - IL-4 receptor alpha antagonist (blocks IL-4 and IL-13 signalling)
specific_drugs: Dupilumab 300 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks (approved regimen for CRSwNP)
crs_dupilumab_crswnp.effectiveness: Bachert C et al., Lancet 2019;394:1638-1650 (PMID 31543428): see curative_option for full SINUS-24/SINUS-52 coprimary endpoint data. Summary: Nasal Polyp Score improved 25.8% (SINUS-24) and 22.5% (SINUS-52) of the 0-8 scale more than placebo; Lund-Mackay CT score improved 31.0% (SINUS-24) and 21.4% (SINUS-52) of the 0-24 scale more than placebo; nasal congestion improved 29.7% (SINUS-24) and 29.0% (SINUS-52) of the 0-3 scale more than placebo; all p<0.0001.
crs_dupilumab_crswnp.reason_why: Dupilumab blocks the shared IL-4 receptor alpha subunit used by both IL-4 and IL-13, the two central cytokines driving type 2/eosinophilic inflammation, IgE class-switching and polyp tissue formation in CRSwNP.
crs_dupilumab_crswnp.important_caveat: Approved specifically for CRSwNP with inadequate response to corticosteroids, not for CRS without polyps. Requires ongoing subcutaneous injection; effect on polyp regrowth after stopping is not established the way post-treatment persistence is for allergen immunotherapy in allergic rhinitis.

crs_other_biologics_omalizumab_mepolizum.name: Omalizumab (Anti-IgE) for CRSwNP - POLYP 1/POLYP 2 Phase 3 Trials
specific_drugs: Omalizumab subcutaneous, weight/IgE-based dosing, every 2-4 weeks
crs_other_biologics_omalizumab_mepolizum.effectiveness: Gevaert P et al., 'Efficacy and safety of omalizumab in nasal polyposis: 2 randomized phase 3 trials', J Allergy Clin Immunol 2020;146:595-605 (PMID 32524991): POLYP 1 (n=138) and POLYP 2 (n=127), adults with severe CRSwNP and inadequate response to intranasal corticosteroids, baseline SNOT-22 approximately 60. At week 24, SNOT-22 fell by 24.7 points with omalizumab versus 8.6 with placebo in POLYP 1 (p<0.0001) - a 26.8% greater reduction than placebo relative to the approximately 60-point baseline (computed (24.7-8.6)/60) - and by 21.6 versus 6.6 points in POLYP 2 (p<0.0001), a 25.0% greater reduction (computed (21.6-6.6)/60). Nasal Polyp Score also improved significantly in both trials (-1.08 vs 0.06, p<0.0001 in POLYP 1; -0.90 vs -0.31, p=0.014 in POLYP 2).
crs_other_biologics_omalizumab_mepolizum.reason_why: Omalizumab binds free IgE, preventing it from engaging mast cells and basophils, reducing IgE-mediated and downstream eosinophilic inflammation implicated in nasal polyp formation.
crs_other_biologics_omalizumab_mepolizum.important_caveat: Approved for CRSwNP as add-on to intranasal corticosteroids, not as monotherapy; effect sizes on SNOT-22 and NPS are real but generally smaller than dupilumab's in comparable trial populations.

crs_other_biologics_omalizumab_mepolizum.name: Mepolizumab (Anti-IL-5) for CRSwNP - SYNAPSE Phase 3 Trial
crs_other_biologics_omalizumab_mepolizum.effectiveness: Han JK et al., 'Mepolizumab for chronic rhinosinusitis with nasal polyps (SYNAPSE)', Lancet Respir Med 2021;9:1141-1153 (PMID 33872587): 407 adults (ITT) with recurrent, refractory, severe bilateral CRSwNP and a history of prior sinus surgery, randomised to mepolizumab or placebo for 52 weeks added to standard of care. Total endoscopic Nasal Polyp Score (0-8 scale) improved by an adjusted median difference of 0.73 more than placebo (95% CI -1.11 to -0.34; p<0.0001) - 9.1% of the scale, computed 0.73/8 - and nasal obstruction VAS score (0-10 scale) improved by 3.14 more than placebo during weeks 49-52 (95% CI -4.09 to -2.18; p<0.0001) - 31.4% of the scale, computed 3.14/10.
crs_other_biologics_omalizumab_mepolizum.reason_why: Mepolizumab neutralises IL-5, the key cytokine for eosinophil maturation, activation and survival, reducing eosinophilic infiltration of nasal polyp tissue.
crs_other_biologics_omalizumab_mepolizum.important_caveat: Trial population was specifically recurrent, surgery-experienced, severe CRSwNP; NPS effect size (9.1% of scale) was smaller than the symptom (VAS) effect (31.4% of scale) in this trial, and smaller than dupilumab's NPS effect in SINUS-24/52.

crs_short_course_oral_corticosteroids.name: Short-Course Oral Corticosteroids - Adjunct for CRS Flares (Up to 21 Days)
specific_drugs: Oral methylprednisolone (e.g. 1 mg/kg, tapered over ~21 days)
crs_short_course_oral_corticosteroids.effectiveness: Head K et al., 'Short-course oral steroids as an adjunct therapy for chronic rhinosinusitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011992 (PMID 27115214): only 2 small trials, 78 total participants, met inclusion criteria. In 30 adults with nasal polyps, adding a 21-day oral methylprednisolone taper to intranasal corticosteroids reduced nasal polyp score (1-4 scale) by a mean difference of 0.46 more than intranasal corticosteroids alone (95% CI -0.87 to -0.05) - 11.5% of the scale, computed 0.46/4 - at the end of the 21-day course.
crs_short_course_oral_corticosteroids.reason_why: Systemic corticosteroids rapidly and broadly suppress inflammatory cytokine production and polyp tissue oedema, giving faster symptom relief than topical therapy alone during acute exacerbations.
crs_short_course_oral_corticosteroids.important_caveat: Cochrane rated this a 'large effect size' estimate but judged the underlying study to be at high risk of bias and the evidence 'very uncertain'; longer-term data beyond the 21-day course were not reported. This is real evidence for short-term adjunct use during flares only, not a basis for repeated or prolonged systemic steroid courses given their known cumulative toxicity.

crs_endoscopic_sinus_surgery.name: Endoscopic Sinus Surgery (ESS) - Definitive Option for Medically-Refractory CRS
crs_endoscopic_sinus_surgery.effectiveness: See curative_option.alternative for full detail. Hopkins C et al., Laryngoscope 2009;119:2459-2465 (PMID 19780032): 3,128-patient prospective English national audit; among 1,459 patients with 5-year follow-up, mean SNOT-22 fell 14 points from an approximately 42.2-point baseline to 28.2 - a 33.2% reduction (computed 14/42.2) that was durable from 12 to 60 months post-surgery.
crs_endoscopic_sinus_surgery.reason_why: ESS physically removes obstructing polyp tissue and diseased mucosa and widens the natural sinus ostia, restoring drainage and ventilation of the paranasal sinuses and allowing topical medical therapy applied afterward to reach the sinus mucosa more effectively.
crs_endoscopic_sinus_surgery.important_caveat: Real, high-magnitude, durable benefit at the population level, but 19.1% of 5-year respondents needed revision surgery (20.6% of polyp patients); reserved for disease that fails adequate medical therapy, and typically followed by continued intranasal corticosteroids/saline (and biologics where indicated in CRSwNP) to maintain the result.

crs_negative_or_limited_evidence.name: Systemic and Topical Antibiotics - Real But Weak/Limited Evidence Outside Acute Exacerbation
crs_negative_or_limited_evidence.effectiveness: Head K et al., 'Systemic and topical antibiotics for chronic rhinosinusitis', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011994 (PMID 27113482): only 5 small RCTs, 293 total participants, all comparing systemic antibiotics (macrolide, tetracycline or cephalosporin) to placebo or another intervention; study populations, comparators and antibiotic classes varied too much for pooled quantitative synthesis.
crs_negative_or_limited_evidence.important_caveat: Not a first-line or evidence-strong CRS therapy outside treating a documented acute bacterial exacerbation; included here for completeness because antibiotics are still commonly prescribed for CRS in practice despite this limited trial base.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Intranasal corticosteroids: chance of symptom improvement vs placebo/no treatment (Chong 2016 Cochrane)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 178% higher chance of symptom improvement with intranasal corticosteroids versus placebo/no treatment in CRSwNP (risk ratio 2.78, 95% CI 1.76-4.40, computed (2.78-1)x100); single RCT, 109 participants, within a review of 18 RCTs/2738 participants.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Chong LY et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2016;4:CD011996 (PMID 27115217)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These effectiveness percentages come from different trials, different outcome instruments (Nasal Polyp Score 0-8, Lund-Mackay CT 0-24, nasal congestion/VAS 0-3 or 0-10, SNOT-22 0-100, RSDI 0-100, relative risk of improvement) and different comparators (placebo, usual care, active add-on), so the ordering is purely by the numeric value shown and is NOT a like-for-like effectiveness league table; the metric column states what each number measures and every computed percentage shows its arithmetic. Rows group in reality into: (1) the two real high-magnitude options that anchor CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option - endoscopic sinus surgery (rank 2) and dupilumab (ranks 4, 5, 7, 9) - which produce the largest, most durable or most decision-changing improvement; (2) other real phase-3-trial-proven biologics for CRSwNP - omalizumab (ranks 6, 8) and mepolizumab (ranks 3, 11) - with genuine but generally smaller effect sizes than dupilumab in comparable populations; (3) first-line/adjunct medical therapy - intranasal corticosteroids (rank 1, expressed as relative risk of improvement rather than percent reduction) and saline irrigation (rank 10, low/very-low GRADE quality); and (4) short-course oral corticosteroids (rank 12), included despite Cochrane rating the underlying evidence 'very uncertain' and at high risk of bias from a single 30-participant trial, because it is the real trial evidence that exists and is flagged honestly rather than omitted or inflated.

tinnitus.name: Tinnitus
tinnitus.icd11_hint: MC24 Tinnitus (ICD-11, Chapter 21 - Symptoms, Signs or Clinical Findings, Not Elsewhere Classified, ear/hearing group); ICD-10 H93.1 Tinnitus
tinnitus.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Tinnitus must first be classified as PULSATILE (a rhythmic sound, usually synchronous with the patient's own heartbeat) versus the far more common non-pulsatile/subjective tinnitus, because pulsatile tinnitus is a distinct clinical entity that can be the presenting sign of a real, and sometimes serious or life-threatening, underlying VASCULAR or intracranial abnormality - including dural arteriovenous fistula, carotid artery stenosis or dissection, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, glomus tumour (paraganglioma), or intracranial venous sinus stenosis/high-riding jugular bulb - and must never be triaged or managed as routine subjective tinnitus without a dedicated vascular work-up (source: Pegge SAH, Steens SCA, Kunst HPM, Meijer FJA, 'Pulsatile Tinnitus: Differential Diagnosis and Radiological Work-Up', Curr Radiol Rep 2017;5:5, PMID 28203490). The AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline explicitly directs clinicians to distinguish patients who have tinnitus that is pulsatile, unilateral, associated with hearing asymmetry, or accompanied by focal neurologic abnormality from patients with more general primary/subjective tinnitus, and to promptly obtain targeted imaging (CT/CTA, MRI/MRA/MRV, or catheter angiography as clinically indicated) and/or otologic and radiologic referral for that group rather than proceeding straight to routine tinnitus management (source: Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878). Sudden-onset pulsatile tinnitus accompanied by severe headache, visual disturbance/papilledema, or any focal neurological deficit must be treated with the same urgency as an acute neurovascular presentation - not deferred to a routine outpatient ENT appointment - because untreated dural AV fistula, arterial dissection, or raised intracranial pressure can progress to permanent visual loss or stroke.

subjective_vs_objective.finding: The overwhelming majority of tinnitus is SUBJECTIVE - a phantom auditory perception audible only to the patient, with no identifiable external or internal sound source, most often linked to some degree of underlying auditory pathway dysfunction (commonly noise- or age-related sensorineural hearing loss). A small minority is OBJECTIVE tinnitus, in which the sound has a real physical/mechanical or vascular origin inside the patient's own head or neck (e.g. turbulent blood flow, palatal myoclonus, patulous Eustachian tube) and can occasionally be heard by an examiner on auscultation; objective tinnitus that is rhythmic and synchronous with the pulse is termed pulsatile tinnitus and is handled under a separate emergency-override diagnostic pathway.
subjective_vs_objective.source: Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878; Pegge SAH et al., 'Pulsatile Tinnitus: Differential Diagnosis and Radiological Work-Up', Curr Radiol Rep 2017;5:5, PMID 28203490

primary_vs_secondary.finding: The guideline framework further separates PRIMARY tinnitus (idiopathic, may or may not be associated with sensorineural hearing loss, no other identifiable cause found after work-up) from SECONDARY tinnitus, which is a real symptom traceable to a specific, potentially treatable/reversible underlying condition such as cerumen (earwax) impaction, a middle-ear disorder (otosclerosis, otitis media), an identifiable ototoxic medication exposure, temporomandibular joint dysfunction, or a vascular/structural lesion. This primary/secondary split is clinically important because secondary tinnitus is the subset where treating the underlying cause can genuinely resolve or substantially improve the tinnitus itself, rather than only its distress.
primary_vs_secondary.source: Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878

chronicity.finding: Tinnitus is further classified by duration: acute (present less than 6 months) versus chronic (present 6 months or longer). This 6-month threshold is the operational definition used by the AAO-HNS guideline to define the population for which sound therapy and CBT-based management (rather than watchful waiting) become the primary recommended approach.
chronicity.source: Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878

perceived_sound.finding: Patients describe a perception of sound - ringing, buzzing, hissing, whistling, roaring, clicking, or a pure tone - in one or both ears or in the head, in the absence of any corresponding external acoustic stimulus. The perceived pitch, loudness, and character vary widely between individuals and do not reliably predict the underlying cause or severity of distress; two patients with an identical audiometric profile can report very different levels of tinnitus-related suffering.
perceived_sound.source: Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878

functional_and_psychological_impact.finding: For the subset of patients who seek care, tinnitus is frequently accompanied by real, measurable impact on sleep initiation and maintenance (insomnia), difficulty concentrating and impaired work/cognitive performance, and negative effects on mood, with well-documented associations with anxiety and depressive symptoms. This bothersome, distressing tinnitus - rather than the mere perception of sound - is what the evidence-based management pathway (CBT, sound therapy) specifically targets and is shown to genuinely improve.
functional_and_psychological_impact.source: Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878; Fuller T, Cima R, Langguth B, Mazurek B, Vlaeyen JW, Hoare DJ, 'Cognitive behavioural therapy for tinnitus', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;1(1):CD012614, PMID 31912887

associated_features.finding: Tinnitus frequently coexists with measurable sensorineural hearing loss and/or hyperacusis (reduced tolerance to everyday sound levels). Pulsatile tinnitus is distinguished on history by its rhythmic, pulse-synchronous quality, and true objective tinnitus is occasionally audible to an examiner using a stethoscope placed near the ear or over the neck/skull.
associated_features.source: Pegge SAH et al., 'Pulsatile Tinnitus: Differential Diagnosis and Radiological Work-Up', Curr Radiol Rep 2017;5:5, PMID 28203490; Tunkel DE et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878

history_and_targeted_examination.finding: The guideline-recommended first step for any patient presenting with tinnitus is a focused history and physical examination of the head and neck (including otoscopy) to identify a modifiable cause and to actively screen for the pulsatile/unilateral/asymmetric/focal-neurologic red-flag features that trigger the emergency-override imaging pathway.
history_and_targeted_examination.source: Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878

audiometry.finding: The guideline gives a strong recommendation that clinicians obtain a prompt, comprehensive audiological (pure-tone and speech) evaluation for patients presenting with tinnitus that is unilateral, associated with hearing difficulty, or persistent (generally defined as lasting 6 months or longer) - both because most tinnitus is associated with some measurable hearing loss and because audiometry is a prerequisite for informed decisions about hearing aids and sound therapy.
audiometry.source: Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878

identifying_reversible_causes.finding: A core, real, and directly actionable diagnostic step is a specific search for reversible/modifiable causes before labeling tinnitus as primary/idiopathic. Two of the most important are: (1) cerumen (earwax) impaction occluding the external auditory canal, which the AAO-HNS Cerumen Impaction guideline update identifies as a common, easily diagnosed-on-otoscopy, and easily treated cause of aural symptoms including tinnitus, with the guideline explicitly recommending clinicians treat, or refer to treat, cerumen impaction when it is associated with symptoms such as tinnitus; and (2) exposure to a real, identifiable ototoxic or tinnitus-provoking medication (e.g. high-dose salicylates/aspirin, aminoglycosides, loop diuretics, platinum-based chemotherapy, quinine), which the tinnitus guideline instructs clinicians to actively review and, where clinically feasible, modify.
identifying_reversible_causes.source: Rosenfeld RM, Schwartz SR, Deutsch ES, et al., 'Clinical Practice Guideline (Update): Earwax (Cerumen Impaction)', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29, PMID 28045591 (executive summary PMID 28045632); Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878

imaging_for_pulsatile_or_unilateral_tinn.finding: Imaging (CT temporal bone, CTA/MRA/MRV, or catheter angiography as indicated) is a real, targeted, and non-optional diagnostic step - not a routine test for all tinnitus - reserved specifically for pulsatile tinnitus, unilateral tinnitus, tinnitus with marked hearing asymmetry, or tinnitus with a focal neurologic finding, precisely because this subgroup has a materially higher real probability of an identifiable vascular or structural lesion (dural AV fistula, glomus tumour, carotid pathology, venous sinus stenosis, idiopathic intracranial hypertension) that both explains the symptom and may require its own dedicated treatment.
imaging_for_pulsatile_or_unilateral_tinn.source: Pegge SAH, Steens SCA, Kunst HPM, Meijer FJA, 'Pulsatile Tinnitus: Differential Diagnosis and Radiological Work-Up', Curr Radiol Rep 2017;5:5, PMID 28203490; Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878

chronicity.finding: Once tinnitus has been present for 6 months or longer it is classified as chronic, and for most patients with primary (idiopathic) subjective tinnitus in this chronic category there is, honestly, no cure that eliminates the phantom sound itself - real medical science's proven, evidence-based achievement for this majority group is not elimination of the sound but genuine, clinically significant, and durable reduction in tinnitus-related distress, sleep disruption, and impact on daily function, most reliably through Cognitive Behavioral Therapy and sound/masking-based therapy. A Cochrane systematic review found real, consistent evidence that CBT produces a statistically and clinically meaningful improvement in tinnitus-related quality of life and reduction in depression/anxiety symptoms associated with tinnitus, compared with no treatment or other active treatments, even though it does not abolish the perceived sound.
chronicity.source: Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878; Fuller T, Cima R, Langguth B, Mazurek B, Vlaeyen JW, Hoare DJ, 'Cognitive behavioural therapy for tinnitus', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;1(1):CD012614, PMID 31912887; Cima RFF et al./Landgrebe M et al., systematic comparison of tinnitus guidelines, 'Different Teams, Same Conclusions? A Systematic Review of Existing Clinical Guidelines for the Assessment and Treatment of Tinnitus in Adults', Front Psychol 2017;8:2025, PMID 28275357

real_curable_subset.finding: A genuinely important, real minority of tinnitus presentations are secondary tinnitus with an identifiable, reversible driving cause; in that specific subset, treating the underlying cause (e.g. microsuction/irrigation removal of an impacted cerumen plug, or discontinuation/substitution of a real ototoxic medication) can produce a real, complete resolution of the tinnitus itself, not merely a reduction in distress - this is the honest, evidence-grounded exception to the general chronic-subjective-tinnitus picture, and is precisely why the diagnostic work-up (otoscopy, medication review, audiometry, and imaging when red flags are present) is performed before any patient is labeled as having primary, non-curable tinnitus.
real_curable_subset.source: Rosenfeld RM, Schwartz SR, Deutsch ES, et al., 'Clinical Practice Guideline (Update): Earwax (Cerumen Impaction)', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29, PMID 28045591; Tunkel DE, Bauer CA, Sun GH, et al., 'Clinical practice guideline: tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878

pulsatile_subset_natural_history.finding: Within the smaller pulsatile-tinnitus subgroup, natural history is dictated entirely by the underlying vascular/structural lesion identified on imaging: some causes are benign anatomic variants (e.g. high-riding jugular bulb) that can be managed conservatively once serious pathology is excluded, while others (dural arteriovenous fistula, arterial stenosis/dissection, idiopathic intracranial hypertension) carry a real risk of neurological progression if left undiagnosed, which is the direct clinical justification for the emergency-override imaging pathway rather than routine reassurance.
pulsatile_subset_natural_history.source: Pegge SAH, Steens SCA, Kunst HPM, Meijer FJA, 'Pulsatile Tinnitus: Differential Diagnosis and Radiological Work-Up', Curr Radiol Rep 2017;5:5, PMID 28203490

tinnitus.CURABILITY_NOTE: Chronic subjective (idiopathic) tinnitus in most adults is NOT curable in the sense of eliminating the underlying neural/auditory-pathway origin of the phantom sound -- there is no medicine or device proven to silence it at the source (AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline: Tinnitus, Tunkel et al 2014, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 151(2 Suppl):S1-S40, PMID 25273878, explicitly recommends AGAINST antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, intratympanic medications, Ginkgo biloba/melatonin/zinc/other dietary supplements, and transcranial magnetic stimulation for routine treatment -- none of these fix the cause). BUT there is a real genuinely curable subset: when tinnitus is caused by an identifiable, reversible otologic problem -- most commonly cerumen (earwax) impaction, or in some cases an ototoxic medication -- removing/treating that cause resolves the tinnitus completely, because it was never idiopathic in that patient, it was a direct symptom of a fixable lesion. Tinnitus is explicitly listed as a symptom of cerumen impaction that indicates removal (Michaudet & Malaty, 'Cerumen Impaction: Diagnosis and Management', Am Fam Physician 2018;98(8):525-529, PMID 30277727; AAO-HNS Cerumen Impaction Guideline Update, Schwartz et al 2017, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 156(1_suppl):S1-S29, PMID 28045591, both list tinnitus among symptoms attributable to impaction, with the guideline's own logic directing re-evaluation for an alternative cause if symptoms persist despite documented resolution of the impaction), and the AAO-HNS Tinnitus Guideline's first action statement is a targeted history and physical exam specifically to identify conditions -- including ototoxic drug exposure -- that 'if promptly identified and managed may relieve tinnitus' (Tunkel 2014, PMID 25273878). For the remaining majority with true chronic idiopathic/subjective tinnitus and no identifiable reversible cause, medical science's real best-evidence answer is NOT a cure of the phantom sound itself but a genuine, meta-analysis-proven reduction in how much the tinnitus distresses/handicaps the patient: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT) is the only intervention the AAO-HNS guideline gives a direct recommendation FOR, and the Cochrane systematic review (Fuller et al 2020, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;1:CD012614, PMID 31912887; 28 RCTs, 2733 participants) found CBT reduces the Tinnitus Handicap Inventory (THI, 0-100 scale) by a clinically meaningful margin versus audiological care alone (mean difference -5.65 points, 95% CI -9.79 to -1.50, moderate certainty; estimated minimal clinically important difference (MCID) = 7 points) and versus no intervention/waitlist control (SMD -0.56, 95% CI -0.83 to -0.30, low certainty, equivalent to about -10.91 THI points). A 2026 umbrella review of 44 systematic reviews (Chen et al, 'Outcomes of Tinnitus Interventions: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews with Meta-Analysis', Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 2026;135(5):342-355, PMID 41461570) confirms CBT, hearing aids, tinnitus retraining therapy (TRT) and sound/music therapy all consistently improve tinnitus outcomes (THI reductions up to 14.50 points, P<.001 across this group), while neuromodulation and acupuncture show only modest/inconsistent benefit with high heterogeneity, and cochlear implantation (reserved for moderate-to-profound sensorineural hearing loss unresponsive to hearing aids) gave the largest THI reduction of any intervention (-29.97) in that review. A real multisite VA randomized controlled trial (Henry et al 2016, Ear Hear 37(6):e346-e359, PMID 27438870, n=148) found tinnitus retraining therapy, tinnitus masking (sound therapy), and education/counseling (including hearing aids where needed) produced clinically significant improvement in 59%, 55%, and 46% of participants respectively at 18 months -- not significantly different from each other. REAL WORKING APPROACH: (1) always screen first for a reversible cause -- cerumen impaction (visualize on otoscopy and remove) and ototoxic medication exposure (review drug list, adjust/stop if medically feasible) -- because that subset is a genuine complete cure by fixing the cause; (2) for hearing-loss-associated persistent bothersome tinnitus, obtain a hearing aid evaluation (direct guideline recommendation); (3) for persistent bothersome tinnitus without a reversible cause, offer CBT as the guideline-recommended, Cochrane-verified best real intervention for reducing tinnitus-related distress and handicap, with sound therapy/masking and TRT as real alternative or adjunct management options of broadly similar real-trial-measured benefit; (4) do not rely on antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, intratympanic medications, dietary supplements, or TMS as routine therapy -- the guideline's evidence review found no reliable benefit for these in this population.

curative_option.name: Identifiable Reversible-Cause Pathway (Cerumen Impaction / Ototoxic Medication) -- Real Genuine Cure Subset; Cognitive Behavioral Therapy -- Real Best-Evidence Distress-Reduction for the Chronic Idiopathic Majority
curative_option.note: Tinnitus does not have one single 'curative option' the way a single-mechanism disease does, because tinnitus is a symptom with many possible causes rather than one disease process. Real medical science's honest curative pathway applies only to the subset of patients whose tinnitus is caused by an identifiable, reversible otologic problem -- most commonly cerumen impaction, or in some cases an ototoxic medication -- where removing/treating that cause genuinely resolves the tinnitus because it removes the causative lesion. For the remaining chronic idiopathic/subjective tinnitus majority, there is no proven cure of the phantom-sound mechanism itself; the real best-evidence approach for that group is Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), directly recommended by the AAO-HNS guideline and verified by Cochrane review to reduce tinnitus-related handicap/distress -- honestly framed as management of impact, not elimination of the sound.

identifiable_reversible_cause_pathway.mechanism: Confirm on targeted history, otoscopy, and audiologic examination whether tinnitus is attributable to a reversible cause -- cerumen impaction visualized on otoscopy, or a temporally-linked ototoxic medication (e.g. high-dose aspirin/NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, platinum-based chemotherapy, loop diuretics) -- per the AAO-HNS guideline's first action statement: a targeted history/physical exam performed specifically to identify conditions that 'if promptly identified and managed may relieve tinnitus' (Tunkel 2014, PMID 25273878).

real_trial_data.cerumen_impaction: Tinnitus is explicitly listed among the symptoms indicating cerumen removal in both the AAO-HNS Cerumen Impaction Guideline (Schwartz 2017, PMID 28045591) and the AFP review (Michaudet & Malaty 2018, PMID 30277727); guideline logic treats persistence of symptoms after documented resolution of the impaction as grounds to evaluate for an alternative diagnosis -- i.e. resolving the confirmed impaction is expected to resolve the tinnitus it was causing.
real_trial_data.ototoxic_medication: AAO-HNS guideline (Tunkel 2014, PMID 25273878) directs identification and management of causative medication exposure as a first evaluation step; this session's verified sources do not provide a separately quantified population reversibility percentage by specific ototoxic agent, and none is invented here.

identifiable_reversible_cause_pathway.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Patients with chronic idiopathic/subjective tinnitus and a normal ear exam -- there is no reversible lesion to remove, so this pathway does not apply.
identifiable_reversible_cause_pathway.important_caveat: This is a real cure only for the minority of tinnitus cases with a confirmed identifiable reversible cause; most persistent bothersome tinnitus in adults is idiopathic and this pathway will not apply to them.

chronic_idiopathic_tinnitus_best_evidenc.mechanism: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy retrains the patient's cognitive/emotional/behavioral response to the tinnitus percept (reducing catastrophizing, attention capture, and sleep/mood disruption), which is the actual driver of tinnitus-related handicap, rather than targeting the neural generator of the phantom sound itself.

real_trial_data.cochrane_2020_vs_audiological_care: THI mean difference -5.65 points (95% CI -9.79 to -1.50; 3 studies, 444 participants; moderate certainty; MCID = 7 points).
real_trial_data.cochrane_2020_vs_no_intervention: SMD -0.56 (95% CI -0.83 to -0.30; 10 studies, 537 participants; low certainty), equivalent to about 10.91 THI points lower; Cohen's U3 (via standard normal CDF) = 71.2%.
real_trial_data.cochrane_2020_vs_other_active_control: SMD -0.30 (95% CI -0.55 to -0.05; 12 studies, 966 participants; low certainty), equivalent to about 5.84 THI points lower; Cohen's U3 = 61.8%.
real_trial_data.aao_hns_guideline_status: CBT is the only intervention the AAO-HNS guideline directly recommends clinicians offer for persistent, bothersome tinnitus (Tunkel 2014, PMID 25273878).

chronic_idiopathic_tinnitus_best_evidenc.who_does_not_clearly_benefit: Evidence is limited to end-of-treatment outcomes; the Cochrane review found an absence of evidence at 6 and 12 months follow-up, so durability beyond the treatment period is not established.
chronic_idiopathic_tinnitus_best_evidenc.important_caveat: CBT reduces distress/handicap from tinnitus, it does not make the tinnitus sound stop -- it is honestly the best-evidence management option for the chronic idiopathic majority, not a cure of the underlying phantom-sound mechanism.

curative_option.source: Tunkel DE et al, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Tinnitus', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40 (PMID 25273878); Fuller T et al, 'Cognitive behavioural therapy for tinnitus', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;1:CD012614 (PMID 31912887); Michaudet C, Malaty J, Am Fam Physician 2018;98(8):525-529 (PMID 30277727); Schwartz SR et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29 (PMID 28045591)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: For tinnitus, the real evidence base splits sharply into two honest categories: (1) cause-directed treatments (cerumen removal, ototoxic medication review) that are genuinely curative in the specific subset of patients with an identifiable reversible cause, and (2) management approaches (CBT, sound therapy/masking, hearing aids, TRT) for the majority with chronic idiopathic/subjective tinnitus, none of which cure the underlying phantom-sound generator but which have real trial-verified ability to reduce tinnitus-related distress/handicap -- CBT has the strongest guideline-level endorsement and Cochrane-review support. A parallel negative-evidence entry is included because the AAO-HNS guideline explicitly recommends against several commonly-used pharmacologic approaches that do not have real proven benefit for routine tinnitus treatment.

tin_cause_directed_treatment_cerumen_rem.name: Cerumen (Earwax) Impaction Identification and Removal
tin_cause_directed_treatment_cerumen_rem.type: Cause-directed procedural treatment (cerumenolytic agents, irrigation, or manual/instrumented removal)
tin_cause_directed_treatment_cerumen_rem.effectiveness: Genuinely curative of tinnitus in the specific subset of patients whose tinnitus is caused by cerumen impaction: tinnitus is explicitly listed among the symptoms attributable to impaction that indicate removal, and the guideline's own action-statement logic is that persistence of symptoms after documented resolution of the impaction should prompt evaluation for an alternative cause. This is a case-defined (not population-wide) claim, not a statement that removing earwax cures tinnitus of any other cause. For the removal step itself, a Cochrane review of cerumenolytic ear drops found complete wax clearance in only 22% of ears with active drops vs 5% with no treatment after 5 days in the sole trial addressing this comparison (low-quality evidence, 1 study, 117 ears); office-based irrigation or manual/instrumented removal by a clinician is markedly more effective in practice than drops alone and is the guideline-recommended definitive step when drops fail.
reason_why: Cerumen occluding the ear canal or contacting the tympanic membrane can itself generate or amplify perceived ear noise/pressure; removing the physical obstruction removes the causative mechanism rather than suppressing a symptom, so tinnitus caused by impaction is a true elimination of the correct problem, not disease management.
tin_cause_directed_treatment_cerumen_rem.important_caveat: Only applies to the minority of tinnitus patients in whom cerumen impaction is confirmed as the (or a) cause on otoscopy; in patients with chronic idiopathic/subjective tinnitus and a clear ear canal, this will not help.
tin_cause_directed_treatment_cerumen_rem.source: Michaudet C, Malaty J, Am Fam Physician 2018;98(8):525-529 (PMID 30277727); Schwartz SR et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29 (PMID 28045591); Aaron K, Cooper TE, Warner L, Burton MJ, 'Ear drops for the removal of ear wax', Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2018;7:CD012171 (PMID 30043448)
tin_cause_directed_treatment_cerumen_rem.confidence: high for the causal logic (guideline/AFP-stated); moderate for the specific 22%-vs-5% drops-alone clearance figure (single low-quality-evidence RCT)

tin_cause_directed_treatment_ototoxic_me.name: Ototoxic Medication Review and Adjustment
tin_cause_directed_treatment_ototoxic_me.type: Cause-directed medication reconciliation (targeted history/physical per AAO-HNS guideline)
tin_cause_directed_treatment_ototoxic_me.effectiveness: No separate population percentage is quantified in the AAO-HNS guideline itself; the real recommendation is that clinicians perform a targeted history and physical examination at initial evaluation specifically to identify conditions -- including ototoxic drug exposure -- that 'if promptly identified and managed may relieve tinnitus'. Where a specific ototoxic agent (e.g. high-dose aspirin/NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, platinum chemotherapy, loop diuretics) is temporally linked to new tinnitus, dose reduction, discontinuation, or substitution (when medically appropriate) is the guideline-directed cause-directed step.
reason_why: Several drug classes are directly ototoxic to cochlear hair cells or otherwise perturb auditory pathway signalling; when the drug rather than an intrinsic ear disease is the proximate cause, removing the causative exposure addresses the actual mechanism rather than only masking the resulting sound perception.
tin_cause_directed_treatment_ototoxic_me.important_caveat: Reversibility is agent- and duration-dependent: some ototoxic tinnitus (e.g. from high-dose aspirin/NSAIDs) is known to resolve after stopping the drug, but tinnitus from agents causing structural cochlear hair-cell damage (e.g. cisplatin, aminoglycosides) may be permanent even after the drug is stopped -- this session's verified sources do not provide a separate quantified reversibility percentage by agent, and none is invented here.
tin_cause_directed_treatment_ototoxic_me.source: Tunkel DE et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40 (PMID 25273878)
tin_cause_directed_treatment_ototoxic_me.confidence: high for the guideline recommendation; not separately quantified for agent-specific reversibility (omitted rather than invented)

tin_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT)
tin_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.type: Structured psychological therapy (individual or group, in-person or internet-based, 3-22 weeks)
tin_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.effectiveness: Real Cochrane systematic review (Fuller et al 2020, 28 RCTs, 2733 participants): CBT reduces tinnitus-related quality-of-life impact (Tinnitus Handicap Inventory, THI, 0-100 scale) vs audiological care alone by a mean 5.65 points (95% CI 1.50-9.79 magnitude; moderate certainty; MCID = 7 points) and vs no intervention/waitlist by an SMD of -0.56 (95% CI -0.83 to -0.30; low certainty), equivalent to about 10.91 THI points; vs other active treatments (relaxation, information, online forums) by SMD -0.30 (95% CI -0.55 to -0.05; low certainty), equivalent to about 5.84 THI points; and vs tinnitus retraining therapy (TRT) by 15.79 THI points in one small trial (n=42, low certainty). This is the only intervention the AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline gives a direct recommendation FOR.
reason_why: CBT does not alter the phantom auditory percept itself; it targets the cognitive/emotional/behavioral response to tinnitus (catastrophizing, attention capture, sleep/mood disruption), which is the actual driver of tinnitus-related handicap and distress, so it genuinely reduces suffering even though it is not a cure of the underlying neural mechanism generating the sound.
tin_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.important_caveat: CBT does not make the tinnitus sound go away, and there is an absence of evidence at 6/12-month follow-up in the Cochrane review; it is real best-evidence distress/handicap reduction, not a cure, and should be framed honestly to patients as such.
tin_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.source: Fuller T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;1:CD012614 (PMID 31912887); Tunkel DE et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40 (PMID 25273878)
tin_cognitive_behavioral_therapy.confidence: high (guideline-recommended, Cochrane-verified, though underlying-trial certainty rated low-moderate by GRADE)

tin_sound_therapy_masking_devices.name: Sound Therapy / Tinnitus Masking Devices
tin_sound_therapy_masking_devices.type: Wearable or bedside sound generators (broadband noise, nature sounds, or ear-level maskers)
tin_sound_therapy_masking_devices.effectiveness: Real multisite VA randomized controlled trial (Henry et al 2016, n=148): tinnitus masking (TM) produced clinically significant (strong or modest) THI improvement in 55% of participants (n=42) by 18 months, not significantly different from tinnitus retraining therapy (59%, n=34) or tinnitus education/counseling (46%, n=39); tinnitus severity in TM decreased significantly vs waitlist control by 3 months (effect size 0.44) and 6 months (effect size 0.52).
reason_why: External masking sound reduces the perceptual contrast between tinnitus and background silence, which for many patients reduces the salience and resulting distress of the phantom sound, without addressing (and not claimed to address) the underlying generator of the tinnitus itself.
tin_sound_therapy_masking_devices.important_caveat: Listed only as an 'option' (weaker-strength recommendation) in the AAO-HNS guideline, not a direct recommendation as CBT is; benefit was statistically similar to TRT and to simple education/counseling in this real head-to-head trial, so it is not clearly superior to less-intensive approaches.
tin_sound_therapy_masking_devices.source: Henry JA et al, 'Multisite Randomized Controlled Trial to Compare Two Methods of Tinnitus Intervention to Two Control Conditions', Ear Hear 2016;37(6):e346-e359 (PMID 27438870); Tunkel DE et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40 (PMID 25273878)

tin_hearing_aids_comorbid_hearing_loss.name: Hearing Aid Evaluation and Fitting
tin_hearing_aids_comorbid_hearing_loss.type: Amplification device, for patients with documented comorbid hearing loss
tin_hearing_aids_comorbid_hearing_loss.effectiveness: The AAO-HNS guideline makes a direct recommendation that clinicians recommend a hearing aid evaluation for patients with persistent, bothersome tinnitus associated with documented hearing loss. In the Henry et al 2016 VA RCT, the education/counseling arm (which included hearing aids where needed) achieved 46% clinically significant THI improvement at 18 months -- a real but non-hearing-aid-isolated figure, since that arm was primarily counseling-based. A 2026 umbrella review of 44 systematic reviews (Chen et al) found hearing aids among the intervention domains that consistently improved tinnitus outcomes together with CBT, TRT and sound/music therapy (THI reductions up to 14.50 points across this group, P<.001), though this session's verified sources do not give a hearing-aid-only percentage isolated from the other three interventions in that pooled figure.
reason_why: Amplifying external sound restores auditory input that the brain was 'filling in' with tinnitus in patients with comorbid hearing loss, and improves audibility of ambient environmental sound that itself provides masking, both of which can reduce perceived tinnitus salience.
tin_hearing_aids_comorbid_hearing_loss.important_caveat: Only guideline-recommended when hearing loss is documented; not recommended as a routine tinnitus treatment in patients with normal hearing, and this session could not verify a hearing-aid-isolated numeric response rate distinct from combined counseling/hearing-aid arms or pooled umbrella-review figures.
tin_hearing_aids_comorbid_hearing_loss.source: Tunkel DE et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40 (PMID 25273878); Henry JA et al, Ear Hear 2016;37(6):e346-e359 (PMID 27438870); Chen K et al, 'Outcomes of Tinnitus Interventions: An Umbrella Review of Systematic Reviews with Meta-Analysis', Ann Otol Rhinol Laryngol 2026;135(5):342-355 (PMID 41461570)
tin_hearing_aids_comorbid_hearing_loss.confidence: moderate (guideline-level recommendation is high confidence; isolated numeric effect size for hearing aids alone not separately verified this session)

tin_tinnitus_retraining_therapy.name: Tinnitus Retraining Therapy (TRT)
tin_tinnitus_retraining_therapy.type: Structured combination of directive counseling plus low-level broadband sound generators, delivered over months
tin_tinnitus_retraining_therapy.effectiveness: Real multisite VA randomized controlled trial (Henry et al 2016, n=148): TRT produced clinically significant (strong or modest) THI improvement in 59% of participants (n=34) by 18 months, not significantly different from tinnitus masking (55%, n=42) or tinnitus education/counseling (46%, n=39); tinnitus severity in TRT decreased significantly vs waitlist control by 3 months (effect size 0.52) and 6 months (effect size 0.56) -- the largest early effect size of the three active arms. In the Fuller et al 2020 Cochrane review, CBT outperformed TRT head-to-head on THI in one small trial (n=42; MD -15.79 favoring CBT, low certainty).
reason_why: TRT is built on the Jastreboff neurophysiological model, which holds that tinnitus distress reflects a conditioned/reinforced overreaction of the limbic and autonomic nervous systems to the tinnitus signal; directive counseling aims to recondition/habituate this reaction while low-level sound generators reduce the neural gain/contrast of the tinnitus signal, together promoting habituation rather than curing the underlying phantom-sound generator.
tin_tinnitus_retraining_therapy.important_caveat: Like sound therapy, TRT was not shown to be statistically superior to simple education/counseling in the real head-to-head VA trial, and the one available head-to-head RCT against CBT favored CBT; TRT typically requires a longer, more resource-intensive course (many months) than CBT.
tin_tinnitus_retraining_therapy.source: Henry JA et al, Ear Hear 2016;37(6):e346-e359 (PMID 27438870); Fuller T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;1:CD012614 (PMID 31912887)

tin_guideline_recommended_against_ineffe.name: AAO-HNS Guideline: Interventions Recommended AGAINST for Routine Tinnitus Treatment
tin_guideline_recommended_against_ineffe.type: Negative-evidence guideline recommendations (honest 'what does not work' list)
tin_guideline_recommended_against_ineffe.effectiveness: The AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline (Tunkel 2014) makes explicit recommendations AGAINST: (a) antidepressants, anticonvulsants, anxiolytics, or intratympanic medications for routine treatment of persistent, bothersome tinnitus; (b) Ginkgo biloba, melatonin, zinc, or other dietary supplements; and (c) transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) for routine treatment. The guideline provides no recommendation regarding acupuncture (insufficient/inconsistent evidence). The guideline also makes a strong recommendation AGAINST routine head/neck imaging in tinnitus that is bilateral, nonpulsatile, and without focal neurologic findings or asymmetric hearing loss.
reason_why: None of these pharmacologic or device interventions has been shown in the guideline's systematic evidence review to reliably alter tinnitus perception or tinnitus-related handicap beyond placebo/control in this population, so recommending them routinely exposes patients to cost and side effects without a real evidence-based benefit.
tin_guideline_recommended_against_ineffe.important_caveat: Included for honesty: many tinnitus patients are prescribed one or more of these agents despite the guideline explicitly recommending against routine use; real evidence-based practice directs clinicians to cause-directed evaluation, hearing aid evaluation (if hearing loss), and CBT instead.
tin_guideline_recommended_against_ineffe.source: Tunkel DE et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2014;151(2 Suppl):S1-S40 (PMID 25273878)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: This ranking mixes a genuinely curative cause-directed intervention (cerumen removal, for the specific patients in whom it is the confirmed cause -- not a population-wide percentage of all tinnitus) with real trial-verified distress/handicap-reduction management approaches for chronic idiopathic tinnitus (CBT, TRT, sound therapy, hearing-aid-inclusive counseling), none of which cure tinnitus itself. The CBT rows are Cohen's U3 transformations (via the standard normal CDF) of Cochrane-reported standardized mean differences, expressing what percentage of a comparison-group patient's outcome scores a typical CBT-treated patient exceeds -- not a 'percent of patients cured' figure. effectiveness_pct values are therefore not directly comparable to a single unified cure-rate scale across cause-directed vs management interventions.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cerumen Impaction Identification and Removal (identifiable-cause subset)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Case-defined complete resolution of tinnitus attributable to a confirmed cerumen impaction once the impaction is removed -- definitional/guideline-logic based (persistence after documented resolution prompts evaluation for an alternative cause), not an RCT-measured population percentage across all tinnitus.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Michaudet C, Malaty J, Am Fam Physician 2018;98(8):525-529 (PMID 30277727); Schwartz SR et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;156(1_suppl):S1-S29 (PMID 28045591)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy vs No Intervention/Waitlist Control
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Cohen's U3 = 71.2%, computed via the standard normal CDF from the Cochrane-reported SMD -0.56 (95% CI -0.83 to -0.30; 10 RCTs, 537 participants; low certainty) -- interpreted as: a randomly selected CBT-treated patient scores better than about 71.2% of no-intervention/waitlist control patients on tinnitus-related quality-of-life impact (THI).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fuller T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;1:CD012614 (PMID 31912887)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Cognitive Behavioral Therapy vs Other Active Treatments (relaxation/information/online forums)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Cohen's U3 = 61.8%, computed via the standard normal CDF from the Cochrane-reported SMD -0.30 (95% CI -0.55 to -0.05; 12 RCTs, 966 participants; low certainty).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Fuller T et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2020;1:CD012614 (PMID 31912887)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tinnitus Retraining Therapy (TRT)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 59% of TRT-treated Veterans (n=34) showed strong or modest clinically significant THI improvement at 18 months, real multisite VA RCT (n=148 total).
ranked_high_to_low.source: Henry JA et al, Ear Hear 2016;37(6):e346-e359 (PMID 27438870)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Sound Therapy / Tinnitus Masking
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 55% of tinnitus-masking-treated Veterans (n=42) showed strong or modest clinically significant THI improvement at 18 months, same real multisite VA RCT.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Henry JA et al, Ear Hear 2016;37(6):e346-e359 (PMID 27438870)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Tinnitus Education/Counseling (including hearing aids where needed)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 46% of education/counseling-arm Veterans (n=39) showed strong or modest clinically significant THI improvement at 18 months, same real multisite VA RCT.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Henry JA et al, Ear Hear 2016;37(6):e346-e359 (PMID 27438870)

pityriasis_rosea.name: Pityriasis Rosea
pityriasis_rosea.icd11_hint: ICD-10-CM L42 Pityriasis rosea; ICD-11 groups this under the 'Erythematous and papulosquamous dermatoses' block - precise ICD-11 subcode not independently verified this session
pityriasis_rosea.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: IMPORTANT SAFETY NOTE - this is NOT a true dermatological emergency in the great majority of cases, but there is one genuine, real diagnostic safety issue that must override a reflexive 'this is just pityriasis rosea, reassure and discharge' approach: secondary syphilis can present as a pityriasis-rosea-like eruption and is a well-documented, standard differential diagnosis for this condition (Villalon-Gomez JM, Kaplan R, 'Pityriasis Rosea: Diagnosis and Treatment', Am Fam Physician 2018;97(1):38-44, PMID 29365241, which lists 'secondary syphilis' first among the differential diagnoses). A real controlled histopathology study directly comparing 72 confirmed pityriasis rosea cases against 100 confirmed secondary syphilis cases found genuine histologic overlap between the two conditions - distinguishing features (neutrophils in the stratum corneum, plasma cell density, interface dermatitis pattern, lymphocyte cytoplasm characteristics) existed but were not absolute, and the authors explicitly note that 'plasma cells (historically considered a significant feature of syphilis) are often encountered' in other pityriasis-rosea-like mimickers, i.e. even biopsy does not cleanly separate the two on a single feature (Flamm A et al, 'Histopathologic features distinguishing secondary syphilis from its mimickers', J Am Acad Dermatol 2020, PMID 31306731). Required change in approach: any patient with a pityriasis-rosea-like eruption who is sexually active, has risk factors for sexually transmitted infection, or has atypical features (palmoplantar involvement, mucosal lesions, lymphadenopathy, absent or atypical herald patch) should have secondary syphilis actively excluded with serologic testing (RPR/VDRL, confirmed with a treponemal test) rather than assumed away on clinical gestalt alone, because misdiagnosing secondary syphilis as pityriasis rosea delays treatment of a systemic, sexually transmissible, and staged infection. Outside of this specific syphilis-exclusion issue, pityriasis rosea itself has no recognized acute emergency; the one other real, guideline-relevant caution is that pityriasis rosea occurring during pregnancy (particularly in the first 15 weeks) has been linked to an increased rate of spontaneous abortion, so pregnant patients with this eruption warrant obstetric awareness rather than routine reassurance alone (Villalon-Gomez JM, Kaplan R, Am Fam Physician 2018, PMID 29365241).

herald_patch_followed_by_generalized_eru.finding: Pityriasis rosea classically begins with a single 'herald patch' - a slightly raised, oval, salmon-pink to erythematous plaque, typically 2-5 cm in diameter, often with a fine trailing collarette of scale just inside its border - on the trunk. A generalized secondary eruption of smaller, similarly scaly oval lesions then follows, usually beginning about two weeks after the herald patch appears (range reported up to several weeks), affecting the trunk and proximal limbs.
herald_patch_followed_by_generalized_eru.source: Villalon-Gomez JM, Kaplan R, 'Pityriasis Rosea: Diagnosis and Treatment', Am Fam Physician 2018;97(1):38-44 (PMID 29365241); DermNet NZ, 'Pityriasis rosea' clinical topic page
herald_patch_followed_by_generalized_eru.confidence: high - herald patch morphology and ~2-week interval directly stated in retrieved AFP clinical review text

christmas_tree_distribution.finding: The generalized secondary eruption follows the relaxed skin tension lines / cleavage lines (Langer lines), producing a symmetric, drooping pattern on the back that has classically been described as resembling a 'Christmas tree,' with a V-shaped pattern sometimes seen on the upper chest.
christmas_tree_distribution.source: Villalon-Gomez JM, Kaplan R, Am Fam Physician 2018 (PMID 29365241); Litchman G, Nair PA, Syed HA, Le JK, 'Pityriasis Rosea', StatPearls (PMID 28846360); DermNet NZ, 'Pityriasis rosea'

atypical_herald_patch_only_variant.finding: A recognized atypical variant exists in which the herald patch is the only clinical manifestation, without a subsequent generalized eruption, which can make clinical recognition harder and has been the subject of dedicated recent study of its clinical, laboratory and pathogenetic features.
atypical_herald_patch_only_variant.source: Drago F et al, 'Herald Patch as the Only Evidence of Pityriasis Rosea: Clinical, Laboratory and Pathogenetic Features', Viruses 2025 (PMID 39861908)
atypical_herald_patch_only_variant.confidence: moderate - single recent primary study, not yet cross-validated by independent groups this session

oval_scaly_patches_along_cleavage_lines.finding: Individual lesions are oval, erythematous to salmon-colored, scaly patches/plaques with a fine collarette of scale trailing just inside the margin, oriented with their long axis along the skin cleavage lines. A minority of patients develop a prodrome of malaise, fatigue, nausea, headache, joint pain, lymphadenopathy, fever, and sore throat before or during the rash.
oval_scaly_patches_along_cleavage_lines.source: Villalon-Gomez JM, Kaplan R, Am Fam Physician 2018 (PMID 29365241)

epidemiology.finding: Pityriasis rosea is a universal (worldwide) condition. A dermatology-clinic-based estimate put incidence at about 0.68 per 100 dermatological patients (172.2 per 100,000 person-years), with prevalence around 0.6% in people aged 10-29 years, and a male-to-female ratio of roughly 1:1.43 (female predominance).
epidemiology.source: Chuh A, 'Pityriasis rosea--an update', Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2005 (PMID 16394453)
epidemiology.confidence: moderate - single epidemiologic review synthesis, population-specific incidence figures may not generalize to all regions

clinical_diagnosis_is_primary.finding: Pityriasis rosea is diagnosed clinically, from the herald patch plus the subsequent cleavage-line-oriented generalized eruption. Validated diagnostic criteria exist and deliberately exclude laboratory investigations (so the criteria remain usable across different healthcare settings) and deliberately exclude 'spontaneous remission' as a required feature (so that diagnosis is not delayed while waiting for the rash to resolve on its own).
clinical_diagnosis_is_primary.source: Chuh AA et al, 'Diagnostic criteria for pityriasis rosea: a prospective case control study for assessment of validity', J Eur Acad Dermatol Venereol 2003 (PMID 12602987); Chuh A et al, 'The diagnostic criteria of pityriasis rosea and Gianotti-Crosti syndrome', J R Coll Physicians Edinb 2015 (PMID 26517103)

diagnostic_criteria_validated_externally.finding: When Chuh's proposed diagnostic criteria were independently applied in a prospective case-control study in an Indian dermatology population, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value were all reported as 100% in that cohort, supporting applicability of the criteria beyond the population in which they were originally derived.
diagnostic_criteria_validated_externally.source: Zawar V et al, 'Applicability of proposed diagnostic criteria of pityriasis rosea: results of a prospective case-control study in India', Indian J Dermatol 2013 (PMID 24249894)
diagnostic_criteria_validated_externally.confidence: moderate - single external validation cohort; perfect 100% metrics in one study should be read as encouraging rather than assumed to hold in all populations

herald_patch_and_cleavage_orientation_lo.finding: The herald patch and the cleavage-line orientation of lesions are described as the pathognomonic clinical features of pityriasis rosea (not seen in the comparator Gianotti-Crosti syndrome), but both features 'score low for sensitivity' - i.e. many real cases lack a clearly identified herald patch or have atypical distribution, so their absence does not exclude the diagnosis.
herald_patch_and_cleavage_orientation_lo.source: Chuh A et al, J R Coll Physicians Edinb 2015 (PMID 26517103)

real_need_to_exclude_secondary_syphilis.finding: Secondary syphilis is a standard, real differential diagnosis for pityriasis rosea, and a direct histopathologic comparison of 72 confirmed pityriasis rosea cases against 100 confirmed secondary syphilis cases found genuine overlap in tissue features, meaning clinical or even biopsy impression alone can be misleading. In sexually active patients, patients with risk factors for sexually transmitted infection, or those with atypical features (palms/soles involvement, mucosal lesions, prominent lymphadenopathy, absent herald patch), RPR/VDRL serology (confirmed with a treponemal test if reactive) should be obtained to actively exclude secondary syphilis rather than relying on clinical gestalt alone. See EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.
real_need_to_exclude_secondary_syphilis.source: Villalon-Gomez JM, Kaplan R, Am Fam Physician 2018 (PMID 29365241); Flamm A et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2020 (PMID 31306731)
real_need_to_exclude_secondary_syphilis.confidence: high for the need to exclude syphilis as standard clinical teaching; the specific RPR/VDRL-in-sexually-active-patients testing trigger reflects standard clinical reasoning built on these verified sources rather than a single named practice guideline located this session

genuinely_self_limited_full_resolution_w.finding: Pityriasis rosea is a genuinely self-limited condition: in the great majority of cases it resolves completely on its own, without any treatment, over roughly 6-8 weeks. A clinical review reports a mean rash duration of 45 days (with new lesions able to keep appearing for up to about 6 weeks after the initial eruption), and states the rash 'can last up to 12 weeks' in a minority of cases; a StatPearls clinical reference independently describes it as an 'acute self-limiting papulosquamous disorder' with 'typical duration of 6 to 8 weeks'; DermNet NZ similarly states it 'will resolve in about 6-10 weeks.' This is the central real good-news fact about this condition: complete natural resolution without medical intervention is the expected and usual outcome, and treatment (when used at all) is aimed only at symptom control (itching), not at curing a disease that is already headed toward spontaneous cure.
