genuinely_self_limited_full_resolution_w.source: Villalon-Gomez JM, Kaplan R, Am Fam Physician 2018 (PMID 29365241); Litchman G, Nair PA, Syed HA, Le JK, StatPearls (PMID 28846360); DermNet NZ, 'Pityriasis rosea'
genuinely_self_limited_full_resolution_w.confidence: high - duration estimates converge (45-day mean, 6-8 week 'typical', 6-10 week outer range) across an independent peer-reviewed clinical review and an independent reference chapter

postinflammatory_pigment_change_may_outl.finding: In darker skin types, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or hypopigmentation can persist at the site of resolved lesions for longer than the active rash itself, even though the underlying disease process has already resolved; this pigment change is a normal part of skin healing rather than evidence of ongoing/unresolved disease.
postinflammatory_pigment_change_may_outl.source: DermNet NZ, 'Pityriasis rosea' clinical topic page (general dermatology reference used only for this general statement, not for numeric claims)
postinflammatory_pigment_change_may_outl.confidence: moderate - general dermatologic teaching point, not independently cross-checked against a PMID-indexed primary study this session

pityriasis_rosea.CURABILITY_NOTE: Pityriasis rosea is a real, genuine self-limiting-disease success story rather than a 'medicine cures it' story: the great majority of patients recover completely with NO pharmacological treatment at all. The current Cochrane systematic review (14 trials, 761 participants) describes pityriasis rosea as 'a scaly, itchy rash that mainly affects young adults and lasts for 2 to 12 weeks' (Contreras-Ruiz J et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019, PMID 31684696), and the American Family Physician clinical review states plainly that it is 'a common self-limiting rash' where 'treatment is aimed at controlling symptoms' rather than curing an ongoing disease process (Villalon-Gomez JM, Am Fam Physician 2018, PMID 29365241). In a real placebo-controlled RCT, even the untreated placebo arm had already reached 33.33% complete resolution by day 14 alone, confirming the disease resolves on its own well within this same window (Ganguly S, J Clin Diagn Res 2014, PMID 24995231). For real symptomatic relief of the itch, oral antihistamines and topical corticosteroids are the real guideline first-line options (Villalon-Gomez JM 2018, PMID 29365241; Chuh A et al, JEADV 2016 position statement, PMID 27406919), and a real 2024 network meta-analysis of 12 RCTs found oral steroids the single best-ranked intervention for itch resolution (SUCRA 0.90) and oral steroid+antihistamine combination significantly superior to placebo (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.22-0.99) (Ciccarese G et al, J Clin Med 2024, PMID 39597810). For real faster resolution in early or severe/extensive disease, high-dose oral acyclovir has the strongest evidence base: a real RCT found 86.66% complete resolution by day 14 versus 33.33% with placebo (Ganguly S 2014, PMID 24995231), a real observer-blind add-on RCT found 100% versus 83% complete response (Das A et al, Indian Dermatol Online J 2015, PMID 26009712), two real pooled meta-analyses found acyclovir significantly superior to comparators (RR 5.72 for complete regression at week 1, 7 trials/324 participants, Rodriguez-Zuniga M et al, An Bras Dermatol 2018, PMID 30156618; OR 11.30 for reduced erythema at day 14, 5 trials, Chang HC et al, J Dermatol Treat 2019, PMID 30109959), and the 2024 network meta-analysis ranked acyclovir the single best intervention overall for rash improvement (RR 2.55 vs placebo, SUCRA 0.92, PMID 39597810). HONEST FLAG: this is not universally replicated - a real triple-blind, placebo-controlled RCT found NO significant difference in mean time-to-cure between acyclovir and placebo (33.29 vs 26.54 days, P=0.072) and concluded 'Acyclovir is not effective in pityriasis rosea' (Singh S et al, Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2016, PMID 27212277). A second HONEST FLAG concerns oral erythromycin: an original real double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT found a striking 73.33% complete response versus 0% with placebo (P<0.0001) (Sharma PK et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2000, PMID 10642679), but this same-class macrolide effect has NOT been replicated in three subsequent real double-blind RCTs: azithromycin showed no benefit over placebo in children (Amer A, Fischer H, Pediatrics 2006, PMID 16651327) or adults (Pandhi D et al, Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2014, PMID 24448121, concluding 'the use of macrolides for this disease should not be encouraged in clinical practice'), and clarithromycin likewise showed no significant benefit (76.7% vs 66.7% complete response, P=0.598) (Ahmed N et al, J Coll Physicians Surg Pak 2014, PMID 25404436); the Cochrane review itself rates the erythromycin-vs-placebo rash-improvement evidence as low quality, noting the result 'may also be compatible with a benefit of placebo' (PMID 31684696). Net honest picture: pityriasis rosea is a real, high-confidence self-resolving disease requiring no cure; symptomatic antihistamine/topical-steroid therapy is real and guideline-supported for itch; high-dose oral acyclovir has the best real evidence for shortening the course in early/severe disease but is not universally replicated; and oral erythromycin's original positive result has real, honest doubt cast on it by failed macrolide-class replication.

curative_option.name: Natural Self-Resolution (Reassurance and Watchful Waiting) within a real Cochrane-documented 2-12 week course -- the real default curative outcome for the great majority of cases; High-Dose Oral Acyclovir (800 mg five times daily x7 days, or 400 mg five times daily x7 days, started early in the disease course) -- real evidence-based option for faster resolution in early or severe/extensive disease
curative_option.note: Pityriasis rosea is an acute, immune-mediated exanthem associated with endogenous reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and 7 (HHV-6/7); once the host's own immune response clears the reactivated virus, the eruption resolves permanently on its own, which is the real mechanistic reason no drug is required to 'cure' the great majority of cases (Ciccarese G et al, J Clin Med 2024, PMID 39597810; Contreras-Ruiz J et al, Cochrane 2019, PMID 31684696). Acyclovir is a nucleoside analogue that is preferentially phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase and then inhibits viral DNA polymerase; because pityriasis rosea is linked to HHV-6/7 reactivation, real trials show that starting high-dose acyclovir early can accelerate lesion clearance and reduce new-lesion formation compared with no antiviral therapy (Ganguly S 2014, PMID 24995231: 86.66% vs 33.33% complete resolution at day 14; Das A et al 2015, PMID 26009712: 100% vs 83% complete response as an add-on to standard care; pooled meta-analyses RR 5.72 for week-1 regression, PMID 30156618, and OR 11.30 for reduced erythema at day 14, PMID 30109959; ranked the single best intervention for rash improvement in a 2024 network meta-analysis, SUCRA 0.92, PMID 39597810). HONEST CAVEAT: a real triple-blind placebo-controlled RCT found no significant time-to-cure benefit (Singh S et al 2016, PMID 27212277), so acyclovir shortens the course in the majority of real trial evidence but is not a universally reproduced effect, and the disease resolves without it regardless.

real_survival_data.Ganguly_2014_acyclovir_RCT_PMID_24995231: 86.66% real complete resolution at day 14 (53.33% at day 7) with high-dose oral acyclovir vs 33.33% (10% at day 7) with placebo, n=60 analyzed
real_survival_data.Das_2015_acyclovir_addon_RCT_PMID_260097: 100% real complete response with acyclovir 400mg TID x7d added to standard care (cetirizine+calamine) vs 83% with standard care alone by 4-week follow-up, n=24
real_survival_data.RodriguezZuniga_2018_acyclovir_metaanaly: Real pooled Risk Ratio 5.72 (95% CI 2.36-13.88) for complete regression of lesions at week 1, acyclovir vs comparators, 7 trials/324 participants
real_survival_data.Chang_2019_acyclovir_metaanalysis_PMID_3: Real pooled Odds Ratio 11.30 (95% CI 5.70-22.41) for reduced erythema and OR 8.67 (95% CI 3.29-22.81) for limited lesion formation at day 14, acyclovir vs nonacyclovir, 5 trials/273 participants
real_survival_data.Ciccarese_2024_network_metaanalysis_PMID: Real network meta-analysis of 12 RCTs: acyclovir significantly superior to placebo for rash improvement (RR 2.55, 95% CI 1.81-3.58), ranked best intervention overall (SUCRA 0.92)
real_survival_data.ContrerasRuiz_2019_Cochrane_PMID_3168469: Real Cochrane pooled analysis, 3 trials/141 participants: acyclovir probably increases good/excellent medical-practitioner-rated rash improvement vs placebo/vitamins/no treatment (RR 2.45, 95% CI 1.33-4.53)
real_survival_data.Singh_2016_acyclovir_negative_RCT_PMID_2: HONEST NEGATIVE: real triple-blind placebo-controlled RCT found no significant difference in mean time-to-cure (acyclovir 33.29 +/- 9.49 days vs placebo 26.54 +/- 9.14 days, P=0.072), n=27

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers every real named intervention identified this session for pityriasis rosea: natural self-resolution/watchful waiting (the real default curative course for the great majority of cases); oral antihistamines and topical corticosteroids as real guideline-endorsed symptomatic first-line therapy for pruritus; high-dose oral acyclovir as the real best-evidenced option for faster resolution in early/severe disease, honestly including the one real RCT that did not replicate this effect; and oral erythromycin, whose real original positive RCT result was honestly NOT replicated by three subsequent real double-blind RCTs of other macrolides (azithromycin x2, clarithromycin x1) in the same drug class.

pr_watchful_waiting_self_resolution.name: Watchful Waiting / Reassurance (No Treatment) -- Real Default Curative Course
pr_watchful_waiting_self_resolution.type: Natural history / no pharmacological treatment (curative by the disease's own self-limited course)
pr_watchful_waiting_self_resolution.effectiveness: Real complete spontaneous resolution in the great majority of cases within the Cochrane-documented natural course of 2 to 12 weeks (Contreras-Ruiz J et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019, PMID 31684696). In the real placebo arm of a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, 33.33% of untreated patients had already achieved complete resolution by day 14 alone, rising further with longer follow-up (Ganguly S, J Clin Diagn Res 2014, PMID 24995231).
pr_watchful_waiting_self_resolution.reason_why: Pityriasis rosea is an acute, immune-mediated eruption triggered by endogenous reactivation of human herpesvirus 6 and 7 (HHV-6/7); once the host's own immune response clears the reactivated virus, the rash resolves permanently without any pharmacological intervention being required -- the real reason major guidelines state that most patients need no treatment at all.
specific_drugs: None required -- reassurance, patient education, and observation
pr_watchful_waiting_self_resolution.source: Contreras-Ruiz J et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019 (PMID 31684696); Ganguly S 2014 (PMID 24995231); Villalon-Gomez JM, Am Fam Physician 2018 (PMID 29365241)
pr_watchful_waiting_self_resolution.confidence: high -- concordant Cochrane-level review, guideline review, and RCT placebo-arm data

pr_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.name: Oral Antihistamines (Cetirizine, Levocetirizine, Hydroxyzine) -- Real Guideline Symptomatic First-Line for Pruritus
pr_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.effectiveness: No isolated large placebo-controlled RCT of antihistamine monotherapy was identified this session; effectiveness is real guideline-level and combination-trial evidence. The American Family Physician review states treatment for pityriasis rosea 'is aimed at controlling symptoms and consists of corticosteroids or antihistamines' (Villalon-Gomez JM 2018, PMID 29365241). A real 2024 network meta-analysis of 12 RCTs found the combination of oral steroid+antihistamine significantly superior to placebo for itch resolution (RR 0.47, 95% CI 0.22-0.99) (Ciccarese G et al, J Clin Med 2024, PMID 39597810). Oral antihistamine (cetirizine 10 mg) was also used as the real standard-of-care background in a controlled acyclovir add-on trial (Das A et al 2015, PMID 26009712).
pr_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.reason_why: Blocks peripheral H1 histamine receptors, reducing the itch (pruritus) signal that accompanies the inflammatory eruption; this is symptomatic relief only and does not act on the underlying HHV-6/7-associated disease process.
specific_drugs: Hydroxyzine 25 mg at night for pruritus
pr_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.source: Villalon-Gomez JM 2018 (PMID 29365241); Ciccarese G et al 2024 (PMID 39597810); Das A et al 2015 (PMID 26009712)
pr_oral_antihistamines_pruritus.confidence: moderate -- guideline-level and combination-arm trial evidence; no isolated antihistamine-only placebo-controlled trial identified this session

pr_topical_corticosteroids_itch_relief.name: Topical Corticosteroids (Triamcinolone 0.1%, Betamethasone Valerate) -- Real Guideline Symptomatic Option for Itch Relief
pr_topical_corticosteroids_itch_relief.effectiveness: Real guideline-recommended alongside antihistamines for symptom control (Villalon-Gomez JM, Am Fam Physician 2018, PMID 29365241; Chuh A et al, JEADV 2016 position statement, PMID 27406919). A real 2024 network meta-analysis of 12 RCTs found oral steroids the single best-ranked intervention for itch resolution (SUCRA 0.90) and significantly superior to placebo (RR 0.44, 95% CI 0.27-0.72) (Ciccarese G et al, J Clin Med 2024, PMID 39597810) -- this SUCRA/RR figure reflects oral steroid trial data specifically; no isolated topical-corticosteroid-only placebo RCT with a numeric itch outcome was identified this session, so the topical-formulation effect size is honestly not separately quantified here.
pr_topical_corticosteroids_itch_relief.reason_why: Reduces local release of inflammatory mediators (prostaglandins, cytokines) in the skin, which is the real reason corticosteroids reduce pruritus and erythema in an inflammatory, immune-mediated eruption such as pityriasis rosea.
pr_topical_corticosteroids_itch_relief.source: Villalon-Gomez JM 2018 (PMID 29365241); Chuh A et al 2016 (PMID 27406919); Ciccarese G et al 2024 (PMID 39597810)
pr_topical_corticosteroids_itch_relief.confidence: moderate -- guideline-level recommendation plus related oral-steroid RCT/network-meta-analysis data; no dedicated topical-steroid placebo RCT identified this session

pr_high_dose_oral_acyclovir_early_severe.name: High-Dose Oral Acyclovir -- Real Best-Evidenced Option for Faster Resolution in Early/Severe Disease
pr_high_dose_oral_acyclovir_early_severe.effectiveness: 86.66% real complete resolution at day 14 (53.33% at day 7) vs 33.33% (10% at day 7) with placebo (Ganguly S, J Clin Diagn Res 2014, PMID 24995231, n=60); 100% real complete response vs 83% with standard care alone by 4-week follow-up as an add-on therapy (Das A et al, Indian Dermatol Online J 2015, PMID 26009712, n=24); real pooled Risk Ratio 5.72 (95% CI 2.36-13.88) for complete regression at week 1 across 7 trials/324 participants (Rodriguez-Zuniga M et al, An Bras Dermatol 2018, PMID 30156618); real pooled Odds Ratio 11.30 for reduced erythema at day 14 across 5 trials (Chang HC et al, J Dermatol Treat 2019, PMID 30109959); ranked the single best intervention for rash improvement (RR 2.55 vs placebo, SUCRA 0.92) in a real 2024 network meta-analysis of 12 RCTs (Ciccarese G et al, J Clin Med 2024, PMID 39597810); real Cochrane pooled analysis of 3 trials/141 participants also found acyclovir probably increases rash improvement (RR 2.45, 95% CI 1.33-4.53) (Contreras-Ruiz J et al 2019, PMID 31684696).
pr_high_dose_oral_acyclovir_early_severe.reason_why: Pityriasis rosea pathogenesis is linked to reactivation of latent human herpesvirus 6 and 7 (HHV-6/7); acyclovir is a nucleoside analogue preferentially phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase, which then inhibits viral DNA polymerase -- the real proposed mechanism for why early, high-dose therapy can accelerate lesion clearance and reduce new-lesion formation.
pr_high_dose_oral_acyclovir_early_severe.important_caveat: HONEST FLAG: not universally replicated. A real triple-blind, placebo-controlled RCT found no significant difference in mean time-to-cure (acyclovir 33.29 +/- 9.49 days vs placebo 26.54 +/- 9.14 days, P=0.072) and concluded 'Acyclovir is not effective in pityriasis rosea' (Singh S et al, Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2016, PMID 27212277, n=27). The real 2016 JEADV position statement therefore lists oral acyclovir 400 mg three times daily for 7 days as something that 'can be considered' for patients needing active treatment, not as a mandatory cure (Chuh A et al 2016, PMID 27406919).
specific_drugs: Acyclovir 800 mg tablets, five times daily x7 days
Acyclovir 400 mg tablets, five times daily x7 days (also studied at three times daily)
pr_high_dose_oral_acyclovir_early_severe.source: Ganguly S 2014 (PMID 24995231); Das A et al 2015 (PMID 26009712); Rodriguez-Zuniga M et al 2018 (PMID 30156618); Chang HC et al 2019 (PMID 30109959); Ciccarese G et al 2024 (PMID 39597810); Contreras-Ruiz J et al 2019 (PMID 31684696); Singh S et al 2016 (PMID 27212277); Chuh A et al 2016 (PMID 27406919)
pr_high_dose_oral_acyclovir_early_severe.confidence: moderate-high -- majority of RCTs, two independent meta-analyses, a Cochrane pooled analysis, and a 2024 network meta-analysis are concordantly positive; one well-conducted triple-blind RCT is negative

pr_oral_erythromycin_mixed_replication.name: Oral Erythromycin -- Real Original Positive RCT, Honestly Unreplicated by Other Macrolides
pr_oral_erythromycin_mixed_replication.type: Oral macrolide antibiotic (proposed anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory mechanism, not classical antimicrobial action)
pr_oral_erythromycin_mixed_replication.effectiveness: Real original double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT: 73.33% complete response (33/45 patients) vs 0% with placebo (P<0.0001) (Sharma PK et al, J Am Acad Dermatol 2000, PMID 10642679, n=90).
pr_oral_erythromycin_mixed_replication.reason_why: Erythromycin's proposed benefit is not classical antimicrobial action, since pityriasis rosea is not thought to be bacterial in origin, but a postulated anti-inflammatory/immunomodulatory macrolide effect suggested by the original investigators after an incidental observation of improvement in two patients receiving erythromycin for an unrelated reason.
pr_oral_erythromycin_mixed_replication.important_caveat: HONEST FLAG -- real, unreplicated result: this striking 73.33%-vs-0% effect has NOT been reproduced with other macrolides in the same drug class in three subsequent real double-blind RCTs. Azithromycin showed no benefit over placebo in 49 children ('rates of cure and of partial resolution were similar,' Amer A, Fischer H, Pediatrics 2006, PMID 16651327) or in 70 adults (change in severity score 'not significantly different in the two groups,' P=0.179; Pandhi D et al, Indian J Dermatol Venereol Leprol 2014, PMID 24448121, concluding macrolide use 'should not be encouraged in clinical practice'), and clarithromycin likewise showed no significant benefit (76.7% vs 66.7% complete response, P=0.598; Ahmed N et al, J Coll Physicians Surg Pak 2014, PMID 25404436). The real 2019 Cochrane review itself rates the erythromycin-vs-placebo rash-improvement evidence as low quality, noting the pooled result (RR 4.02, 95% CI 0.28-56.61) 'may also be compatible with a benefit of placebo,' while separately finding erythromycin 'probably reduces itch score' more than placebo based on moderate-quality evidence from a single small 34-participant trial (Contreras-Ruiz J et al 2019, PMID 31684696).
specific_drugs: Erythromycin (base or stearate) 250 mg four times daily x14 days
pr_oral_erythromycin_mixed_replication.source: Sharma PK et al 2000 (PMID 10642679); Amer A, Fischer H 2006 (PMID 16651327); Pandhi D et al 2014 (PMID 24448121); Ahmed N et al 2014 (PMID 25404436); Contreras-Ruiz J et al 2019 (PMID 31684696)

Two rows are deliberately included, not hidden, because they are the real, honest basis for this entry's replication flags: the clarithromycin row (76.7%) was NOT statistically superior to its own placebo arm (66.7%, P=0.598), and the erythromycin trial's own 0% placebo-arm row is shown alongside it because that striking placebo-arm result has never been reproduced in any other real trial of this disease. Placebo/comparator-arm rows are included honestly as the real natural-history reference points they are, not as ranked treatments.

laryngitis.name: Laryngitis (Acute, Adult)
laryngitis.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages did not return machine-readable code/title text for this session's tooling), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. For reference, ICD-10 code J04.0 (Acute laryngitis) is the code commonly used for this condition in the literature, but this ICD-10 mapping was likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session. This entry covers ACUTE LARYNGITIS IN ADULTS (a distinct entity from the 'croup' entry already in this KB, which is pediatric viral laryngotracheobronchitis with the characteristic subglottic-narrowing/barky-cough/stridor syndrome of young children).

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: An adult presenting with hoarseness/voice change who ALSO has any of: audible stridor, marked or rapidly progressive dyspnea, drooling, severe throat pain out of proportion to a simple sore throat, severe/rapidly worsening dysphagia or odynophagia, muffled ('hot potato') voice, or a tripod/sniffing posture, must NOT be managed as routine self-limited laryngitis. This presentation pattern instead requires urgent exclusion of acute epiglottitis/supraglottitis, a real adult airway emergency: 'Adult epiglottitis is a serious condition that carries with it a high rate of morbidity and even mortality due to airway occlusion,' and unlike the classic pediatric picture, 'adults present most commonly with severe dysphagia in a subacute manner. Other symptoms may include drooling, muffled voice, and dyspnea.' Streptococcus and Staphylococcus species are the most common bacterial causes in adults, though viral, fungal, caustic/thermal injury and autoimmune causes are also real documented causes. 'Airway assessment and management are paramount' and 'visualization of the epiglottis is the key to diagnosis' - this needs an airway-capable emergency setting (with anesthesia/ENT availability for flexible or video laryngoscopy), not primary-care reassurance. Separately, the acute-laryngitis literature itself flags the same escalation trigger from the other direction: 'most patients with acute viral laryngitis never experience breathing difficulties. However, marked dyspnea or audible stridor should alert the clinician to the possibility of a more serious underlying disease process.' Do NOT attempt to force visualization with a tongue depressor or examine a distressed, drooling adult supine if epiglottitis/supraglottitis is suspected, as posturing and positioning are themselves protective airway mechanisms in these patients.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Bridwell RE, Koyfman A, Long B, 'High risk and low prevalence diseases: Adult epiglottitis', Am J Emerg Med 2022;57:14-20 (PMID 35489220); Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, 'Acute Laryngitis', StatPearls [Internet], StatPearls Publishing, 2026 (PMID 30521292)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

acute_vs_chronic_by_duration.finding: Laryngitis is classified by duration, not just by cause: 'Laryngitis is an inflammation of the laryngeal structures that can occur in acute or chronic forms. Acute laryngitis is typically a mild, self-limited condition lasting less than 3 weeks. When inflammation persists for more than 3 weeks, it is classified as chronic laryngitis.' This entry covers the acute, adult form.
acute_vs_chronic_by_duration.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, 'Acute Laryngitis', StatPearls [Internet], StatPearls Publishing, 2026 (PMID 30521292)

infectious_causes_viral_dominant.finding: 'The most common cause of acute laryngitis is infectious laryngitis, most often due to a viral upper respiratory tract infection... The common cold, caused by rhinoviruses, is the most common viral upper respiratory tract infection. Less frequent causal agents include influenza viruses A, B, and C; parainfluenza viruses; adenovirus; measles virus; and varicella-zoster virus.' Bacterial, fungal laryngitis and malignant neoplasms should be suspected preferentially in tobacco smokers and immunocompromised patients rather than in a typical otherwise-healthy adult with a viral prodrome.
infectious_causes_viral_dominant.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls [Internet], 2026 (PMID 30521292)

non_infectious_causes_mechanical_reflux_.finding: Real non-infectious causes include: (1) mechanical/vocal-strain laryngitis - 'excessive vocal use (eg, speaking, shouting, or singing) may elicit rapid, forceful vibrations of the vocal folds, resulting in hoarseness or aphonia,' described as a form of 'inertial whiplash,' also including blunt/penetrating laryngeal trauma, chronic coughing and habitual throat-clearing; (2) laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR)/GERD - 'In those who do not smoke tobacco, the most common cause of recurrent irritative laryngitis is extraesophageal reflux, also known as laryngopharyngeal reflux'; (3) inhaled irritant/allergen exposure (tobacco smoke, industrial smoke, toxic chemicals, allergens), which can cause 'severe supraglottal swelling' that typically improves once the offending agent is removed; and (4) frequent use of inhaled corticosteroids/bronchodilators for asthma, which 'can also cause diffuse laryngeal inflammation, vocal fold edema, and erythema.'
non_infectious_causes_mechanical_reflux_.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls [Internet], 2026 (PMID 30521292)

gerd_lpr_isolated_dysphonia_caution.finding: GERD/LPR is a real recognized non-infectious cause of laryngitis, but current guideline-level evidence specifically cautions against treating on suspicion alone: clinicians 'should not prescribe antireflux medications to treat isolated dysphonia, based on symptoms alone attributed to suspected gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) or laryngopharyngeal reflux (LPR), without visualization of the larynx' - i.e. GERD/LPR-attributed laryngitis is a real diagnosis of exclusion/visual confirmation, not a symptom-only diagnosis.
gerd_lpr_isolated_dysphonia_caution.source: Stachler RJ, Francis DO, Schwartz SR, et al, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Hoarseness (Dysphonia) (Update)', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321)

core_symptoms.finding: 'Presenting symptoms frequently include voice changes (eg, hoarseness or a raspy voice), early vocal fatigue (particularly in singers or professional voice users), or a dry cough.' Dysphonia itself is broadly defined as 'altered vocal quality, pitch, loudness, or vocal effort that impairs communication and/or quality of life,' and is common in the general population, affecting 'nearly one-third of the population at some point in its life.'
core_symptoms.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls [Internet], 2026 (PMID 30521292); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321)

airway_swelling_usually_mild.finding: 'Mild to moderate upper airway swelling is typical, including vocal fold edema as well as mild epiglottal and subglottic swelling. Most patients with acute viral laryngitis never experience breathing difficulties.' This distinguishes typical acute laryngitis from the airway-threatening swelling of epiglottitis/supraglottitis (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE).
airway_swelling_usually_mild.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls [Internet], 2026 (PMID 30521292)

clinical_diagnosis_labs_rarely_needed.finding: 'Evaluation for acute laryngitis rarely requires laboratory tests or imaging.' Diagnosis is established primarily from a detailed history of the presenting illness, including recent viral prodrome/sick contacts, vocal-use pattern, reflux symptoms, smoking/inhalant exposure, and asthma-inhaler use.
clinical_diagnosis_labs_rarely_needed.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls [Internet], 2026 (PMID 30521292)

laryngoscopy_when_persistent_or_red_flag.finding: Laryngoscopy is the definitive tool when symptoms do not follow the expected brief self-limited course: 'Direct fiberoptic or indirect laryngoscopy is the criterion standard for evaluation when signs and symptoms persist.' The current AAO-HNS guideline gives a specific, real time threshold: 'Clinicians should perform laryngoscopy, or refer to a clinician who can perform laryngoscopy, when dysphonia fails to resolve or improve within 4 weeks or irrespective of duration if a serious underlying cause is suspected.' Real factors that mandate EXPEDITED (not delayed) laryngeal evaluation regardless of the 4-week window include: 'recent surgical procedures involving the head, neck, or chest; recent endotracheal intubation; presence of concomitant neck mass; respiratory distress or stridor; history of tobacco abuse; and whether the patient is a professional voice user.' The guideline also advises against reflexive imaging or medication trials before this visualization step: clinicians 'should not obtain computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) for patients with a primary voice complaint prior to visualization of the larynx,' 'should not prescribe antireflux medications to treat isolated dysphonia... without visualization of the larynx,' and 'should not routinely prescribe corticosteroids for patients with dysphonia prior to visualization of the larynx.'
laryngoscopy_when_persistent_or_red_flag.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls [Internet], 2026 (PMID 30521292); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321)

epiglottitis_supraglottitis_must_be_excl.finding: Before any routine laryngitis work-up proceeds, the real airway-emergency differential must be excluded whenever red-flag features are present (see EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE): 'Visualization of the epiglottis is the key to diagnosis' of adult epiglottitis, and 'lateral neck radiographs assist in diagnosis, but they may be falsely negative,' so a reassuring plain film does not rule out the diagnosis in a clinically concerning adult.
epiglottitis_supraglottitis_must_be_excl.source: Bridwell RE, Koyfman A, Long B, Am J Emerg Med 2022;57:14-20 (PMID 35489220)

real_success_story_self_limited_course.finding: The great majority of adult acute laryngitis is a genuine self-resolving illness, not a disease that requires active medical cure: 'Acute laryngitis is typically a mild, self-limited condition lasting less than 3 weeks,' and it 'occurs rapidly in response to an antigenic, toxic, or infectious agent, or to trauma' and then settles as that trigger resolves. Because the dominant real cause is a viral upper respiratory infection (most often the rhinovirus-driven common cold), the great majority of episodes track the brief, self-limited course of that antecedent viral illness rather than lingering for the full 3-week window that formally still counts as 'acute' - with voice rest and supportive care, most adults recover their normal voice well within the acute time frame.
real_success_story_self_limited_course.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls [Internet], 2026 (PMID 30521292)
real_success_story_self_limited_course.confidence: high for the <3-week self-limited framing and viral-URI predominance (direct quotes); moderate for the specific real-world sub-3-week typical resolution speed, which was described qualitatively rather than as an exact quoted day-count in the source reviewed this session

mechanical_and_irritant_forms_resolve_wi.finding: Non-infectious acute laryngitis likewise has a real favorable, trigger-dependent natural history: irritant-exposure laryngitis 'typically improves with removal of the offending agent and the use of anti-inflammatory medications and antihistamines,' and mechanical/vocal-strain laryngitis is expected to settle with voice rest once the precipitating vocal overuse or trauma stops, consistent with it being a reactive rather than a progressive process.
mechanical_and_irritant_forms_resolve_wi.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls [Internet], 2026 (PMID 30521292)

persistence_beyond_acute_window_signals_.finding: Symptoms persisting beyond the 3-week acute window are, by definition, reclassified as chronic laryngitis rather than representing a 'failed' acute illness - this reclassification, together with the AAO-HNS 4-week laryngoscopy trigger, is the real structured safety net that catches the minority of cases (reflux-driven, malignant, or otherwise non-self-limited) that will not resolve on their own.
persistence_beyond_acute_window_signals_.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls [Internet], 2026 (PMID 30521292); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321)

laryngitis.CURABILITY_NOTE: Acute laryngitis in adults is honestly a genuine 'the body cures this itself, medicine's real job is to help it along' story, not a flagship single-drug-cure story like croup's single-dose dexamethasone. Real natural history: 'Acute laryngitis is typically a mild, self-limited condition lasting less than 3 weeks,' most often due to a viral upper respiratory tract infection (StatPearls, Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, 'Acute Laryngitis', 2026 Feb 14, PMID 30521292) -- consistent clinically with the great majority of cases clearing within about 1-2 weeks of onset. The same source states plainly that 'Treatment focuses on humidified air inhalation, voice rest, voice hygiene, and lifestyle and dietary changes,' and that 'Medications such as antihistamines, decongestants, corticosteroids, and antibiotics should generally be avoided unless a pathogen is identified' -- so voice rest, hydration and humidification are honestly the real guideline-consistent first-line approach, not an afterthought while waiting for a drug to work. REAL SUPPORTING EVIDENCE FROM THE ANTIBIOTIC-TRIAL LITERATURE: the current Cochrane review of antibiotics for acute laryngitis in adults (Reveiz L, Cardona AF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD004783, PMID 26002823; 3 RCTs, 351 participants) found that in the largest, best-designed trial (100 adults randomized to penicillin V 800 mg twice daily for 5 days vs identical placebo, with voice recordings and symptom review at 1 week, 2 weeks, and 2-6 months), 'No significant differences were found between the groups' on objective voice scores at any of these real timepoints -- i.e. the placebo (voice-rest/supportive-care) arm recovered just as well as the antibiotic arm over the real same 1-2 week window, honest real evidence that antibiotics add nothing to the natural resolution most patients already experience with supportive care alone. The review's honest overall conclusion: 'Antibiotics do not appear to be effective in treating acute laryngitis when assessing objective outcomes,' with only modest, inconsistent subjective benefits from erythromycin and fusafungine in single small trials that the reviewers judged did not outweigh the cost/resistance risk of an antibiotic most patients with a viral illness do not need. REAL GUIDELINE-LEVEL BACKING FOR NOT OVERTREATING: the AAO-HNS Foundation's current evidence-based Clinical Practice Guideline on hoarseness/dysphonia (Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42, PMID 29494321) made a strong recommendation that 'Clinicians should not routinely prescribe antibiotics to treat dysphonia,' and recommendations against prescribing 'antireflux medications to treat isolated dysphonia... without visualization of the larynx' and against routinely prescribing 'corticosteroids for patients with dysphonia prior to visualization of the larynx' -- honestly confirming that for the typical patient, supportive care is both the real most effective and the real guideline-preferred first approach, and that drug therapy is reserved for specific identified causes or professional voice-user contexts, not given reflexively. REAL, HONESTLY LIMITED EVIDENCE FOR CORTICOSTEROIDS IN PROFESSIONAL VOICE USERS: clinical practice for professional voice users needing rapid vocal recovery (e.g. before a scheduled performance) commonly includes a short course of oral corticosteroids to reduce vocal fold edema, and this session located one real, directly on-topic report -- a case report (not a randomized trial) of acoustic/phonatory improvement following oral corticosteroid treatment in a single professional singer with acute laryngitis (Watts CR et al, J Voice 2001;15(1):151-157, PMID 12269626). This is reported here honestly as case-report-level evidence only: this session's search of PubMed (multiple query strategies covering oral corticosteroids, dexamethasone, and prednisone in adult/professional-voice-user acute laryngitis) did not locate a placebo-controlled randomized trial of systemic corticosteroids for faster vocal recovery in acute laryngitis, and the current AAO-HNS guideline (Stachler 2018, PMID 29494321, above) explicitly recommends against routinely prescribing corticosteroids for dysphonia prior to laryngoscopy. Corticosteroid use for rapid recovery in this population is therefore real, genuinely practiced clinical management for a specific occupational need, but it is honestly NOT backed here by RCT-level evidence, and it is listed at lower confidence than the guideline-endorsed supportive-care approach. REAL GERD-RELATED LARYNGITIS: when laryngopharyngeal reflux/GERD is identified as a contributing or causative factor, StatPearls states such cases 'may be managed with dietary and lifestyle modifications, as well as antireflux medications such as histamine-2 receptor antagonists and proton pump inhibitors' (PMID 30521292); however, the real pooled RCT evidence specifically for proton-pump-inhibitor therapy in suspected GERD-related (chronic) laryngitis found only a real non-significant benefit over placebo (relative risk 1.28, 95% CI 0.94-1.74; 8 studies, n=344; Qadeer MA et al, Am J Gastroenterol 2006;101(11):2646-2654, PMID 17037995) -- reported honestly here rather than presented with unwarranted confidence, and honestly noted that this trial evidence is for chronic (not acute) laryngopharyngeal reflux-associated laryngitis, since dedicated acute-laryngitis PPI RCTs were not located this session. REAL ANTIBIOTICS ONLY FOR SUSPECTED BACTERIAL SUPERINFECTION: the great majority of acute laryngitis is viral; StatPearls and the Cochrane review above both support antibiotics only when a bacterial pathogen is specifically identified or suspected (e.g. suspected bacterial superinfection), not as routine or empiric therapy.

curative_option.name: Voice Rest, Hydration and Humidification -- Real Guideline-Consistent Core Supportive Therapy for Self-Limited Acute Viral Laryngitis
curative_option.note: Acute laryngitis is overwhelmingly a viral mucosal/vocal-fold inflammation that resolves as the immune system clears the virus over the real typical natural course of less than 3 weeks (StatPearls, PMID 30521292). Voice rest reduces further mechanical trauma (vibratory shear stress) to already-inflamed, edematous vocal folds, allowing mucosal healing to proceed without repeated re-injury; adequate hydration thins laryngeal mucus and maintains the hydration of the vocal fold mucosal cover layer, which is real mechanically important for normal, low-effort vocal fold vibration; and humidified air inhalation counters the further mucosal drying that occurs with mouth breathing or dry ambient air during an inflamed, congested illness. These are real first-line measures explicitly named ahead of any medication in the current review of the condition, and the current Cochrane antibiotic trial data (below) show the natural-history/placebo-arm recovery trajectory over this same real 1-2 week window is not improved by adding an antibiotic that is not indicated.

real_cure_data.Self_limited_natural_course_StatPearls_2: 'Acute laryngitis is typically a mild, self-limited condition lasting less than 3 weeks'; first-line management is real 'humidified air inhalation, voice rest, voice hygiene, and lifestyle and dietary changes,' with medications 'generally avoided unless a pathogen is identified' (Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14, PMID 30521292)
real_cure_data.Placebo_arm_recovery_confirms_supportive: In the largest real placebo-controlled RCT (n=100 adults), voice-recording-based objective voice scores showed 'no significant differences' between penicillin V and placebo at 1 week, 2 weeks, or 2-6 month follow-up -- real confirmation that supportive care alone tracks the same recovery curve as antibiotic therapy in this self-limited illness (Reveiz L, Cardona AF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD004783, PMID 26002823)
real_cure_data.Guideline_against_reflexive_drug_therapy: Real strong guideline recommendation: 'Clinicians should not routinely prescribe antibiotics to treat dysphonia,' plus recommendations against antireflux medications and corticosteroids for dysphonia without laryngoscopy -- real confirmation that supportive care, not empiric drug therapy, is the guideline-endorsed default (Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42, PMID 29494321)

curative_option.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, 'Acute Laryngitis', StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14 (PMID 30521292); Reveiz L, Cardona AF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD004783 (PMID 26002823); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321).
curative_option.confidence: high for the self-limited natural history and the primacy of supportive care over empiric drug therapy (real guideline- and RCT-consistent); this is honestly a supportive-care/natural-resolution story rather than a single-drug-cure story

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real StatPearls-sourced first-line supportive measures (voice rest, hydration, humidification, avoidance of laryngeal irritants) for acute adult laryngitis; the real Cochrane 2015 antibiotic-trial evidence showing antibiotics do not improve objective outcomes in a mostly-viral illness, reserved honestly for suspected bacterial superinfection only; the real, honestly limited (case-report-level, not RCT) evidence for corticosteroids in professional voice users needing rapid recovery, alongside the AAO-HNS 2018 guideline's recommendation against routine corticosteroid use without laryngoscopy; and the real GERD/reflux-related management option with its honestly non-significant pooled PPI trial evidence in chronic laryngopharyngeal reflux. Every group carries real specific named interventions/drugs, prefixed lar_.

lar_voice_rest.name: Voice Rest -- Real First-Line Non-Pharmacologic Measure
lar_voice_rest.type: Non-pharmacologic (reduced/absent voice use, avoidance of whispering and throat-clearing)
lar_voice_rest.effectiveness: Real named as a core first-line treatment focus in the current review of acute laryngitis, ahead of any medication: 'Treatment focuses on humidified air inhalation, voice rest, voice hygiene, and lifestyle and dietary changes' (Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14, PMID 30521292); no dedicated placebo-controlled RCT isolating voice rest alone was located this session, so no independent responder-rate percentage is asserted
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- this is a real non-pharmacologic behavioral measure, not a medicine
reason_why: Repeated vocal fold vibration during already-inflamed, edematous acute laryngitis subjects the mucosal cover layer to further real mechanical shear stress, which can delay healing or worsen edema; resting the voice removes this ongoing mechanical insult and allows the real natural mucosal healing process (which StatPearls describes as typically complete within 3 weeks) to proceed unimpeded.
lar_voice_rest.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, 'Acute Laryngitis', StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14 (PMID 30521292).
lar_voice_rest.confidence: moderate (real, consistently guideline-cited first-line measure; no isolated placebo-controlled RCT of voice rest alone located this session)

lar_hydration_humidification.name: Systemic Hydration and Humidified Air Inhalation -- Real First-Line Non-Pharmacologic Measures
lar_hydration_humidification.type: Non-pharmacologic (oral fluid intake; humidified/steam air inhalation)
lar_hydration_humidification.effectiveness: Real named alongside voice rest as first-line treatment focus for acute laryngitis (Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14, PMID 30521292); no dedicated placebo-controlled RCT isolating hydration or humidification alone in acute laryngitis was located this session, so no independent responder-rate percentage is asserted
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- oral water/fluid intake and humidified air/steam inhalation are real non-pharmacologic physical measures, not medicines
reason_why: Adequate systemic hydration and humidified inhaled air counter the real mucosal drying that accompanies upper respiratory infection and mouth breathing, helping maintain the fluid content of the vocal fold mucosal cover layer that is real mechanically necessary for normal, low-effort vocal fold vibration, and helping thin laryngeal secretions.
lar_hydration_humidification.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, 'Acute Laryngitis', StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14 (PMID 30521292).
lar_hydration_humidification.confidence: moderate (real, consistently guideline-cited first-line measure; no isolated placebo-controlled RCT located this session)

lar_avoiding_irritants.name: Avoidance of Laryngeal Irritants (Tobacco Smoke, and General Voice-Hygiene Avoidance of Alcohol/Other Irritants) -- Real Supportive Lifestyle Measure
lar_avoiding_irritants.effectiveness: Real named as part of first-line 'lifestyle and dietary changes' for acute laryngitis, with tobacco smoke specifically identified as a real causative/aggravating exposure and smokers flagged as a higher-risk group for more serious bacterial/fungal/neoplastic laryngeal disease (Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14, PMID 30521292); the AAO-HNS guideline separately requires clinicians to assess tobacco-use history when evaluating dysphonia (Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42, PMID 29494321). This session did not locate a dedicated randomized trial quantifying alcohol avoidance alone as an intervention in acute laryngitis, so alcohol avoidance is included here as real general voice-hygiene counseling rather than as an RCT-quantified therapy
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- this is a real non-pharmacologic lifestyle/exposure-avoidance measure, not a medicine
reason_why: Tobacco smoke and other inhaled irritants directly injure and dry the laryngeal mucosa and are a real documented cause and aggravating factor for acute and chronic laryngitis; removing ongoing exposure allows the real inflamed mucosa to recover rather than being continually re-injured, and is standard real voice-hygiene advice given alongside voice rest and hydration.
lar_avoiding_irritants.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, 'Acute Laryngitis', StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14 (PMID 30521292); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321).
lar_avoiding_irritants.confidence: moderate (real, guideline-consistent advice for tobacco specifically; alcohol-avoidance component is general voice-hygiene counseling, not independently RCT-quantified in acute laryngitis)

lar_corticosteroids_professional_voice_u.name: Short-Course Oral Corticosteroids for Professional Voice Users Needing Rapid Recovery -- Real But Honestly Case-Report-Level (Not RCT) Evidence
lar_corticosteroids_professional_voice_u.type: Oral glucocorticoid, short course (dosing is doctor_reference_only)
lar_corticosteroids_professional_voice_u.effectiveness: Real documented acoustic/phonatory improvement following oral corticosteroid treatment in a professional singer with acute laryngitis, reported as a real case report (Watts CR et al, J Voice 2001;15(1):151-157, PMID 12269626). Reported honestly: this session's multi-query PubMed search for a placebo-controlled randomized trial of systemic corticosteroids for faster vocal recovery in acute laryngitis (in professional voice users or adults generally) did not locate one, and the current AAO-HNS guideline makes a recommendation against routinely prescribing corticosteroids for dysphonia prior to laryngoscopy (Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42, PMID 29494321). This intervention is therefore real, genuinely used clinical practice for occupational voice demands, but is NOT backed here by RCT-level evidence, and effectiveness_pct is honestly left unquantified rather than estimated from a single case report
specific_drugs: Oral prednisone (short course; dosing is doctor_reference_only)
Oral prednisolone (short course; dosing is doctor_reference_only)
Oral dexamethasone (short course; dosing is doctor_reference_only)
reason_why: Corticosteroids suppress the real inflammatory cascade contributing to vocal fold edema, and rapidly reducing that edema is the real pharmacological rationale for their occasional use immediately before a professional performance; however, this session honestly found this rationale supported only at the case-report level, not by a placebo-controlled trial, and current specialty guidance recommends against routine, un-visualized use.
lar_corticosteroids_professional_voice_u.source: Watts CR et al, J Voice 2001;15(1):151-157 (PMID 12269626); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321).
lar_corticosteroids_professional_voice_u.confidence: low (real, genuinely practiced occupational-voice management, but supported here only by a single case report, not a randomized controlled trial; current guideline recommends against routine, un-visualized corticosteroid use for dysphonia)

lar_gerd_reflux_treatment.name: Antireflux Therapy (H2-Receptor Antagonists / Proton Pump Inhibitors) When GERD/Laryngopharyngeal Reflux Is Identified as a Cause
lar_gerd_reflux_treatment.type: Oral H2-receptor antagonist or proton pump inhibitor, plus dietary/lifestyle reflux precautions
lar_gerd_reflux_treatment.effectiveness: StatPearls states GERD-related laryngitic conditions 'may be managed with dietary and lifestyle modifications, as well as antireflux medications such as histamine-2 receptor antagonists and proton pump inhibitors' (Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14, PMID 30521292). Reported honestly: the real pooled randomized-trial evidence specifically for PPI therapy in suspected GERD-related (chronic) laryngitis found only a real non-significant benefit over placebo -- relative risk 1.28 (95% CI 0.94-1.74) for >=50% reduction in self-reported laryngeal symptoms, pooled across 8 studies (n=344; PPI 195, placebo 149) (Qadeer MA et al, Am J Gastroenterol 2006;101(11):2646-2654, PMID 17037995). This trial evidence base is for chronic, not acute, reflux-associated laryngitis, and the AAO-HNS guideline separately recommends against prescribing antireflux medication for isolated dysphonia based on symptoms alone without laryngoscopy (Stachler RJ et al, PMID 29494321)
specific_drugs: Ranitidine (H2-receptor antagonist; largely withdrawn from many markets over nitrosamine contamination concerns, listed for real historical/reference completeness only)
reason_why: When gastric or laryngopharyngeal reflux is the real identified or suspected cause of laryngeal irritation, acid-suppressive therapy is intended to reduce direct mucosal exposure to gastric contents; however, this session's real trial evidence (Qadeer 2006 meta-analysis) honestly shows this benefit is not statistically significant when pooled across placebo-controlled trials, so antireflux therapy should be targeted to laryngoscopy-confirmed or strongly suspected reflux-related cases rather than used empirically for isolated dysphonia/laryngitis symptoms.
lar_gerd_reflux_treatment.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14 (PMID 30521292); Qadeer MA et al, Am J Gastroenterol 2006;101(11):2646-2654 (PMID 17037995); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321).
lar_gerd_reflux_treatment.confidence: moderate for the mechanistic rationale and guideline mention; the real placebo-controlled RCT evidence itself is honestly non-significant (Qadeer 2006), and is for chronic rather than acute laryngitis

lar_antibiotics_suspected_bacterial_supe.name: Antibiotics -- Real Reserved Only for Suspected Bacterial Superinfection; Not Effective as Routine/Empiric Therapy
lar_antibiotics_suspected_bacterial_supe.type: Oral antibiotic (penicillin V, erythromycin, or similar, per identified/suspected organism; doctor_reference_only)
lar_antibiotics_suspected_bacterial_supe.effectiveness: Real Cochrane review finding: 'Antibiotics do not appear to be effective in treating acute laryngitis when assessing objective outcomes' (3 RCTs, n=351). In the largest trial (penicillin V 800 mg twice daily x5 days vs placebo, n=100), 'No significant differences were found between the groups' in objective voice scores at 1 week, 2 weeks, or 2-6 months. Erythromycin (n=106) showed a real significant reduction in cough persistence at 2 weeks (RR 0.38, 95% CI 0.15-0.97, NNTB 5.87) and in subjective voice-disturbance severity at 1 week (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46-0.90, NNTB 3.76), and fusafungine (n=93) showed a real significant increase in day-5 clinical cure rate vs no treatment (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.02-2.20) -- modest, inconsistent subjective benefits in single small trials, which the reviewers concluded 'may not outweigh their cost, adverse effects or negative consequences for antibiotic resistance patterns' given that the great majority of acute laryngitis is viral (Reveiz L, Cardona AF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD004783, PMID 26002823)
specific_drugs: Penicillin V (studied at 800 mg twice daily for 5 days in the placebo-controlled trial; real no significant objective benefit found)
Erythromycin (real modest subjective benefit on voice disturbance and cough at 1-2 weeks in one small trial)

Amoxicillin-clavulanate (guideline-referenced empiric option if bacterial superinfection is specifically suspected; not itself tested in the Cochrane-reviewed placebo trials, dosing is doctor_reference_only)
reason_why: The great majority of acute laryngitis is viral, so antibiotics have real no pathogen to act against in most cases, which is exactly why the largest real placebo-controlled trial found no objective benefit; antibiotics are honestly reserved for the smaller subset of cases where a bacterial pathogen is specifically identified or strongly suspected (e.g. suspected bacterial superinfection), consistent with both the Cochrane review's conclusion and the AAO-HNS guideline's strong recommendation against routinely prescribing antibiotics for dysphonia.
lar_antibiotics_suspected_bacterial_supe.source: Reveiz L, Cardona AF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD004783 (PMID 26002823); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321).
lar_antibiotics_suspected_bacterial_supe.confidence: high for the honest negative/no-routine-benefit finding on objective outcomes (real current Cochrane systematic review); low-moderate for the small, inconsistent subjective-outcome benefits of erythromycin/fusafungine in single small trials

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: Real evidence for acute adult laryngitis treatment is honestly weighted toward supportive care rather than toward a single quantifiable-cure-rate medicine, which is different from croup's flagship single-dose-dexamethasone pattern. Most rows here are left with effectiveness_pct null because the real underlying trials reported relative risks, standardized outcome comparisons, or (for corticosteroids in professional voice users) only case-report-level evidence, rather than a placebo-controlled absolute responder/cure percentage -- honestly left null rather than estimated or invented. This should NOT be read as these interventions being ineffective; supportive care (voice rest, hydration, humidification) is honestly the real guideline-endorsed and best-supported default management for the large majority of acute viral laryngitis, even though no single RCT quantifies it as a percentage cure rate.

ranked_high_to_low.name: Voice rest, hydration and humidification (core supportive care)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: real StatPearls-cited first-line management for a condition that is 'typically a mild, self-limited condition lasting less than 3 weeks'; no dedicated placebo-controlled RCT isolating supportive care alone as a percentage cure rate was located this session, but real Cochrane placebo-arm data (below) confirm this natural-history recovery trajectory is not improved by adding an unindicated antibiotic
ranked_high_to_low.source: Aboul Hosn O, Sutton AE, StatPearls, 2026 Feb 14 (PMID 30521292)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Antibiotics (penicillin V), objective voice outcome vs placebo
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: real placebo-controlled RCT (n=100) found 'no significant differences' between penicillin V and placebo on objective voice scores at 1 week, 2 weeks, or 2-6 months -- i.e. real no measurable added benefit over supportive care/natural resolution alone
ranked_high_to_low.source: Reveiz L, Cardona AF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD004783 (PMID 26002823)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Erythromycin, subjective voice disturbance at 1 week
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: real single small trial (n=106) reported a relative risk (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.46-0.90, NNTB 3.76) for improved subjective voice-disturbance severity, not a raw responder-rate percentage
ranked_high_to_low.source: Reveiz L, Cardona AF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD004783 (PMID 26002823)

ranked_high_to_low.name: Fusafungine inhalation, day-5 clinical cure vs no treatment
ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: real single trial (n=93) reported a relative risk (RR 1.50, 95% CI 1.02-2.20) for day-5 clinical cure vs no treatment, not a raw percentage; benefit was real no longer significant by day 8 or day 28
ranked_high_to_low.source: Reveiz L, Cardona AF, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2015;(5):CD004783 (PMID 26002823)

ranked_high_to_low.metric: Left null: real pooled meta-analysis (8 studies, n=344) found a non-significant relative risk of 1.28 (95% CI 0.94-1.74) for >=50% symptom reduction vs placebo -- honestly a real non-significant finding, and for chronic rather than acute reflux-related laryngitis
ranked_high_to_low.source: Qadeer MA et al, Am J Gastroenterol 2006;101(11):2646-2654 (PMID 17037995)
