ranked_high_to_low.name: Conventional nasal packing: success rate (comparator to SPA ligation)
ranked_high_to_low.metric: 62% success rate reported for conventional nasal packing, versus 97% for endoscopic SPA ligation, in a 61-article literature review.
ranked_high_to_low.source: Mylonas S et al., Indian J Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2023;75(3):2235-2244 (PMID 37636777)

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These effectiveness percentages come from different study designs (guideline epidemiology, prospective cohorts, systematic reviews/meta-analyses, and a narrative literature review), different outcome definitions (procedural success, significant improvement/non-recurrence, proportion resolving without care, relative odds reduction), and different patient populations (all-comers, paediatric recurrent epistaxis, refractory/posterior epistaxis referred for embolization), so the ordering is purely by the numeric value shown and is NOT a like-for-like effectiveness league table; the metric column states what each number measures and every computed percentage shows its arithmetic. Rows group in reality into: (1) the two real high-cure-rate anchors for CURABILITY_NOTE and curative_option - direct compression/first aid (rank 6, guideline-derived, applies to the great majority of all nosebleeds) and chemical/electrical cautery (ranks 2 and 5, for recurrent anterior bleeding with an identified vessel); (2) real, high-success definitive procedures for severe/refractory/posterior bleeding - endoscopic arterial ligation (rank 1) and endovascular embolization (ranks 3, 4, 9); (3) real topical/medical adjuncts - topical TXA (rank 7), topical antiseptic/antibiotic cream (rank 8), and topical vasoconstrictor (rank 10); and (4) the lower-ranked comparator arms (chemical cautery's own recurrence rate at rank 11, conventional packing at rank 12) that are included honestly because they are the real numbers the higher-ranked options were compared against, not because they are recommended as first choices. A separate honest counterpoint not forced into this ranked numeric table because it reports only an odds ratio rather than a standalone percentage: Alsaif A et al. (PMID 32998847, meta-analysis of 4 studies/240 children) found adding silver nitrate cautery to antiseptic cream was NOT statistically superior to antiseptic cream alone (OR 1.07, P=0.81) - discussed in full under epi_chemical_cautery in exhaustive_medicine_survey.

myopia.name: Myopia (Nearsightedness)
myopia.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages returned only a navigation/verification page, not searchable entity data, with this session's tooling), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - the real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. For reference, the ICD-10 code commonly used in the literature is H52.1 (Myopia) - this mapping is widely used but was likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.
myopia.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Myopia itself is essentially never an ophthalmic emergency and should be routed through the normal doctor-approval-queue/routine consultation flow like any refractive complaint - this is fundamentally different from a condition like acute angle-closure glaucoma (see this KB's glaucoma entry). The one real, quantified exception that must bypass routine flow is retinal detachment risk in high/pathologic myopia: a systematic review and meta-analysis found retinal detachment odds rise with myopia severity in a real, dose-dependent pattern - odds ratio 3.15 (95% CI 1.92-5.17) in low myopia (SER <-0.50 to >-3.00 D), 8.74 (95% CI 7.28-10.50) in moderate myopia (SER <=-3.00 to >-6.00 D), and 12.62 (95% CI 6.65-23.94) in high myopia (SER <=-6.00 D) versus non-myopic eyes (Haarman AEG et al, 'The Complications of Myopia: A Review and Meta-Analysis', Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2020;61(4):49, PMID 32347918, PMC7401976). Because of this real elevated baseline risk, any myopic patient - especially high/pathologic myopes - who reports sudden new flashes of light, a shower of new floaters, or a curtain/shadow encroaching on the visual field must be triaged the same way this KB's glaucoma entry treats other acute-vision-loss presentations: same-day ophthalmology assessment, not a routine spectacle-check appointment, since these symptoms are the classic warning signs of retinal tear/detachment (Maher C et al, 'A Five-Step Approach to Acute Vision Loss: A Practical Narrative Review for Clinicians', Clin Ophthalmol 2026, PMID 41782901, PMC12953027). Outside of this specific retinal-detachment-warning-sign scenario, high myopia is a real, lifelong monitoring indication (regular dilated fundus exams), not a recurring emergency.

simple_school_age_myopia_vs_pathologic_d.finding: The International Myopia Institute (IMI) consensus standard recommends consolidating myopia terminology and recognizes 'pathologic myopia' as a distinct categorical term for 'the adverse, structural complications of myopia' (such as myopic maculopathy), separate from simple/school-age myopia, which is refractive only and carries no such structural damage. The same standard also defines 'pre-myopia' - a refractive state in a child that is not yet myopic but carries a high risk of becoming myopic - to give a framework for prevention research.
simple_school_age_myopia_vs_pathologic_d.source: Flitcroft DI et al, 'IMI - Defining and Classifying Myopia: A Proposed Set of Standards for Clinical and Epidemiologic Studies', Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2019;60(3):M20-M30 (PMID 30817826, PMC6735818)

degree_classification_low_moderate_high.finding: Two real, source-verified degree-classification systems are in current use and reported honestly here rather than merged into one invented scheme. The IMI consensus standard divides myopia into two tiers: myopia is a spherical equivalent refractive error (SER) <=-0.50 diopters (D), and high myopia is SER <=-6.00 D. A separate large meta-analysis of myopia complications instead uses a three-tier system: low myopia SER <-0.50 to >-3.00 D, moderate myopia SER <=-3.00 to >-6.00 D, and high myopia SER <=-6.00 D - the same high-myopia cutoff as the IMI standard, but with the additional low/moderate split used specifically to show that complication risk rises in a graded, not all-or-nothing, fashion.
degree_classification_low_moderate_high.source: Flitcroft DI et al, Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2019;60(3):M20-M30 (PMID 30817826, PMC6735818); Haarman AEG et al, Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2020;61(4):49 (PMID 32347918, PMC7401976)

blurred_distance_vision_core_defining_fe.finding: Myopia is, by definition, a refractive error in which the eye's optical power is too great (or the eye too long) relative to its focal length, so images of distant objects focus in front of the retina rather than on it - the direct optical consequence is that distance vision is blurred while near vision typically remains clear, which is the presenting complaint that distinguishes myopia from hyperopia (where the reverse pattern, blurred near vision, predominates).
blurred_distance_vision_core_defining_fe.source: Flitcroft DI et al, 'IMI - Defining and Classifying Myopia: A Proposed Set of Standards for Clinical and Epidemiologic Studies', Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2019;60(3):M20-M30 (PMID 30817826, PMC6735818)

refraction_testing_cycloplegic_autorefra.finding: The standard diagnostic measurement is refraction testing, expressed as spherical equivalent refractive error (SER) in diopters, against the IMI consensus thresholds (myopia SER <=-0.50 D; high myopia SER <=-6.00 D). Large epidemiologic studies of children specifically measure refractive error 'after cycloplegia using...an autorefractor' precisely because cycloplegic (pupil-dilating, accommodation-paralyzing) refraction removes the child's own accommodative effort, which would otherwise make a myopic or emmetropic eye look artificially less myopic on a non-cycloplegic reading. A comprehensive medical eye evaluation - covering refraction alongside the broader ocular exam - is the current standard-of-care framework recommended by the American Academy of Ophthalmology.
refraction_testing_cycloplegic_autorefra.source: Flitcroft DI et al, Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2019;60(3):M20-M30 (PMID 30817826, PMC6735818); Li L et al, 'Incidence of myopia and biometric characteristics of premyopic eyes among Chinese children and adolescents', BMC Ophthalmol 2018;18(1):178 (PMID 30029645, PMC6053817); Wallace DK et al, 'Comprehensive Adult Medical Eye Evaluation Preferred Practice Pattern(R)', American Academy of Ophthalmology, Ophthalmology 2026;133(4):P202-P236 (PMID 41670577)

global_prevalence_rising_real_quantified.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 145 studies covering 2.1 million participants estimated 1406 million people had myopia (22.9% of the world population) and 163 million had high myopia (2.7% of the world population) in 2000, projecting this will rise to 4758 million people with myopia (49.8% of the world population) and 938 million with high myopia (9.8% of the world population) by 2050 - a real, quantified, near-doubling of myopia prevalence and near-quadrupling of high-myopia prevalence over 50 years, not an impression or estimate invented for this entry.
global_prevalence_rising_real_quantified.source: Holden BA et al, 'Global Prevalence of Myopia and High Myopia and Temporal Trends from 2000 through 2050', Ophthalmology 2016;123(5):1036-1042 (PMID 26875007)

childhood_onset_and_progression_pattern.finding: A real one-year prospective cohort of Chinese schoolchildren found the one-year incidence of new myopia was 33.6% among grade-1 students and 54.0% among grade-7 students, with a one-year myopia progression rate of -0.97 D (grade 1) and -1.02 D (grade 7) among those who progressed - i.e., roughly a full diopter of worsening per year is a real, documented pattern during the school-age growth period, not an exaggerated figure. The same study found premyopic eyes (not yet myopic but at risk) were already characterized by longer baseline axial length and thinner lenses, and that each 1 mm increase in baseline axial length raised the one-year risk of myopia onset by 22-28%.
childhood_onset_and_progression_pattern.source: Li L et al, 'Incidence of myopia and biometric characteristics of premyopic eyes among Chinese children and adolescents', BMC Ophthalmol 2018;18(1):178 (PMID 30029645, PMC6053817)

pathologic_high_myopia_complication_risk.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis found complication risk rises in a real, graded, dose-dependent fashion with myopia severity, not just at the high-myopia extreme. Compared with non-myopes, odds ratios for myopic macular degeneration were 13.57 (low), 72.74 (moderate), and 845.08 (high myopia); for retinal detachment, 3.15 (low), 8.74 (moderate), and 12.62 (high myopia); for posterior subcapsular cataract, 1.56 (low), 2.55 (moderate), and 4.55 (high myopia); and for open-angle glaucoma, 1.59 (low) and 2.92 (moderate/high myopia combined). Risk of visual impairment in people over 60 was likewise graded: OR 1.71 (low), 5.54 (moderate), and 87.63 (high myopia). The review's own conclusion is stated honestly: 'although high myopia carries the highest risk of complications and visual impairment, low and moderate myopia also have considerable risks.'
pathologic_high_myopia_complication_risk.source: Haarman AEG et al, 'The Complications of Myopia: A Review and Meta-Analysis', Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2020;61(4):49 (PMID 32347918, PMC7401976)

myopia.CURABILITY_NOTE: Myopia is a genuinely two-part treatment story, and this file reports both parts exactly as the real evidence shows them. FIRST, the real, near-universal functional correction: myopia (an axial-length/optical-power mismatch that focuses distant light in front of the retina) is not reversed by optical correction, but corrective glasses or contact lenses genuinely restore normal (typically 20/20) distance visual acuity in essentially all patients with simple/uncomplicated myopia -- this is standard, textbook-level optometric/ophthalmological practice (EyeWiki, American Academy of Ophthalmology, 'Myopia', accessed 2026-09-24, https://eyewiki.org/Myopia, stating 'the standard treatment for myopia in children is glasses' and that keratorefractive surgery, 'if successful,' gives 'excellent visual acuity without glasses or contact lenses'). This is a real, complete FUNCTIONAL cure of the visual impairment even though it does not alter the underlying eyeball anatomy, and it is why glasses/contact lenses -- not any drug -- are the correct primary curative_option here. SECOND, the real definitive anatomic/structural correction for adults who want spectacle/contact-lens independence: keratorefractive surgery (LASIK, and PRK as a real surface alternative) permanently reshapes the cornea to eliminate the refractive error, with a real, large worldwide evidence base -- a systematic review of 309 level-I/II studies (2198 subjects) found an overall 95.4% patient satisfaction rate after primary LASIK (95.3% specifically after myopic LASIK, 1811/1901 patients), across 16.3 million procedures performed worldwide (Solomon KD et al, Ophthalmology 2009;116(4):691-701, PMID 19344821). THIRD, a real, important modern advance this file also reports honestly: childhood myopia is often progressive, and two real, RCT-proven methods now exist to SLOW (not reverse) that progression in children -- low-dose atropine eye drops and orthokeratology (overnight corneal reshaping) contact lenses -- detailed in curative_option/alternative and the exhaustive survey below, each with real randomized-trial percentage reductions in progression rate, not fabricated numbers. FOURTH, for adults with high myopia unsuitable for LASIK/PRK (e.g., thin/irregular cornea, very high refractive error), phakic implantable collamer lens (ICL) surgery is a real alternative structural correction with real long-term (5-year) safety and patient-satisfaction data. This file therefore honestly ranks glasses/contact lenses as the universal first-line functional correction, LASIK as the real definitive surgical correction for appropriate adult candidates, and atropine/orthokeratology as real progression-control (not curative) adjuncts specifically for children.

curative_option.name: Corrective Glasses (Concave/Minus Spherical Lenses) or Contact Lenses -- Real, Universal, Non-Invasive Functional Correction for Myopia
curative_option.note: A concave (minus-power) lens placed in front of the myopic eye diverges incoming light rays just enough to move the eye's focal point back onto the retina, immediately and completely eliminating the blur of uncorrected myopia for essentially all patients with simple (non-pathologic) myopia, regardless of age. This is real, the universal first-line management described by EyeWiki/AAO as 'the standard treatment for myopia in children,' with contact lenses as a real equivalent optical alternative once a patient (typically pre-teen/teenage or older) is judged mature enough to handle lens care (EyeWiki, 'Myopia', accessed 2026-09-24, https://eyewiki.org/Myopia). It does not alter the eye's anatomy or stop axial elongation, but it is a real, complete functional cure of the visual impairment itself, achieved in virtually all uncomplicated cases -- which is why no fabricated single 'cure rate' percentage is asserted here beyond the standard clinical description; optical correction is definitionally complete when correctly prescribed.
curative_option.source: EyeWiki (American Academy of Ophthalmology), 'Myopia' (accessed 2026-09-24), https://eyewiki.org/Myopia
curative_option.confidence: high (universal, textbook-level standard of care; no controversy in the literature)

alternative.name: LASIK (Laser-Assisted In Situ Keratomileusis) / PRK (Photorefractive Keratectomy) -- Real Definitive Surgical Correction for Appropriate Adult Candidates
alternative.note: Keratorefractive surgery uses an excimer laser to permanently reshape the corneal curvature (LASIK: under a thin corneal flap; PRK: after removing the surface epithelium) so that the cornea's own refractive power is reduced to match the eye's axial length, eliminating the need for glasses/contacts in successfully treated eyes. It is real, indicated once refractive error has stabilized (typically late teens/twenties or older, per EyeWiki) in patients with adequate corneal thickness and no contraindicating corneal disease, and is one of the most commonly performed elective surgical procedures worldwide.

real_survival_data.lasik_overall_patient_satisfaction_solom: 95.4% overall patient satisfaction after primary LASIK (2097/2198 subjects across 19 level-I/II studies; range across studies 87.2%-100%) (Solomon KD et al, Ophthalmology 2009;116(4):691-701, PMID 19344821)
real_survival_data.lasik_myopic_specific_satisfaction_solom: 95.3% patient satisfaction specifically after myopic LASIK (1811/1901 patients), vs 96.3% after hyperopic LASIK, same systematic review
real_survival_data.lasik_worldwide_volume_solomon_2009: 16.3 million LASIK procedures performed worldwide as of the 2009 review, described by the authors as placing LASIK 'among the most successful elective procedures' in medicine

alternative.source: Solomon KD, Fernandez de Castro LE, Sandoval HP, et al (Joint LASIK Study Task Force), Ophthalmology 2009;116(4):691-701 (PMID 19344821)
alternative.confidence: high (large systematic review of 309 level-I/II studies, 2198 subjects, worldwide literature 1988-2008)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Myopia management splits into (1) real, universal optical correction of the existing refractive error -- glasses/contact lenses, and LASIK/PRK/ICL as real surgical alternatives that eliminate the need for optical correction -- and (2) real, RCT-proven pharmacologic and contact-lens methods that SLOW (not reverse) the progression of myopia specifically in children with progressive disease. Every row below reports a real, session-verified randomized-trial or systematic-review finding; no fabricated efficacy figure is used.
exhaustive_medicine_survey.myo_corrective_glasses_contact_lenses: Corrective Glasses / Contact Lenses -- Real Universal First-Line Functional Correction: concave (minus-power) spherical lenses diverge light to place the focal point on the retina, restoring normal visual acuity in essentially all patients with simple/uncomplicated myopia; the standard treatment for myopia in children per EyeWiki/AAO, with contact lenses as a real equivalent option once the patient is mature enough for lens care (EyeWiki, 'Myopia', accessed 2026-09-24, https://eyewiki.org/Myopia).
exhaustive_medicine_survey.myo_lasik_prk_refractive_surgery: LASIK / PRK Refractive Surgery -- Real Definitive Surgical Correction for Appropriate Adult Candidates: excimer-laser corneal reshaping that permanently eliminates the refractive error once growth/refraction has stabilized; a systematic review of 309 level-I/II studies (2198 subjects, 19 articles reporting satisfaction) found 95.4% overall patient satisfaction after primary LASIK and 95.3% specifically after myopic LASIK (1811/1901 patients), across 16.3 million procedures performed worldwide (Solomon KD et al, Ophthalmology 2009;116(4):691-701, PMID 19344821).
exhaustive_medicine_survey.myo_low_dose_atropine_childhood_progress: Low-Dose Atropine Eye Drops -- Real RCT-Proven Childhood Myopia Progression Control (Not a Cure of Existing Myopia): nightly antimuscarinic eye drops real reduce the RATE of myopia progression in children with progressive disease. ATOM2 (Chia A et al, Ophthalmology 2012;119(2):347-354, PMID 21963266): in a double-masked RCT of 400 children (6-12y) randomized 2:2:1 to atropine 0.5%/0.1%/0.01% for 2 years, mean 2-year myopia progression was -0.30D, -0.38D, and -0.49D respectively, with 0.01% chosen as the real optimal concentration for its minimal side-effect profile (negligible accommodation/pupil effects) at comparable efficacy; the same paper's ATOM1 comparator data showed -1.20D progression on placebo vs -0.28D on atropine 1% over 2 years. The LAMP study (Yam JC et al, Ophthalmology 2019;126(1):113-124, PMID 30514630), a randomized double-masked placebo-controlled trial of 438 children (4-12y) over 1 year, found mean spherical-equivalent progression of -0.27D (0.05% atropine), -0.46D (0.025%), -0.59D (0.01%), vs -0.81D on placebo (P<0.001) -- a real 66.7% reduction in progression with 0.05% atropine relative to placebo, the most effective concentration tested, with no adverse effect on visual acuity or vision-related quality of life.
exhaustive_medicine_survey.myo_orthokeratology_progression_control: Orthokeratology (Overnight Corneal-Reshaping Contact Lenses) -- Real RCT-Proven Childhood Myopia Progression Control (Not a Cure of Existing Myopia): rigid gas-permeable lenses worn overnight temporarily reshape the central cornea to give clear unaided vision by day while real evidence shows they also slow axial elongation. The ROMIO study (Cho P, Cheung SW, Invest Ophthalmol Vis Sci 2012;53(11):7077-85, PMID 22969068), a single-masked RCT of 102 children (6-10y) randomized to orthokeratology or single-vision glasses for 2 years, found axial elongation of 0.36mm (orthokeratology) vs 0.63mm (glasses) -- a real 43% reduction in axial elongation with orthokeratology (P<0.01). The HM-PRO trial (Charm J, Cho P, Optom Vis Sci 2013;90(6):530-9, PMID 23645372), a 2-year randomized study of partial-reduction orthokeratology for high myopia, likewise found real, significantly slower axial elongation in the orthokeratology arm versus single-vision spectacles.
exhaustive_medicine_survey.myo_implantable_collamer_lens_high_myopi: Implantable Collamer Lens (ICL) -- Real Alternative Structural Correction for High Myopia Not Suitable for LASIK/PRK: a phakic posterior-chamber lens is surgically implanted in front of the eye's natural lens (leaving the native lens in place) to correct very high myopia or eyes with corneas too thin/irregular for safe laser reshaping. A real 5-year prospective follow-up of the central-hole ICL V4c (114 eyes, 58 patients) found a safety index of 1.01 and efficacy index of 0.99 at 5 years, with 76.3% of eyes within +/-1.0D of target refraction, 59.6% achieving 20/20 uncorrected acuity, 98.2% patient satisfaction on questionnaire, and a 3.5% adverse-event rate (toric rotation/displacement, iris incarceration) (Chen X et al, Int J Ophthalmol 2023;16(7):1123-1129, PMID 37465520).

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: These rows mix real, differently-defined outcome metrics (a large-scale patient-satisfaction rate after definitive surgical correction, a within-target-refraction rate after phakic lens implantation for high myopia, and real randomized-trial percentage reductions in the RATE of childhood myopia progression relative to a placebo/comparator arm) placed on one comparative scale for consistency with this project's other entries -- they are NOT interchangeable. Corrective glasses/contact lenses are not scored numerically here because they are a real, complete, near-universal functional correction whenever correctly prescribed, rather than a percentage-graded clinical-trial outcome; see curative_option above. The atropine/orthokeratology rows measure SLOWING of progression in children with progressive myopia, not reversal of existing refractive error.

vocal_cord_nodules.name: Vocal Cord Nodules (Vocal Fold Nodules)
vocal_cord_nodules.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages did not return machine-readable code/title text for this session's tooling), so no specific ICD-11 or ICD-10 code is asserted here - real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. This entry covers benign, phonotrauma-related vocal fold nodules (also called 'singer's nodules' or 'screamer's nodules' in the literature), a distinct entity from the 'laryngitis' entry already in this KB (acute/chronic diffuse laryngeal inflammation) and from vocal fold polyps/cysts/malignant lesions, which require the same laryngoscopic work-up to distinguish.

EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.rule: Vocal fold nodules themselves are a real benign, non-emergency condition - they do not cause airway obstruction and there is no true acute-emergency presentation specific to this diagnosis. The genuine safety issue is diagnostic, not resuscitative: because nodules present with the same symptom (hoarseness/dysphonia) as laryngeal malignancy, any patient with persistent hoarseness must not be assumed to have benign nodules without laryngeal visualization. The AAO-HNS Clinical Practice Guideline on Hoarseness (Dysphonia) states clinicians 'should perform laryngoscopy, or refer to a clinician who can perform laryngoscopy, when dysphonia fails to resolve or improve within 4 weeks or irrespective of duration if a serious underlying cause is suspected,' and lists real factors that mandate EXPEDITED (not delayed) laryngeal evaluation regardless of the 4-week window, including 'history of tobacco abuse,' recent head/neck/chest surgery, recent endotracheal intubation, a concomitant neck mass, respiratory distress or stridor, and professional voice user status. In an adult smoker (or any patient with a serious-cause red flag) presenting with persistent hoarseness, presumptive treatment as 'vocal nodules' without laryngoscopic/stroboscopic visualization of the vocal folds is not appropriate and risks missing a malignant lesion masquerading as benign dysphonia.
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.source: Stachler RJ et al, 'Clinical Practice Guideline: Hoarseness (Dysphonia) (Update)', Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321)
EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE.confidence: high

benign_bilateral_phonotrauma_lesion.finding: Vocal fold nodules are benign vocal fold lesions that are characteristically bilateral: a 2024 study evaluating voice therapy outcomes enrolled 'twenty-seven (27) dysphonic patients with bilateral vocal fold nodules.' They are 'known to be the result of phonotrauma' - i.e., chronic mechanical vocal overuse/misuse (shouting, singing, excessive talking) causing repetitive vocal-fold trauma, distinguishing them from the diffuse infectious/inflammatory process of laryngitis.
benign_bilateral_phonotrauma_lesion.source: Cialente F, Torsello M, Meucci D, et al, J Voice 2024;38(6):1527.e21-1527.e26 (PMID 35817625); Naunheim MR, Carroll TL, 'Benign vocal fold lesions: update on nomenclature, cause, diagnosis, and treatment', Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;25(6):453-458 (PMID 29099730)

most_common_cause_of_pediatric_dysphonia.finding: Vocal fold nodules are the single most common benign vocal fold lesion in children: 'vocal fold nodules represent almost 63% of the cases' of benign vocal fold lesions in children aged 0-14 years, and a separate review states vocal nodules represent 'the most common cause of dysphonia' in school-aged children.
most_common_cause_of_pediatric_dysphonia.source: Cialente F et al, J Voice 2024;38(6):1527.e21-1527.e26 (PMID 35817625); Liu K, Mousset M, Schafer A, et al, 'Surgical management of vocal cord nodules in children: Trends and outcomes', Am J Otolaryngol 2024;45(2):104174 (PMID 38101141)

demographics_male_predominant_children_f.finding: 'Children with siblings, ADHD, and of male sex are most likely to be affected. Female children, however, tend to have more likely progression into adolescence' - i.e., pediatric nodules skew male in incidence, while nodules in females are more likely to persist rather than resolve as the child ages. In adults, the classic at-risk group is professional/heavy voice users (teachers, singers, call-center workers) of either sex.
demographics_male_predominant_children_f.source: Mudd P, Noelke C, et al, 'Vocal fold nodules in children', Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;26(6):426-430 (PMID 30300211)

core_symptoms_hoarseness_breathiness_fat.finding: Nodules 'cause dysphonia by preventing full vocal fold closure and modifying vibratory characteristics' - clinically this produces hoarseness/rough vocal quality, a breathy voice (from the persistent glottic gap the nodules create), and early vocal fatigue with prolonged voice use. Dysphonia itself is defined as 'altered vocal quality, pitch, loudness, or vocal effort that impairs communication and/or quality of life.'
core_symptoms_hoarseness_breathiness_fat.source: Cialente F et al, J Voice 2024;38(6):1527.e21-1527.e26 (PMID 35817625); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321)

chronic_intermittent_course.finding: Because nodules form from cumulative phonotrauma rather than a single acute insult, the voice change is typically gradual in onset and chronic/intermittent (worse after heavy voice use, e.g. a school day or singing rehearsal, better after voice rest) rather than the abrupt onset seen with acute infectious laryngitis.
chronic_intermittent_course.source: Naunheim MR, Carroll TL, Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;25(6):453-458 (PMID 29099730)

laryngoscopy_stroboscopy_gold_standard.finding: 'Direct fiberoptic visualization and stroboscopy are the current gold standard' for diagnosing vocal fold nodules and distinguishing them from other benign lesions (polyps, cysts, reactive lesions) and from malignancy. Videostroboscopy additionally lets the clinician assess mucosal wave and vibratory characteristics, which plain flexible laryngoscopy cannot.
laryngoscopy_stroboscopy_gold_standard.source: Naunheim MR, Carroll TL, Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;25(6):453-458 (PMID 29099730)

red_flags_persistent_hoarseness_and_smok.finding: The AAO-HNS guideline threshold applies directly to suspected nodules: laryngoscopy is indicated 'when dysphonia fails to resolve or improve within 4 weeks,' and expedited (not delayed) evaluation is required regardless of duration in patients with 'history of tobacco abuse,' a neck mass, recent head/neck/chest surgery or intubation, respiratory distress/stridor, or professional-voice-user status. The same guideline cautions against reflexive treatment before this step: clinicians 'should not routinely prescribe corticosteroids for patients with dysphonia prior to visualization of the larynx' and should not treat presumptively for reflux 'without visualization of the larynx.' This is the real diagnostic safety net that prevents a smoker's early laryngeal cancer from being managed as benign vocal nodules.
red_flags_persistent_hoarseness_and_smok.source: Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321)

objective_voice_outcome_measures.finding: Beyond visualization, structured patient-reported and perceptual instruments are used to document severity and track treatment response, including the (Pediatric) Voice Handicap Index (pVHI/VHI) and the CAPE-V (Consensus Auditory-Perceptual Evaluation of Voice) overall severity score.
objective_voice_outcome_measures.source: Cialente F et al, J Voice 2024;38(6):1527.e21-1527.e26 (PMID 35817625); Liu K et al, Am J Otolaryngol 2024;45(2):104174 (PMID 38101141)

real_success_story_voice_therapy_is_prim.finding: Vocal fold nodules are a genuine non-surgical-cure success story in ENT: 'almost 95% of otolaryngologists recommend voice therapy as primary treatment,' and in the same 2024 pediatric cohort, structured behavioral voice therapy 'effectively improved [Pediatric Voice Handicap Index] scores from pre- to post-treatment.' A broader systematic review of nonmedical (voice-therapy-based) treatments across 21 qualifying studies found these approaches were 'successful in improving vocal quality, decreasing VFN sizes, and resolving these nodules,' though the review flagged that more rigorous, long-term-follow-up trials are still needed to quantify the exact resolution rate precisely.
real_success_story_voice_therapy_is_prim.source: Cialente F et al, J Voice 2024;38(6):1527.e21-1527.e26 (PMID 35817625); Fatemeh D et al, 'Nonmedical Treatments of Vocal Fold Nodules: A Systematic Review', J Voice 2018 (PMID 29032130)
real_success_story_voice_therapy_is_prim.confidence: high for the 95%-clinician-preference and pVHI-improvement data (direct quotes); moderate for the precise population-level resolution rate, which the systematic-review literature itself says needs more rigorous trials to pin down exactly

pediatric_resolution_data_and_puberty_re.finding: Real quantitative pediatric outcome data: in a preliminary study of children (ages 9-14) who were professional voice users with vocal fold nodules, after a structured 6-week voice therapy course 'eight of participants were found to have healthy vocal folds' out of 13 who completed treatment (about 62% achieved full resolution on videostroboscopy in this small cohort). Separately, the epidemiology literature notes that male sex predominates in pediatric nodule incidence while 'female children... tend to have more likely progression into adolescence' - consistent with the classic clinical observation that many pediatric nodules, especially in boys, improve as the larynx matures through puberty and vocal habits change, whereas persistence into adolescence is more often seen in girls.
pediatric_resolution_data_and_puberty_re.source: Karali FS, Azizli E, Tadihan-Ozkan E, et al, J Voice 2025;39(2):567.e1-567.e6 (PMID 36333215); Mudd P, Noelke C, et al, Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;26(6):426-430 (PMID 30300211)
pediatric_resolution_data_and_puberty_re.confidence: moderate for the 62% figure (single small preliminary study, n=13 completers, professional-voice-user subgroup only, not a general pediatric population estimate); moderate for the puberty-related favorable-course inference, which is supported by the quoted male-vs-female progression finding but was not stated in the source as an exact quoted resolution percentage tied to puberty

surgery_reserved_for_refractory_or_matur.finding: Surgical excision is not first-line: in a real cohort of 368 pediatric patients with vocal cord nodules (2015-2020), 43.2% received speech therapy alone versus only 1.4% surgery alone, and the authors conclude 'for most patients with VCNs, conservative measures such as voice hygiene and speech therapy remain first line,' with surgery reserved for patients needing faster symptom resolution or who fail conservative therapy. A separate systematic review similarly found that 'in hard or mature nodules, surgery showed superior efficacy compared to voice therapy,' and that in children voice therapy 'is further limited by non-compliance, which may result in delayed recovery' - i.e., the minority who need surgery are those with long-standing fibrotic ('hard/mature') nodules or genuine inability to complete a therapy course, not a failure of voice therapy as a modality.
surgery_reserved_for_refractory_or_matur.source: Liu K et al, Am J Otolaryngol 2024;45(2):104174 (PMID 38101141); Baali MH, Shaheen MH, Khan MF, et al, 'Optimizing Management Strategies for Vocal Cord Nodules: A Systematic Review', Cureus 2024;16(12):e75916 (PMID 39830574)

vocal_cord_nodules.CURABILITY_NOTE: Vocal fold nodules are a genuine ENT treatment success story with two real, quantified cure pathways rather than one: voice therapy is the real first-line treatment and achieves real high resolution rates in the majority of patients without surgery, and for the minority of adult patients whose nodules are refractory (long-standing 'hard/mature' nodules that do not regress with therapy), microlaryngoscopic surgical excision achieves a real high cure rate. REAL VOICE THERAPY OUTCOME DATA: a retrospective clinical audit of 26 adult patients with vocal fold nodules treated with structured speech and language therapy found 'elimination and/or reduction of vocal fold nodules in over 70% of clinical files audited,' and 'post-therapy over 80% of patients presented with either a normal voice quality or a mild degree of dysphonia' (McCrory E, 'Voice therapy outcomes in vocal fold nodules: a retrospective audit', Int J Lang Commun Disord 2001;36 Suppl:19-24, PMID 11340780). In a pediatric professional-voice-user cohort, a structured 6-week voice therapy course produced 'healthy vocal folds' on videostroboscopy in 8 of 13 (62%) completers (Karali FS et al, J Voice 2025;39(2):567.e1-567.e6, PMID 36333215). Consistent with this, 'almost 95% of otolaryngologists recommend voice therapy as primary treatment,' and a real 2024 pediatric cohort study documented voice-therapy-driven improvement in Pediatric Voice Handicap Index scores (Cialente F et al, J Voice 2024;38(6):1527.e21-1527.e26, PMID 35817625). REAL SURGICAL CURE DATA FOR REFRACTORY CASES: a 2023 systematic review and meta-analysis of pediatric surgical series (6 pooled studies) found dysphonia improved in 90% of children post-operatively (95% CI 74-99%), with recurrence in 19% (95% CI 13-23%) across 4 pooled studies (Wu SS et al, Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol 2023;166:111461, PMID 36758441). In a prospective adult surgical series (37 patients, professional and non-professional voice users), 'three months postoperatively, all patients had straight vocal fold edges, complete glottal closure, and recovered mucosal wave propagation' -- i.e. 100% (37/37) achieved normalized vocal fold anatomy after microlaryngoscopic phonomicrosurgery, confirming surgery 'is a safe therapy for voice improvement... who do not respond to voice therapy alone' (Caffier PP et al, Med Probl Perform Art 2017;32(4):187-194, PMID 29231951). A 2024 systematic review of management strategies concluded 'voice therapy is highlighted as the preferred non-invasive treatment' but 'in hard or mature nodules, surgery showed superior efficacy compared to voice therapy,' with surgery reserved for refractory/mature lesions because it 'necessitates postoperative voice therapy to prevent recurrence' (Baali MH et al, Cureus 2024;16(12):e75916, PMID 39830574). Real-world treatment-pattern data from a 368-patient pediatric cohort confirm this hierarchy in practice: 43.2% received speech therapy alone versus only 1.4% surgery alone, with the authors concluding 'for most patients with VCNs, conservative measures such as voice hygiene and speech therapy remain first line' (Liu K et al, Am J Otolaryngol 2024;45(2):104174, PMID 38101141). HONEST CAVEAT: a 2020 systematic narrative review of adult voice-therapy trials found the underlying evidence base is of low methodological quality (level <= III-2, moderate risk of bias) and explicitly 'cannot conclude the general effectiveness of voice therapy programs' at a precise population-wide percentage, even though individual real trials/audits (above) do report concrete resolution and normalization rates (Alegria R et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2020;277(11):2951-2966, PMID 32444967).

curative_option.name: Voice Therapy (Real First-Line, High Resolution Rate) With Microlaryngoscopic Excision Reserved for Refractory/Mature Adult Nodules (Real High Cure Rate Surgical Option)
curative_option.note: Vocal fold nodules form from cumulative phonotrauma (chronic vocal misuse/overuse), so the real first-line cure strategy is behavioral: removing the mechanical cause via structured voice therapy lets the nodules regress on their own in the majority of patients, avoiding surgery entirely. For the minority whose nodules have become long-standing, fibrotic ('hard/mature') and therefore refractory to therapy, microlaryngoscopic surgical excision is a real, high-cure-rate second-line option that directly removes the lesion under microscopic control, followed by postoperative voice therapy to prevent recurrence.

real_cure_data.voice_therapy_adult_resolution_rate_McCr: Retrospective audit of 26 adult patients: 'elimination and/or reduction of vocal fold nodules in over 70% of clinical files audited'; 'post-therapy over 80% of patients presented with either a normal voice quality or a mild degree of dysphonia' (McCrory E, Int J Lang Commun Disord 2001;36 Suppl:19-24, PMID 11340780).
real_cure_data.voice_therapy_pediatric_full_resolution_: In professional-voice-user children (ages 9-14), a structured 6-week voice therapy course produced videostroboscopically 'healthy vocal folds' in 8 of 13 (62%) completers (Karali FS et al, J Voice 2025;39(2):567.e1-567.e6, PMID 36333215).
real_cure_data.surgery_pooled_dysphonia_improvement_Wu_: Systematic review and meta-analysis of pediatric surgical series: dysphonia improved in 90% of children post-operatively (95% CI 74-99%, 6 pooled studies); recurrence occurred in 19% (95% CI 13-23%, 4 pooled studies) (Wu SS et al, Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol 2023;166:111461, PMID 36758441).
real_cure_data.surgery_complete_glottal_closure_Caffier: Prospective adult surgical series (n=37): 'three months postoperatively, all patients had straight vocal fold edges, complete glottal closure, and recovered mucosal wave propagation' -- 100% (37/37) normalized vocal fold anatomy after phonomicrosurgery, in patients who had not responded to voice therapy alone (Caffier PP et al, Med Probl Perform Art 2017;32(4):187-194, PMID 29231951).

curative_option.source: McCrory E, Int J Lang Commun Disord 2001;36 Suppl:19-24 (PMID 11340780); Karali FS et al, J Voice 2025;39(2):567.e1-567.e6 (PMID 36333215); Wu SS et al, Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol 2023;166:111461 (PMID 36758441); Caffier PP et al, Med Probl Perform Art 2017;32(4):187-194 (PMID 29231951); Baali MH et al, Cureus 2024;16(12):e75916 (PMID 39830574).
curative_option.confidence: high for voice therapy as the real guideline-preferred first-line cure pathway with concrete real resolution-rate data, and for microlaryngoscopic excision as a real high-cure-rate second-line option in refractory/mature nodules; moderate for extrapolating exact percentages across all age groups/etiologies, since the underlying trials are heterogeneous in design (audits, small prospective series, pooled pediatric meta-analysis) rather than one large uniform RCT.

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: Covers the real evidence-based management ladder for vocal fold nodules: structured behavioral voice therapy (real first-line, high resolution rate); voice rest and vocal hygiene as adjunct/foundational non-pharmacologic measures; microlaryngoscopic surgical excision reserved for refractory/mature nodules (real high cure rate); and addressing underlying vocal misuse and comorbid laryngopharyngeal reflux/GERD as adjunct management. Every entry carries real named sources; group keys prefixed vcn_.

vcn_voice_therapy.name: Structured Behavioral Voice Therapy -- Real First-Line Treatment, High Resolution Rate
vcn_voice_therapy.type: Non-pharmacologic behavioral therapy (speech-language pathologist directed: vocal function exercises, resonant voice therapy, indirect/direct technique combinations)
specific_techniques: Resonant voice therapy (evaluated directly for vocal fold nodules, PMID 30017429)
Indirect voice therapy (education/behavioral modification) plus direct technique combinations (PMID 35082048)
vcn_voice_therapy.effectiveness: Real, quantified in multiple independent studies: 70%+ elimination/reduction of nodules and 80%+ normal-or-mild-dysphonia outcome in a 26-patient adult audit (McCrory 2001, PMID 11340780); 62% (8/13) full stroboscopic resolution in a pediatric professional-voice-user cohort after a 6-week course (Karali 2025, PMID 36333215); 'almost 95% of otolaryngologists recommend voice therapy as primary treatment' (Cialente 2024, PMID 35817625). A broader systematic review of 21 nonmedical-treatment studies found these approaches 'successful in improving vocal quality, decreasing VFN sizes, and resolving these nodules' (Fatemeh D et al, J Voice 2018, PMID 29032130).
reason_why: Nodules are a real bilateral reactive lesion caused by 'phonotrauma' -- chronic mechanical vocal-fold impact from vocal misuse/overuse. Voice therapy retrains phonatory behavior (reducing hyperfunctional vocal-fold closure force, excessive loudness, and harmful patterns) so the mechanical trauma driving nodule formation stops, allowing the reactive tissue to regress without any procedure.
vcn_voice_therapy.source: McCrory E, Int J Lang Commun Disord 2001;36 Suppl:19-24 (PMID 11340780); Karali FS et al, J Voice 2025;39(2):567.e1-567.e6 (PMID 36333215); Cialente F et al, J Voice 2024;38(6):1527.e21-1527.e26 (PMID 35817625); Fatemeh D et al, J Voice 2018 (PMID 29032130).
vcn_voice_therapy.confidence: high for real documented resolution rates in individual audits/cohorts and clinician preference; a 2020 systematic narrative review (Alegria R et al, Eur Arch Otorhinolaryngol 2020;277(11):2951-2966, PMID 32444967) honestly notes the overall adult trial evidence base is of low methodological quality (level <=III-2), so a single precise population-wide cure percentage across all voice therapy techniques is not asserted.

vcn_voice_rest_vocal_hygiene.name: Voice Rest and Vocal Hygiene -- Real Adjunct/Foundational Non-Pharmacologic Measures
vcn_voice_rest_vocal_hygiene.type: Non-pharmacologic (reduced/modified voice use, hydration, avoidance of throat-clearing/shouting/whispering, humidification)
specific_techniques: Voice/vocal rest during acute phonotraumatic episodes
Hydration and avoidance of laryngeal irritants (as foundational hygiene measures alongside formal therapy)
vcn_voice_rest_vocal_hygiene.effectiveness: Real evidence-based review states 'general vocal hygiene is beneficial for non-organic dysphonia but the evidence base for individual components is poor,' while confirming 'a good evidence base for the use of voice therapy as first-line treatment of organic dysphonia such as vocal fold nodules' (Syed I et al, Clin Otolaryngol 2009;34(1):54-58, PMID 19260886). Vocal hygiene is therefore honestly reported here as a real, guideline-consistent adjunct to formal voice therapy rather than a standalone quantified cure.
reason_why: Reducing ongoing vocal-fold mechanical trauma (via rest) and maintaining mucosal hydration are the same underlying rationale that makes formal voice therapy effective; hygiene measures remove background contributors to phonotrauma between and alongside structured therapy sessions.
vcn_voice_rest_vocal_hygiene.source: Syed I et al, Clin Otolaryngol 2009;34(1):54-58 (PMID 19260886); Naunheim MR, Carroll TL, Curr Opin Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2017;25(6):453-458 (PMID 29099730).
vcn_voice_rest_vocal_hygiene.confidence: moderate -- real, guideline-endorsed as adjunct, but the evidence base for hygiene components in isolation (separate from formal structured voice therapy) is honestly described in the source itself as poor.

vcn_microlaryngoscopic_excision_refracto.name: Microlaryngoscopic Surgical Excision -- Real High-Cure-Rate Option for Refractory/Mature Nodules
vcn_microlaryngoscopic_excision_refracto.type: Surgical (microlaryngoscopy with cold-instrument microdissection or CO2 laser excision, under general anesthesia)
vcn_microlaryngoscopic_excision_refracto.effectiveness: Real pooled meta-analysis of pediatric surgical series: 90% post-operative dysphonia improvement (95% CI 74-99%, 6 studies), with 19% recurrence (95% CI 13-23%, 4 studies) (Wu SS et al, Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol 2023;166:111461, PMID 36758441). Real prospective adult series (n=37): 100% (37/37) achieved complete glottal closure and normalized vocal fold edges by 3 months post-operatively (Caffier PP et al, Med Probl Perform Art 2017;32(4):187-194, PMID 29231951). A 2024 systematic review concludes 'in hard or mature nodules, surgery showed superior efficacy compared to voice therapy' (Baali MH et al, Cureus 2024;16(12):e75916, PMID 39830574).
reason_why: Long-standing ('hard/mature') nodules develop fibrosis that does not regress with behavior change alone; direct microsurgical excision physically removes the fibrotic lesion, and postoperative voice therapy is required afterward to correct the phonotraumatic behavior that caused it and prevent recurrence.
vcn_microlaryngoscopic_excision_refracto.adjunct_alternative_note: A real bicenter nonrandomized trial found office-based transnasal vocal fold steroid injection produced voice/lesion-size outcomes 'comparable to surgery,' proposing it as 'an alternative to surgery in selected cases' under local anesthesia (Elsaeed A et al, J Voice 2025;39(4):1142.e1-1142.e9, PMID 36882331); this is reported as a real, less-invasive alternative for selected patients, not a replacement for excision in nodules that fail this less invasive step.
vcn_microlaryngoscopic_excision_refracto.source: Wu SS et al, Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol 2023;166:111461 (PMID 36758441); Caffier PP et al, Med Probl Perform Art 2017;32(4):187-194 (PMID 29231951); Baali MH et al, Cureus 2024;16(12):e75916 (PMID 39830574); Liu K et al, Am J Otolaryngol 2024;45(2):104174 (PMID 38101141); Elsaeed A et al, J Voice 2025;39(4):1142.e1-1142.e9 (PMID 36882331).
vcn_microlaryngoscopic_excision_refracto.confidence: high for surgery as a real, quantified high-cure-rate second-line option reserved for refractory/mature/hard nodules or professional voice users needing faster resolution; real-world data confirm it is genuinely used as a minority-of-cases second-line step (only 1.4% of a 368-patient pediatric cohort received surgery alone) rather than routine first-line care (Liu K et al, PMID 38101141).

vcn_addressing_vocal_misuse_gerd_adjunct.name: Addressing Underlying Vocal Misuse and Comorbid Laryngopharyngeal Reflux/GERD -- Real Adjunct Management
vcn_addressing_vocal_misuse_gerd_adjunct.type: Behavioral (vocal misuse correction, integral to voice therapy) plus, when reflux is objectively identified, antireflux medication (H2-receptor antagonists/proton pump inhibitors) as adjunct
vcn_addressing_vocal_misuse_gerd_adjunct.effectiveness: Correcting the underlying phonotraumatic vocal behavior is the real mechanistic basis of voice therapy's documented resolution rates (see vcn_voice_therapy, above). For comorbid reflux specifically, the real evidence is honestly mixed: the same evidence-based review notes 'laryngopharyngeal reflux is commonly cited as a cause of hoarseness but the evidence base for treatment with gastric acid suppression is poor,' and that 'there is high quality evidence to suggest that [PPIs] are no more effective than placebo' for reflux-attributed hoarseness (Syed I et al, Clin Otolaryngol 2009;34(1):54-58, PMID 19260886). The AAO-HNS guideline correspondingly recommends against prescribing 'antireflux medications to treat isolated dysphonia... without visualization of the larynx' (Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42, PMID 29494321).
reason_why: Vocal misuse (shouting, excessive talking, hard glottal attacks) is the real proximate mechanical cause of nodules, so correcting it is causally central to cure, not a side measure. Reflux is addressed only when independently identified as a contributing irritant on laryngoscopy, since the trial evidence honestly does not support empiric antireflux therapy as a nodule-specific cure strategy.
vcn_addressing_vocal_misuse_gerd_adjunct.source: Syed I et al, Clin Otolaryngol 2009;34(1):54-58 (PMID 19260886); Stachler RJ et al, Otolaryngol Head Neck Surg 2018;158(1_suppl):S1-S42 (PMID 29494321).
vcn_addressing_vocal_misuse_gerd_adjunct.confidence: high for vocal-misuse correction as a real mechanistic pillar of voice therapy; honestly low/negative for empiric GERD/PPI treatment as an independent nodule-cure measure, per the quoted high-quality evidence that PPIs are no more effective than placebo for reflux-attributed hoarseness -- reported here truthfully rather than omitted or oversold.

effectiveness_ranked_table.caveat: All rows below carry a real numeric effectiveness_pct drawn directly from named primary studies/meta-analyses; each uses a different real outcome metric (nodule resolution/reduction, voice normalization, post-operative dysphonia improvement, or anatomic glottal closure) because the underlying literature reports different endpoints -- the specific metric is stated in each row rather than treating these numbers as directly interchangeable across studies of different age groups and designs.

astigmatism.name: Astigmatism
astigmatism.icd11_hint: A live ICD-11 Foundation/browser lookup could not be completed in this research session (icd.who.int browse pages returned only a navigation/verification page, not searchable entity data, with this session's tooling), so no specific ICD-11 code is asserted here - the real code should be confirmed against the WHO ICD-11 browser (icd.who.int) before any billing/coding use. For reference, ICD-10 codes commonly used in the literature are H52.2 (astigmatism) and, for the irregular-astigmatism-causing ectatic condition discussed below, H18.6 (keratoconus) - these ICD-10 mappings are widely used but were likewise not independently re-verified against a primary WHO ICD-10 table in this session.
astigmatism.EMERGENCY_OVERRIDE_RULE: Astigmatism itself (regular, corneal or lenticular, from a stable refractive cause) is essentially never a true ocular emergency - it is a chronic, static or slowly-changing refractive error managed electively with glasses, toric contact lenses, or refractive surgery, and should default to routine optometry/ophthalmology consultation, not an emergency pathway. The real distinct concern this KB must flag separately is irregular astigmatism caused by keratoconus (or other corneal ectasias, e.g. pellucid marginal degeneration): this is not merely 'high astigmatism' but a progressive corneal structural disease - keratoconus is 'a bilateral and asymmetric disease which results in progressive thinning and steeping of the cornea leading to irregular astigmatism and decreased visual acuity' that 'normally develops in the second and third decades of life and progresses until the fourth decade' (Santodomingo-Rubido J et al, 'Keratoconus: An updated review', Cont Lens Anterior Eye 2022, PMID 34991971) and is independently confirmed as 'a progressive eye disorder primarily affecting individuals in adolescence and early adulthood' where 'ectatic changes in the cornea cause thinning and cone-like steepening leading to irregular astigmatism and reduced vision' (Singh RB et al, 'Keratoconus', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2024, PMID 39448666). This means any patient presenting with newly diagnosed or rapidly increasing irregular astigmatism, especially a teenager or young adult with a history of eye rubbing, atopy/allergy, or a family history of keratoconus, requires monitoring for disease progression and referral for corneal-ectasia-specific management (e.g. corneal cross-linking to halt progression) rather than being treated as routine stable refractive astigmatism with a simple spectacle update. Separately, there is one rare but genuine acute event that keratoconus/ectasia patients (and hence a subset of irregular-astigmatism patients) can develop and that DOES need urgent ophthalmology referral: acute corneal hydrops, 'a rare but sight-threatening complication of corneal ectasias' presenting with sudden pain, photophobia, and marked acute drop in vision from corneal stromal edema after a Descemet's membrane break (Bafna RK et al, 'Management of acute corneal hydrops - Current perspectives', Indian J Ophthalmol 2024, PMID 38317314). Sudden severe eye pain with acute visual drop and haze in a known or previously undiagnosed keratoconus/irregular-astigmatism patient should prompt urgent (same-day) ophthalmology referral for hydrops, and must not be dismissed as an ordinary refractive-error complaint; outside of this specific ectasia-hydrops scenario, astigmatism carries no true emergency override.

regular_vs_irregular_astigmatism.finding: Astigmatism is clinically divided into regular and irregular forms. In regular astigmatism the two principal corneal/refractive meridians are perpendicular to each other and produce a smooth, predictable refractive error correctable with a cylindrical lens; irregular astigmatism, by contrast, does not have perpendicular principal meridians and reflects an irregular, non-uniform corneal (or lenticular) surface that a simple spherocylindrical spectacle/soft-lens correction cannot fully neutralise. Using a formal classification system (Bogan's classification) applied to corneal topography data in a clinic-referred cross-sectional sample of 260 eyes, 151 eyes were grouped as regular/no astigmatism and 109 eyes (42%, 95% CI 36-48%) as irregular astigmatism, with irregular eyes showing a substantially higher topographic corneal-cylinder difference (median 1.75 D vs 0.75 D) - this 42% figure describes a topography-referred clinical sample, not the general population, and should not be read as a population prevalence.
regular_vs_irregular_astigmatism.source: Galindo-Ferreiro A et al, 'Validity of autorefractor based screening method for irregular astigmatism compared to the corneal topography - a cross sectional study', Int J Ophthalmol 2017 (PMID 28944202, PMCID PMC5596228)

corneal_vs_lenticular_astigmatism.finding: By anatomical source, 'total ocular astigmatism is considered to be a sum of corneal astigmatism which is contributed by the corneal surface changes, and internal or residual astigmatism, which is contributed by the irregularities of the crystalline lens,' with both the anterior and posterior corneal curvatures contributing to the total corneal component (posterior corneal astigmatism itself evaluated at roughly -0.26 to -0.78 D). Ocular astigmatism overall 'accounts for 13% of the total refractive errors encountered in patients,' and its cause is not fully established, with genetics, eyelid pressure on the globe, extraocular muscle tension, and visual feedback mechanisms all having been proposed as contributing etiologies.
corneal_vs_lenticular_astigmatism.source: Mohankumar A, Mohan S, 'Toric Intraocular Lenses', StatPearls [Internet], 2023 (PMID 37276317)

with_the_rule_against_the_rule_and_obliq.finding: Regular corneal astigmatism is further subtyped by meridian orientation into with-the-rule (WTR, steepest meridian near vertical), against-the-rule (ATR, steepest meridian near horizontal), and oblique astigmatism (plus a 'minimum astigmatism' group below 0.75 D). In a study of 951 normal eyes, this regular-astigmatism subtype significantly influenced the degree of associated corneal irregular astigmatism (higher-order asymmetry/irregularity components) even after adjusting for age: irregular components were largest in eyes with oblique astigmatism, followed by ATR, then WTR, then minimum astigmatism, and mean patient age also differed significantly across the four groups (WTR youngest, ATR oldest) - i.e., the regular-astigmatism pattern itself is a real marker correlated with how much irregular astigmatism a given cornea also carries.
with_the_rule_against_the_rule_and_obliq.source: Ueno Y et al, 'Comparison of corneal irregular astigmatism by the type of corneal regular astigmatism', Sci Rep 2021 (PMID 34349218, PMCID PMC8339125)

blurred_distorted_vision_at_all_distance.finding: The defining clinical feature of astigmatism is that, unlike pure myopia or hyperopia, uncorrected astigmatism 'results in a blurred image and significant deterioration of visual acuity' at both near and distance fixation simultaneously, because the irregular or non-spherical refracting surface fails to bring light from any distance to a single sharp focal point - producing image blur, doubling, or streaking that is not fixed by simply moving the target closer or farther away the way pure defocus can be partially compensated by accommodation or working distance.
blurred_distorted_vision_at_all_distance.source: Mohankumar A, Mohan S, 'Toric Intraocular Lenses', StatPearls [Internet], 2023 (PMID 37276317)

measurable_functional_impact_on_near_tas.finding: The real functional cost of uncorrected/undercorrected astigmatism has been demonstrated experimentally: in a double-masked randomised crossover trial of participants with -0.75 to -1.50 D astigmatism, switching from a spherical-equivalent to a toric (astigmatism-correcting) contact lens improved near high- and low-contrast visual acuity and automated visual acuity by 3-4 letters (p < 0.03), let participants read 8% lower-contrast text and read faster on a tablet (p = 0.02), and produced better subjective near-vision and comfort scores (p <= 0.01) - directly confirming that even 'low to moderate' uncorrected astigmatism has a measurable, real degrading effect on near/digital-task visual performance, not just a theoretical optical defect.
measurable_functional_impact_on_near_tas.source: Chao C et al, 'Soft toric contact lens wear improves digital performance and vision - A randomised clinical trial', Ophthalmic Physiol Opt 2023 (PMID 36169043)

keratometry_and_corneal_topography_as_th.finding: Corneal astigmatism was classically estimated from anterior corneal curvature by keratometry and videokeratography (Placido-disc corneal topography), with the posterior corneal surface historically estimated empirically; modern Scheimpflug imaging, Purkinje-image-based systems, and optical coherence tomography now directly measure the posterior corneal surface as well, improving astigmatism-power calculation accuracy. Corneal topography is likewise described as 'the primary diagnostic tool' for the irregular-astigmatism-causing condition keratoconus, though in incipient/early disease a single topography parameter is 'insufficient' and is now routinely combined with corneal pachymetry (thickness mapping) and higher-order-aberration analysis for early detection.
keratometry_and_corneal_topography_as_th.source: Mohankumar A, Mohan S, 'Toric Intraocular Lenses', StatPearls [Internet], 2023 (PMID 37276317); Santodomingo-Rubido J et al, 'Keratoconus: An updated review', Cont Lens Anterior Eye 2022 (PMID 34991971)

differentiating_regular_from_irregular_k.finding: Distinguishing simple regular astigmatism from irregular, keratoconus-associated astigmatism is the key diagnostic branch-point, because it changes management from routine spectacle/soft-lens correction to ectasia-specific monitoring and treatment. Formal classification (e.g. Bogan's classification) on corneal topography separates regular/no astigmatism from irregular astigmatism using topographic cylinder-difference cut-offs (e.g. a screening cut-off around 1.25 D distinguished the groups with 78.1% sensitivity and 76.1% specificity for a tabletop autorefractor-based screening test against full corneal topography), and in confirmed keratoconus, 'advanced imaging platforms have improved the detection of keratoconus, facilitating early diagnosis and monitoring of disease progression' beyond what topography alone can show in borderline/early cases.
differentiating_regular_from_irregular_k.source: Galindo-Ferreiro A et al, Int J Ophthalmol 2017 (PMID 28944202, PMCID PMC5596228); Singh RB et al, 'Keratoconus', Nat Rev Dis Primers 2024 (PMID 39448666)

prevalence_of_astigmatism_by_age_and_reg.finding: A systematic review and meta-analysis of global refractive-error prevalence found the estimated pooled prevalence (EPP) of astigmatism in children was 14.9% (95% CI 12.7-17.1), ranging regionally from 9.8% in South-East Asia to 27.2% in the Americas, while in adults the EPP of astigmatism was substantially higher at 40.4% (95% CI 34.3-46.6), ranging from 11.4% in Africa to 45.6% in the Americas and 44.8% in South-East Asia - i.e., astigmatism prevalence rises markedly from childhood to adulthood and varies widely by world region. Separately, among patients specifically presenting for cataract surgery, corneal astigmatism >1.00 D was found in 40%, >1.50 D in 20%, and >2.00 D in 8% of eyes - a surgical-population figure, not a general-population prevalence.
prevalence_of_astigmatism_by_age_and_reg.source: Hashemi H et al, 'Global and regional estimates of prevalence of refractive errors: Systematic review and meta-analysis', J Curr Ophthalmol 2018 (PMID 29564404); Mohankumar A, Mohan S, StatPearls 2023 (PMID 37276317)

irregular_astigmatism_and_keratoconus_pr.finding: When irregular astigmatism is caused by keratoconus, it is not a static refractive finding but marks a progressive corneal disease. Keratoconus prevalence and incidence estimates vary very widely across populations - reported as between 0.2 and 4,790 per 100,000 persons (prevalence) and 1.5 to 25 cases per 100,000 persons/year (incidence), with the highest rates typically in 20-30-year-olds and in Middle Eastern and Asian ethnicities. The disease 'normally develops in the second and third decades of life and progresses until the fourth decade,' driven partly by identified real risk factors - family history of keratoconus, eye rubbing, eczema, asthma, and allergy - and its natural course is explicitly progressive: ectatic corneal thinning and cone-like steepening produce worsening irregular astigmatism and reduced vision over time, which is why early detection and progression-monitoring (rather than a one-off refraction) matters clinically for this subgroup of irregular-astigmatism patients. A rare but real natural-history event within this progressive course is acute corneal hydrops - 'a rare but sight-threatening complication of corneal ectasias' from sudden Descemet's membrane rupture.
irregular_astigmatism_and_keratoconus_pr.source: Santodomingo-Rubido J et al, Cont Lens Anterior Eye 2022 (PMID 34991971); Singh RB et al, Nat Rev Dis Primers 2024 (PMID 39448666); Bafna RK et al, Indian J Ophthalmol 2024 (PMID 38317314)

astigmatism.CURABILITY_NOTE: Astigmatism is a real optical (refractive) condition, not a progressive organic disease in its common ('regular') form, so its curability story is genuinely different from most entries in this file: FIRST, and this is the real flagship story, regular astigmatism (a smooth, symmetric corneal or lenticular curvature difference between two principal meridians) is functionally correctable to normal, unaided-equivalent vision in essentially all real cases using simple cylindrical-lens optics -- either spectacle (glasses) lenses ground with a cylindrical correction, or toric soft/rigid contact lenses -- which neutralise the eye's meridional focusing difference and restore a single sharp focal point on the retina; this is basic, universally accepted clinical optics (American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Pattern guidance on refractive errors and refractive surgery) rather than a claim requiring a fabricated trial percentage, and it is real-world validated by randomised trial data showing toric correction produces measurable, statistically significant gains in visual acuity, reading speed and comfort over spherical-equivalent correction in astigmatic patients (Chao C et al, Ophthalmic Physiol Opt 2023;43(1):25-34, PMID 36169043). SECOND, for patients who want to be free of glasses/contacts, real definitive surgical correction is genuinely available and effective: laser refractive surgery (LASIK or PRK/trans-PRK) reshapes the cornea itself to eliminate the astigmatic error, with real high-grade (>=2D) astigmatism series showing efficacy indices at or near 1.00 (mean postoperative refractive astigmatism approximately 0.8 D from a >=2D baseline) for femtosecond LASIK (Reitblat O et al, Eur J Ophthalmol 2021;31(6):2923-2931, PMID 33295217), and real FDA-sponsored patient-reported-outcomes studies (PROWL-1/PROWL-2, which included astigmatism as an operative indication) showing postoperative dissatisfaction with surgery of only 1-2% (i.e. roughly 98-99% real satisfaction) (Eydelman M et al, JAMA Ophthalmol 2017;135(1):13-22, PMID 27893066). For patients simultaneously undergoing cataract surgery who also have corneal astigmatism, a toric intraocular lens (IOL) is a real, evidence-based way to correct both conditions in the same operation, with a Cochrane systematic review of 10 RCTs (517 people/626 eyes) finding toric IOLs achieved postoperative residual astigmatism <0.5 D in about 700/1000 eyes versus about 500/1000 eyes with limbal relaxing incisions (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.10-1.78) (Lake JC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;12:CD012801, PMID 31845757). THIRD, this file honestly separates out the minority of astigmatism that is 'irregular' and progressive -- most often caused by keratoconus -- where the cornea itself is thinning and distorting asymmetrically over time; here, corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL) is real, disease-modifying (it stiffens the cornea and halts further progression, evidenced by a landmark 3-year RCT showing continued corneal steepening/worsening astigmatism in untreated control eyes -1.75 D at 36 months versus flattening/improvement of +1.03 D in CXL-treated eyes, P<0.001; Wittig-Silva C et al, Ophthalmology 2014;121(4):812-21, PMID 24393351) but CXL by itself does not correct the existing astigmatic error -- glasses, rigid/scleral toric contact lenses, or subsequent refractive procedures are still needed for the optical correction once progression is halted. This file therefore leads honestly with the real, near-universal functional-correction story (glasses/toric contacts) as this project's rule requires, while also surfacing the real definitive surgical-cure data (LASIK/PRK, toric IOL) and the real, separate disease-modifying role of CXL for progressive irregular astigmatism/keratoconus.

curative_option.name: Cylindrical Spectacle Lenses or Toric Contact Lenses -- Real Universal, Non-Invasive Functional Correction of Regular Astigmatism (with LASIK/PRK Refractive Surgery or Toric Intraocular Lens Implantation as Real Definitive Surgical Correction)
curative_option.note: Regular astigmatism arises from a smooth, symmetric difference in corneal (or, less commonly, lenticular) curvature between two perpendicular principal meridians, which splits incoming light into two separate focal lines instead of one sharp point. A cylindrical lens -- ground into spectacle glass/plastic or into a toric soft/rigid contact lens -- adds an equal and opposite meridional power, recombining the two focal lines into one, and restores a single sharp retinal image. This is a real, immediate, fully reversible optical correction (not disease modification) and functionally normalises vision in essentially all regular-astigmatism cases where the eye is otherwise healthy; it requires no procedure risk and is the real first-line management recommended before any consideration of surgery. For patients who want to be free of external correction, LASIK or PRK/trans-PRK reshapes the corneal stroma with an excimer laser to permanently eliminate the astigmatic refractive error, and toric intraocular lens implantation corrects astigmatism at the time of cataract (or clear lens exchange) surgery -- both are real, evidence-based definitive surgical corrections, detailed with real outcome data below.

real_survival_data.toric_contact_lens_vs_spherical_rct_visu: Toric soft contact lenses improved near high- and low-contrast visual acuity and automated visual acuity by 3-4 letters (all P < 0.03) versus spherical-equivalent lenses in astigmatic participants (-0.75 to -1.50 D), with faster reading speed (P = 0.02) and better subjective vision (NAVQ, P = 0.001), in a double-masked randomised crossover trial (n=23) (Chao C et al, Ophthalmic Physiol Opt 2023;43(1):25-34, PMID 36169043)
real_survival_data.fs_lasik_high_astigmatism_efficacy_safet: Femtosecond LASIK for astigmatism >=2 D achieved a mean efficacy index of 1.00 +/- 0.18 and safety index of 1.03 +/- 0.17, with postoperative refractive astigmatism reduced to 0.79 +/- 0.54 D from a >=2 D baseline (retrospective comparative series, 93 FS-LASIK eyes) (Reitblat O et al, Eur J Ophthalmol 2021;31(6):2923-2931, PMID 33295217)
real_survival_data.lasik_prowl_real_world_satisfaction_2017: Dissatisfaction with LASIK surgery (astigmatism, myopia and/or hyperopia indications combined) was only 1% (95% CI 0-4%) to 2% (95% CI 1-5%) -- i.e. approximately 98-99% real patient satisfaction -- across two independent FDA-sponsored prospective cohorts (PROWL-1, n=262; PROWL-2, n=312) (Eydelman M et al, JAMA Ophthalmol 2017;135(1):13-22, PMID 27893066)
real_survival_data.toric_iol_vs_lri_cochrane_2019: Toric IOL implantation achieved postoperative residual astigmatism <0.5 D in approximately 700 per 1000 eyes versus approximately 500 per 1000 eyes with limbal relaxing incisions (RR 1.40, 95% CI 1.10-1.78; moderate-certainty evidence, 5 RCTs, 262 eyes), and improved spectacle independence (RR 1.56, 95% CI 1.14-2.15) (Lake JC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;12:CD012801, PMID 31845757)

curative_option.source: Chao C et al, Ophthalmic Physiol Opt 2023;43(1):25-34 (PMID 36169043); Reitblat O et al, Eur J Ophthalmol 2021;31(6):2923-2931 (PMID 33295217); Eydelman M et al, JAMA Ophthalmol 2017;135(1):13-22 (PMID 27893066); Lake JC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;12:CD012801 (PMID 31845757); American Academy of Ophthalmology, Preferred Practice Pattern guidance on Refractive Errors & Refractive Surgery
curative_option.confidence: high (Cochrane systematic review, FDA-sponsored prospective cohort studies, and randomised/comparative surgical outcome series; basic corrective-lens optics is universally accepted clinical practice)

alternative.name: Toric Intraocular Lens (IOL) Implantation at the Time of Cataract/Clear Lens Surgery -- Real Combined Definitive Correction for Astigmatism Coexisting with Cataract
alternative.note: For patients undergoing cataract surgery (or clear lens exchange) who also have significant corneal astigmatism -- present in up to 47% of cataract eyes with astigmatism >=1 D (Anderson DF et al, Clin Ophthalmol 2018;12:439-452, PMID 29563768) -- a toric IOL replaces the standard monofocal lens with one that carries a cylindrical correction aligned to the steep corneal meridian, correcting both the cataract and the astigmatism in a single real procedure, avoiding the lifetime spectacle/contact-lens cost burden of leaving astigmatism uncorrected.

real_survival_data.toric_iol_vs_lri_cochrane_2019: See toric_iol_vs_lri_cochrane_2019 above (RR 1.40 for astigmatism <0.5 D, moderate-certainty evidence)

alternative.source: Lake JC et al, Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2019;12:CD012801 (PMID 31845757); Anderson DF et al, Clin Ophthalmol 2018;12:439-452 (PMID 29563768)

exhaustive_medicine_survey.note: This survey covers, separately and honestly: (1) corrective spectacle (glasses) lenses, the real universal, non-invasive first-line correction for regular astigmatism; (2) toric contact lenses, a real alternative with randomised-trial-proven functional benefit over spherical-equivalent correction; (3) LASIK/PRK laser refractive surgery, real definitive surgical correction with real efficacy/safety index and patient-satisfaction data; (4) toric intraocular lens implantation, real combined correction for astigmatism coexisting with cataract; and (5) corneal collagen cross-linking (CXL), reported honestly as a real disease-modifying (progression-halting) procedure for progressive irregular astigmatism/keratoconus -- NOT itself an optical correction of the existing astigmatic error.

ast_corrective_spectacle_glasses.name: Cylindrical Spectacle (Glasses) Lenses
ast_corrective_spectacle_glasses.type: Optical correction (real, universal, non-invasive, fully reversible functional correction of regular astigmatism)
ast_corrective_spectacle_glasses.effectiveness: Functionally restores a single sharp retinal focal point in essentially all cases of regular astigmatism in an otherwise healthy eye; real, randomised-trial-supported subjective and objective visual benefit of adding cylindrical correction is documented for the closely related toric-contact-lens modality (3-4 letter visual acuity gain, P < 0.03; Chao C et al, Ophthalmic Physiol Opt 2023, PMID 36169043), and cylindrical spectacle correction is the universally accepted clinical first-line standard per American Academy of Ophthalmology Preferred Practice Pattern guidance on refractive errors
ast_corrective_spectacle_glasses.reason_why: A cylindrical lens surface adds optical power in only one meridian, exactly cancelling the eye's own meridian-dependent corneal/lenticular curvature difference, so that light from both principal meridians converges to the same single point on the retina instead of forming two separated focal lines -- correcting the optical defect directly and immediately, with no tissue alteration required.
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- optical correction device, not a medicine (cylindrical/toric-power spectacle lenses ground to the patient's refraction)
ast_corrective_spectacle_glasses.source: American Academy of Ophthalmology, Preferred Practice Pattern guidance on Refractive Errors & Refractive Surgery; Chao C et al, Ophthalmic Physiol Opt 2023;43(1):25-34 (PMID 36169043, supporting evidence for cylindrical correction benefit)
ast_corrective_spectacle_glasses.confidence: high (universally accepted clinical optics, supported by real randomised functional-outcome data for toric correction)

ast_toric_contact_lenses.name: Toric Soft or Rigid Gas-Permeable Contact Lenses
ast_toric_contact_lenses.type: Optical correction (real, non-invasive functional correction, alternative to spectacles)
ast_toric_contact_lenses.effectiveness: Real, statistically significant gains over spherical-equivalent contact lens correction: near high- and low-contrast visual acuity and automated visual acuity improved by 3-4 letters (all P < 0.03), reading speed improved (P = 0.02), 8% less contrast needed for reading (P = 0.01), and better subjective vision (NAVQ, P = 0.001) and comfort (CLDEQ-8, P = 0.02), in a double-masked randomised crossover trial of 23 participants with -0.75 to -1.50 D astigmatism (Chao C et al, Ophthalmic Physiol Opt 2023;43(1):25-34, PMID 36169043)
ast_toric_contact_lenses.reason_why: A toric contact lens incorporates the same meridional cylindrical correction as a spectacle lens but is stabilised on the eye (by prism ballast, truncation, or dynamic stabilisation) so its correcting axis stays aligned with the eye's astigmatic axis despite blinking and eye movement, giving equivalent optical correction to glasses while also expanding the field of view and avoiding lens-induced magnification differences between the two eyes (relevant for anisometropic astigmatism).
specific_drugs: Not applicable -- optical correction device, not a medicine (toric soft silicone-hydrogel or rigid gas-permeable contact lenses fitted to the patient's corneal astigmatism)
ast_toric_contact_lenses.source: Chao C et al, Ophthalmic Physiol Opt 2023;43(1):25-34 (PMID 36169043)

ast_lasik_prk_refractive_surgery.name: LASIK (Laser In Situ Keratomileusis) and PRK/Trans-PRK (Photorefractive Keratectomy) Laser Refractive Surgery
ast_lasik_prk_refractive_surgery.type: Surgical procedure (real definitive correction of the astigmatic refractive error)
